title_key: deepdomain ai system design and validation for enterprise ai talent training|he
title: DeepDomain AI: System Design and Validation for Enterprise AI Talent Training
abstract: Enterprise AI roles evolve faster than conventional course catalogs, while direct use of large language models (LLMs) for training-content generation introduces risks such as unsupported claims, non-executable code, and incomplete audit trails. This paper presents DeepDomain AI, a prototype platform for personalized enterprise AI training. Built with React 18 and FastAPI, the platform compares learner evidence with a structured catalog of 15 AI roles, identifies readiness gaps, and organizes role-oriented training paths. Its resource workflow produces foundation-oriented and project-oriented candidates, records structured review results, and applies a publish/correct/reject quality gate. Pydantic schemas constrain model outputs, and a Docker sandbox scores code through task-specific executable assertions rather than source-code keywords. Functional tests cover job analysis, path generation, knowledge recommendation, state persistence, and sandbox execution. In an offline evaluation of 45 constructed learner profiles, dynamic ranking achieved a Top-3 hit rate of 93.33%; on the 30 same-direction profiles used for comparison, the static-label baseline achieved 80.00%. A 20-sample threshold-consistency test produced a 100% interception rate for rule-violating resources and a 0% false-positive rate for rule-compliant resources. In this study, the system was tested with constructed learner profiles rather than data collected from employees. The results therefore describe how the implemented rules and ranking method performed in our test setting; they do not yet show whether the generated resources improve learning or meet expert expectations in practice.
venue: Journal of Big Data and Computing

title_key: research trends in career education in the era of digital transformation in south korea|cho
title: Research Trends in Career Education in the Era of Digital Transformation in South Korea
abstract: This study analyzed research trends in career education in the era of digital transformation in South Korea, with the aim of identifying research gaps and providing an evidence base for future inquiry. In accordance with the PRISMA guidelines, 103 studies were selected for analysis. The findings are as follows. Research in this field began with a single study in 2014 and fluctuated thereafter before expanding rapidly from 2023 onward, a surge that coincided with the commercialization of generative AI. Students constituted the predominant participant group, accounting for 59 studies (57.3%), whereas teachers were the focus of only seven studies (6.8%). Survey research was the most common research design (35 studies, 34.0%), and qualitative approaches were the most frequently employed method of data analysis (46 studies, 44.7%). With duplicate coding permitted, AI-related technologies-both generative and non generative were the most prevalent technology type (115 instances, 47.7%), and career and academic guidance emerged as the most frequently addressed career-related construct (100 instances, 12.1%). Drawing on these findings, this study delineates the gaps in career education research in the era of digital transformation and discusses their implications for future research.

title_key: agentic university collaborative agents for personalized learning|fan
title: Agentic University: Collaborative Agents for Personalized Learning
abstract: Large language models support personalized tutoring, content generation, and adaptive learning paths. However, capability development requires these resources and interactions to form a coherent learning process that evolves with the learner. A central challenge is to align goals, activities, and assessment while using learning evidence to decide what should follow. We introduce Human-Participatory Multi-Agent Organization and instantiate it in Agentic University (AU). In AU, learners participate as organization members and work with specialized agents to maintain a revisable Capability Program. The program connects personal goals, learning activities across modalities, and layered assessment, while learner feedback and performance guide subsequent support. Our evaluation shows advantages in program organization, assessment design, and revision quality. Users achieved larger mean assessment gains (12.19 versus 5.61 points on a 50-point scale) and reported stronger cognitive support. This work contributes an organizational approach to adaptive learning that makes learner participation a continuing basis for multi-agent coordination. The Agentic University project is available at \href{https://github.com/AgenticOrgLab/AgenticUniversity.git}.

title: Practice patterns, determinants, and outcomes of artificial intelligence use in research writing among postgraduate health science students in South Karnataka, India
abstract:
Artificial intelligence (AI) technology is increasingly supporting research writing, raising concerns about academic integrity, intellectual skill development, and ethics in academics and research.
 
 
 
 A cross-sectional survey was conducted from February to May 2026 among 383 postgraduate students from four randomly selected health science institutions in Mangalore, Karnataka, to assess AI usage, determinants of utilization, and perceived outcomes. Descriptive statistics were used to summarize the data, while Chi-square tests and multivariable logistic regression analyses were performed to examine associations and identify factors associated with AI utilization.
 
 
 
 
 Majority of respondents reported familiarity with ChatGPT (98.2%) and previous AI usage (68.7%). Age, program of study, research experience, and prior AI usage were statistically associated with AI utilization (all
 P
 < 0.05). AI application was mostly to paraphrase (62.8%), summarize (61.9%), and check grammar (57.4%). Major facilitators included perceived usefulness (mean [
 M
 ] = 3.82, ±standard deviation: ±0.91) and ease-of-use (
 M
 = 3.91 ± 0.83). Among the facilitators assessed, institutional norms (perceived institutional support and expectations regarding AI use) (
 M
 = 3.01 ± 1.01) and confidence in AI output (
 M
 = 2.98 ± 0.895) had the lowest mean scores. The highest-rated perceived benefit of AI use was improved time efficiency gained (
 M
 = 3.95 ± 0.83), followed by enhanced academic performance (
 M
 = 3.66 ± 0.84). Concern about plagiarism received the highest concern rating (
 M
 = 3.99 ± 0.80). Regression analysis identified ethical awareness as the only statistically significant independent predictor of AI use (β = 0.100,
 P
 = 0.019).
 
 
 
 
 Postgraduate students widely adopt AI tools to support academic and research writing, particularly to improve writing efficiency. However, AI utilization appears to be influenced more by students’ ethical awareness than by conventional demographic or academic factors. Responsible and effective integration of AI into postgraduate education and research within health science institutions requires clear institutional AI in research guidelines that promote ethical, transparent, and accountable AI use.

title_key: integrating generative ai into chemistry education a chatgpt assisted pjbl stem framework for improving scientific literacy on reaction rate|wulandari
title: Integrating Generative AI into Chemistry Education: A ChatGPT-Assisted PJBL-STEM Framework for Improving Scientific Literacy on Reaction Rate
abstract: Low scientific literacy among students poses a challenge in 21st-century learning, necessitating the development of relevant and innovative instructional models. This study aims to analyze the effectiveness of a ChatGPT-assisted science, technology, engineering, and mathematics-integrated (STEM-integrated) project-based learning (PjBL) model in improving scientific literacy regarding reaction rate. The study employed a quasi-experimental design of the nonequivalent control group type, with the experimental class implementing ChatGPT-assisted PjBL-STEM and the control class using PjBL-STEM. Data were collected through scientific literacy tests and student response questionnaires, then analyzed using the N-gain test and the independent t-test. The results showed that the implementation of ChatGPT-assisted PjBL-STEM effectively improved students’ scientific literacy, with a higher increase compared to the control class, and yielded student responses in the “very good” category. These findings indicate that the integration of ChatGPT has the potential to serve as an innovative learning alternative to enhance students’ scientific literacy

title_key: determinants of university students intent to adopt artificial intelligence ai a case study of the national university of battambang cambodia|leng
title: Determinants of University Students' Intent to Adopt Artificial Intelligence (AI): A Case Study of the National University of Battambang, Cambodia
abstract: This research investigated the factors that affect students' intention to adopt artificial intelligence (AI). This included examining students' adoption of AI technologies, the factors that affect their intention to adopt AI, and the relationship between AI technology use and the factors that affect adoption intention. This research used a quantitative approach, collecting data through a questionnaire from 316 university students at the National University of Battambang using simple random sampling. The data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, reliability analysis, Pearson correlation, and multiple linear regression. All respondents (100%) adopted AI technologies such as ChatGPT (84.8%), Google Gemini (14.2%), and Microsoft Copilot (0.9%). Students' behavioral intention to adopt AI was high (M = 2.84 on a 4-point scale). Mean scores for the factors affecting students' intention to adopt AI all fell within the high-agreement band (M = 2.63–3.03). Among the factors that influence students' intention to adopt AI, performance expectancy had the highest mean (M = 3.03; highest item M = 3.142). Social influence was the strongest regression predictor (β = .293, p < .001). Furthermore, multiple linear regression indicated a statistically significant positive relationship between the five independent constructs and behavioral intention (F(5, 310) = 53.65, p < .001, R2 = .464), supporting all proposed hypotheses (H1, H2, H3, H4, and H5). Importantly, the students expressed a strong commitment to ethical AI usage and maintaining academic integrity (M = 3.174). Higher education institutions should integrate dedicated AI training modules into curricula and strengthen digital support.

title_key: university students disciplinary perspectives on generative ai after two years of its widespread use|elaal
title: University students' disciplinary perspectives on generative AI after two years of its widespread use
abstract:
This study explores how university students use generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) across various disciplines, including STEM, Business, Education Futures, Clinical & Health Sciences (CHS), Creative and Allied Health & Human Performance (AHHP). It aims to identify discipline-based perspectives, perceived benefits, ethical boundaries and the support needs required for responsible use of GenAI tools.
 
 
 
 A survey was conducted approximately two years after the widespread use of GenAI, by which time participants were expected to be familiar with its use. Students were categorised based on their discipline, English fluency, mode of learning and level of study. Their responses were analysed to compare usage patterns, satisfaction levels and ethical considerations across disciplines.
 
 
 
 The results highlight that student perspectives on GenAI tools are discipline-dependent. STEM and Education Futures showed the highest acceptance, while CHS and Business students were more cautious and sceptical about accuracy and ethical issues. Non-native English speakers rated GenAI tools more favourably as aids for writing and comprehension. Novice users expressed enthusiasm, while expert users showed dissatisfaction due to errors and false information.
 
 
 
 The study relied on self-reported perceptions and represents a single institutional context. Broader investigations are recommended, with a particular focus on equity groups such as students with disabilities, low-SES students and remote learners.
 
 
 
 Different approaches were suggested for integrating GenAI into learning. STEM students favoured comparative tasks; CHS recommended support for diagnostic reasoning; Allied Health preferred role-playing simulations; Education Futures highlighted lesson planning; and Business students suggested case-based and productivity uses.
 
 
 
 The study provides cross-disciplinary analyses of GenAI use by students and proposes approaches for ethical and discipline-specific integration into university curricula.

title_key: digital age ethics for elementary teachers challenges and strategies for professional integrity|mujahidah
title: Digital-Age Ethics for Elementary Teachers: Challenges and Strategies for Professional Integrity
abstract: Digital transformation has expanded elementary teachers’ work into learning platforms, social media, messaging applications, data systems, and generative artificial intelligence. These tools support collaboration and instructional improvement but raise ethical concerns about professional boundaries, children’s privacy and safety, information integrity, copyright, equity, and accountability. This article synthesizes the ethical challenges faced by elementary school teachers in digital environments and identifies strategies for maintaining professional integrity while prioritizing children’s best interests. A narrative literature review was conducted through exploratory searches of scholarly articles, academic books, international frameworks, policy documents, and Indonesian legislation, prioritizing publications from 2020 to 2026 alongside foundational theories. The thematic synthesis identifies risks involving blurred personal and professional boundaries, children’s data governance, unsafe online communication, unverified digital and AI-generated content, and unequal access to technology. It proposes a Five-Dimension Framework of Teachers’ Digital Integrity comprising pedagogical, relational, information-and-data, epistemic, and civic-professional integrity. Recommendations are directed to teachers, schools, teacher education programs, families, and professional associations. The framework is a conceptual synthesis, not a validated instrument, and requires empirical testing in Indonesian elementary schools

title_key: do large language models hallucinate more in uzbek a cross lingual measurement of factual reliability and its implications for non english higher education|olimov
title: Do large language models hallucinate more in Uzbek? A cross-lingual measurement of factual reliability and its implications for non-English higher education
abstract:
Students in non-English higher education are increasingly using large language models (LLMs) as informal study aids; however, the factual reliability of these systems in lower-resource languages - and its consequences for learning - remain largely unmeasured.
 
 
 
 We report a controlled, fully reproducible evaluation of factual hallucination in eight open-weight LLMs answering 100 verifiable factual questions in English, Russian, and Uzbek. Uzbek, an agglutinative and comparatively low-resource Turkic language, is the primary language of instruction at our institution. Responses were scored with a deterministic answer-key procedure.
 
 
 
 
 The factual error rate increased monotonically with the resource level of the query language: 3.5% in English, 10.9% in Russian, and 15.9% in Uzbek (pooled over models; chi-square = 68.5, df = 2,
 p
 < 10
 -14
 ). The gap was present in nearly every model, but its size varied widely: a 12B general-purpose model answered reliably across all three languages, whereas the smaller 1-4B models had an error rate of 24%-27% in Uzbek. Language-adapted models - open checkpoints continued-pretrained or fine-tuned on Uzbek - closed the gap almost entirely, reaching an error rate of 2%-8% in Uzbek, comparable to their reliability in English.
 
 
 
 
 A student querying an off-the-shelf model in Uzbek is several times more likely to receive an incorrect fact than an English-speaking peer, which is both an equity concern and a hazard for academic integrity when unverified output enters student work. The risk, however, is not intrinsic to the language: it can be substantially reduced by preferring language-adapted models and by auditing per-language reliability before classroom deployment. All questions, code, and model outputs are released to support replication.

title_key: cognitive tutoring systems for programming and learner modeling|deriyeva
title: Cognitive Tutoring Systems for Programming and Learner Modeling
abstract: The overarching goal of this doctoral project is to attempt to combine the Intelligent Tutoring Systems with aspects from cognitive science to help learners on their way to acquiring programming skills. First, I describe the previous work: intelligent tutoring systems, knowledge tracing, and combining learning analytics with the LLMs. Following, I describe the immediate future research directions: theoretical modeling in knowledge tracing, as well as a study to investigate how stress impacts self-regulated learning.

title_key: when code is no longer enough for programming assessment in the genai era|oyelere
title: When Code Is No Longer Enough for Programming Assessment in the GenAI Era
abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) has made a long-standing assumption in programming assessment markedly more fragile: that submitted code is sufficiently good evidence of what a student knows and can do. This discussion paper argues that the central assessment problem in higher computing education is not only cheating, plagiarism, or whether GenAI should be banned. It is a validity problem. When high-quality code can be generated, explained, transformed, and repaired externally, grades attached to programming submissions may overstate, understate, or misidentify the student’s actual capability. The paper introduces the idea of assessment evidence debt: the growing gap between the claims programming assessments make about student competence and the evidence that final artefacts alone can support. It then proposes a claim-evidence approach to GenAI-era programming assessment, in which educators design assessment around explicit claims, evidence channels, and threats to inference. The paper outlines five evidence channels for programming courses: constrained performance, process provenance, executable verification, interpretive defence, and transfer probes. These channels are read alongside recent 2025–2026 work on authentic assessment, code interviews, executable exams, and assessment validity. They are not presented as a single solution or an AI-proof recipe. Rather, they offer a discussion framework for redesigning programming assessment so that grades are grounded in defensible evidence of learning, not merely in code that runs.

title_key: in context learning chain of thought vs tree of thoughts prompting on multi step reasoning|cakal
title: In-Context Learning: Chain-of-Thought vs. Tree-of-Thoughts Prompting on Multi-Step Reasoning
abstract: We present an empirical comparison of four In-Context Learning (ICL) prompting strategies on the GSM8K grade-school mathematics benchmark—Zero-Shot Chain-of-Thought (CoT), Few-Shot CoT (8-shot), Tree-of-Thoughts (ToT) with BFS at two search depths, and Self-Consistency voting—using Llama 3.1 8B via the Groq API without fine-tuning. ZeroShot CoT achieves 95.0%, Self-Consistency 92.0%, and ToT (BFS-2, depth=6) and Few-Shot CoT each 85.0% on the same 100-problem seed-42 sample. A single answer-extraction format instruction raises Zero-Shot CoT by 7 pp (88.0% → 95.0%) and reorders the strategies—a parsing confound, not a reasoning gain—placing it alone on the accuracy–cost Pareto frontier at the 8B scale. A depth ablation yields only +4.0 pp at 2.1× cost, indicating diminishing returns when the evaluator is the same 8B backbone. A cross-model replication on Claude Haiku 4.5 with full evaluation identity preserved collapses the inter-strategy gap from 14 to 2 pp, revealing a ceiling effect: deliberation-and ensemble-style strategies pay off only when the base model has headroom to lose and identifiable wrong branches to prune. A pairwise Cohen’s κ analysis confirms this—ToT depths on Llama reach near-zero agreement (κ=0.011) versus perfect agreement on Haiku (κ=1.000).

title_key: adaptive generative tutoring in resource limited secondary education effects on participation achievement and digital equity in nigeria|trujillo
title: Adaptive Generative Tutoring in Resource-Limited Secondary Education: Effects on Participation, Achievement, and Digital Equity in Nigeria
abstract: This study examines the short-term educational contribution of teacher-guided generative tutoring through a secondary analysis of a randomized trial in nine public secondary schools in Benin City, Nigeria. Among 1328 randomized students, 657 were offered twelve 90 min sessions combining Microsoft Copilot, curriculum-aligned English activities, and pair work, while 671 received regular instruction. Intention-to-treat models used ordinary least squares, school fixed effects, baseline performance adjustment, and HC3 standard errors, with conditional estimates on observed endline outcomes and required covariates. The overall assessment effect was 0.310 SD (95% CI 0.176–0.444; n = 654), with positive estimates for English (0.238 SD), AI knowledge (0.309 SD), and school examination performance (0.206 SD). The digital-skills estimate was positive but imprecise (0.139 SD; p = 0.066). Attendance was positively associated with achievement, and effects were larger at higher baseline performance. The female interaction was positive, with caution warranted by the smaller male subsample. The digital-access interaction was negative but imprecise (−0.182 SD; 95% CI −0.370–0.005; 457 complete cases). These findings support short-term learning gains from the complete tutoring package relative to regular instruction. They provide a basis for further evaluation of structured programs integrating generative AI with curriculum, collaborative practice, and teacher guidance in resource-limited urban schools.

title_key: learnmate a personalized learning resource generation system based on multi agent collaboration|guo
title: LearnMate: A Personalized Learning Resource Generation System Based on Multi-Agent Collaboration
abstract: Digital teaching platforms today tend to deliver homogenized learning resources with little room for personalized adaptation. Meanwhile, general-purpose large language models frequently produce hallucinated content, which forces teachers to carry heavy repetitive workloads during lesson preparation, while students can hardly find materials that actually match their own proficiency. To address these practical difficulties, we developed LearnMate, a higher-education-oriented platform for curriculum-resource generation and dynamic evaluation that relies on multi-agent collaboration. The system first builds a course-specific RAG knowledge base so that teaching materials remain structurally traceable. It then uses LangGraph to coordinate several agents that generate multimodal resources including courseware, exercises, and teaching videos, and a two-tier quality review mechanism is put in place to mitigate model hallucinations. A six-dimensional learner profile is updated from learning events and used to produce adaptive learning paths and personalized resource recommendations, forming a bidirectional closed loop for teaching and learning. Full-scale practical validation was carried out on the course Big-Data Computing Cluster Technology. In the evaluation, the retrieval hit rate of the course knowledge base reaches 100%, and teachers' lesson-preparation time per lecture drops by 73.3%. The knowledge-absorption rate of underperforming students also improves significantly. The platform supports domestic large-language models and domestic databases, and offers plug-and-play multi-course extension capability. Taken together, the system reduces teachers' lesson-preparation costs and enable hierarchical adaptive learning. It provides a feasible, complete engineering solution for applying large-language models to specialized university courses.

title_key: peningkatan kemampuan pemecahan masalah matematis melalui pembelajaran spldv berbantuan interactive flat panel dan chatgpt pada siswa kelas viii smpn 5 gegerbitung|luthfitasari
title: PENINGKATAN KEMAMPUAN PEMECAHAN MASALAH MATEMATIS MELALUI PEMBELAJARAN SPLDV BERBANTUAN INTERACTIVE FLAT PANEL DAN CHATGPT PADA SISWA KELAS VIII SMPN 5 GEGERBITUNG
abstract: Students’ mathematical problem-solving skills in Systems of Linear Equations in Two Variables (SPLDV) need to be improved through interactive learning that supports the exploration of solution strategies. This study aimed to analyze changes in students’ mathematical problem-solving skills through learning supported by an Interactive Flat Panel (IFP) and ChatGPT . A quantitative approach with a one-group pretest-posttest design was employed, involving 32 eighth-grade students at SMPN 5 Gegerbitung. The research instrument was a constructed-response test administered before and after the learning intervention. Data were collected through testing and analyzed using a paired-samples t-test, effect size, and normalized gain (N-gain). The results showed an increase in the mean score from 27.00 to 40.41 out of 48, with an N-gain of 0.64 (moderate category). The greatest improvement occurred in the indicator of checking the solution. Learning supported by IFP and ChatGPT has the potential to support mathematical problem-solving skills. Its implementation should include answer verification and teacher guidance.

title_key: ai use environmental awareness and moral disengagement among gen z business students|daveluy
title: AI Use, Environmental Awareness and Moral Disengagement Among Gen Z Business Students
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has become a defining feature of how Generation Z business students learn, work, and produce knowledge. It is also among the most resource-intensive consumer technologies ever deployed, requiring substantial water and electricity for both training and use. Yet the environmental costs of AI remain largely invisible to its end users, and existing AI literacy frameworks systematically exclude environmental considerations from their account of responsible AI use. Drawing on four focus groups and 42 open-response questionnaires conducted at an international business school, this study examines how environmentally aware Gen Z business students reconcile intensive AI use with their stated environmental commitments. Using reflexive thematic analysis of 395 double-coded segments, we identify a four-stage moral disengagement architecture for AI sustainability. The architecture begins with productivity primacy with AI use framed as professionally unavoidable, proceeds through rationalisation and collective disengagement, then responsibility delegation to governments and corporations, and culminates in technological solutionism, in which future innovation is expected to resolve environmental concerns. Each stage closes a specific cognitive and moral gap left open by the previous one, producing an internally coherent structure that allows pro-environmental values to coexist with high-intensity AI use without moral incongruence. The findings also reveal asymmetry in AI education. Participants demonstrated awareness of cognitive and academic risks associated with AI, largely reflecting institutional messaging, while environmental risks remained fragmented, informal, and weakly connected to behavioural decision-making. Although many students expressed concern about sustainability, environmental considerations rarely entered their ethical evaluation of AI use. The study extends Bandura's moral disengagement theory by demonstrating its sequential, architecture-like operation in a high-uptake technology context. It also proposes Green AI Literacy as a missing dimension of existing AI literacy frameworks. Finally, it provides preliminary insights into how higher education institutions might better integrate environmental sustainability into AI literacy education.
venue: European Conference on Management Leadership and Governance

title_key: more than marks the broader educational contribution of generative ai in biomedical science|zhu
title: More than marks: The Broader Educational Contribution of Generative AI in Biomedical Science.
abstract: In higher education, discussion surrounding generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) often centers on academic integrity and potential grade inflation. However, much less attention has been given to how GenAI may be reshaping the learning process itself, including how students reason and construct understanding. This gap limits our ability to evaluate GenAI in educational terms that extend beyond performance outcomes. This study examined the association between declared GenAI use and academic performance in undergraduate biomedical science courses, using physiology and biochemistry as disciplinary contexts. Student grades were analyzed between declared GenAI Users and Non-users within each course and across assignments. Contrary to common assumptions that using GenAI would advantage or disadvantage students academically, no measurable difference in performance was observed between Users and Non-users in any analysis. This consistent absence of a grade effect occurred alongside evidence that students primarily declared using GenAI for tasks such as concept explanation rather than core content generation. As such, the findings support the interpretation that the influence of GenAI use are concentrated at the level of reasoning and self-regulation, rather than having significant effects on grades. These findings suggest that incorporating measures of learning processes alongside summative outcomes may better support and guide the integration of GenAI in biomedical science education.

title_key: development of aicbl learning materials to promote pre service physics teachers representational competence in solid state physics|nurdini
title: Development of AI–CBL Learning Materials to Promote Pre-Service Physics Teachers’ Representational Competence in Solid-State Physics
abstract: This study aimed to develop and validate AI–CBL learning materials for solid-state physics that were designed to support pre-service physics teachers’ representational competence. A research and development approach using the ADDIE framework was applied and limited to the Analysis, Design, and Development stages. The analysis stage identified key learning difficulties and representational demands in solid-state physics instruction for pre-service physics teachers. Based on these findings, an AI-integrated Case-Based Learning package was designed and developed, consisting of contextual case studies, structured learning tasks aligned with case-based learning phases, and guidelines for responsible interaction with open-access generative artificial intelligence. The materials were organized through a learning management system to support consistent access, structured sequencing, and documentation of learning artifacts. The developed materials were reviewed by three expert validators using the Learning Object Review Instrument (LORI) 2.0 across eight aspects on a five-point scale. The validation data were analyzed descriptively and supported by Many-Facet Rasch Measurement using Minifac to examine rater consistency and measurement quality. The expert validation results showed an average feasibility percentage of 76.50% across the eight LORI aspects, indicating that the developed materials were feasible for further implementation. Rasch-based analysis also indicated good unidimensionality, with 47.84% of variance explained by Rasch measures, and acceptable rater consistency, with reliability of 0.87. Revisions were made based on validators’ comments to improve clarity, learning-goal alignment, usability, and responsible artificial intelligence integration. These findings indicate that the developed AI–CBL learning materials are feasible as a validated instructional product and provide a foundation for subsequent classroom implementation studies in solid-state physics.

title_key: generative ai empowered reform of key elements in ict talent cultivation|lv
title: Generative AI-Empowered Reform of Key Elements in ICT Talent Cultivation
abstract: The rapid advancement of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) and intelligent agent technologies is continuously reshaping job structures, work patterns, and competency requirements within the Information and Communication Technology (ICT) industry, thereby creating new demands for vocational ICT talent cultivation. Addressing challenges such as the mismatch between program structures and industrial needs, insufficient transformation of authentic engineering projects into instructional tasks, delayed updating of teaching materials and resources, inadequate digital-intelligence competencies among teachers, and the disconnect between training environments and real workplace scenarios, this study follows the reform requirements for the five key elements of vocational education: programs, curricula, teaching materials, teachers, and practical training. A “5×3” vocational education agent matrix is proposed, taking the five key teaching elements as the vertical dimension and industry–education integration, teaching reform, and research and industry engagement as the horizontal dimension, thereby establishing a collaborative reform framework. Based on this framework, reform pathways are developed for dynamic mapping of industrial demands, transformation of enterprise engineering tasks, dynamic construction of teaching resources, teacher competency development, and engineering-oriented training environment construction. Furthermore, a collaborative teaching model involving teachers, intelligent agents, and students is established. Real-world smart shipping projects are employed to support project-based learning, while multi-source learning evidence is integrated to diagnose and support student development. This study provides a practical framework for systematically empowering the reform of key teaching elements in vocational ICT education through Generative AI and offers an industry-oriented implementation pathway for cultivating interdisciplinary talents in the “Information Technology + Shipping” domain.
venue: Journal of Educational Development and Social Sciences

title_key: cognitive inclusivity in ai coding assistants evidence from github copilot|kerr
title: Cognitive Inclusivity in AI Coding Assistants: Evidence from GitHub Copilot
abstract: AI coding assistants are commonly used for daily software development tasks. While prior research has examined their impact on productivity and code quality, less is understood about how these tools support diverse ways of thinking. Evidence from non-AI software engineering tools suggests that mismatches between tool design and users'cognitive styles can introduce inclusivity barriers, but it remains unclear whether similar issues arise in AI coding assistants. We investigate how developers with different cognitive styles experience and interact with these tools and whether they exhibit cognitive inclusivity challenges. We conducted a controlled laboratory study with 20 student participants using GitHub Copilot to complete code generation, debugging, and refactoring tasks. Using think-aloud protocols, semi-structured interviews, and inductive thematic analysis, we identify patterns in user interaction. We then apply the GenderMag framework to examine how these patterns differ across cognitive styles. We identify five inclusivity issues concerning how Copilot explains suggestions, supports validation, facilitates learning, exposes its features, and influences the problem-solving process. Our findings suggest that common interaction paradigms in AI coding assistants can privilege certain cognitive styles while introducing additional cognitive effort for others. We derive design implications for more inclusive AI coding assistants.

title_key: visualizing use of generative artificial intelligence in higher education|shah
title: Visualizing use of generative artificial intelligence in higher education
abstract:
Higher education students are engaged with academic learning and research using generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) applications. A major shift in pedagogical approach surfaces many challenges to academic integrity that urging to redefining assessment model and ethical literacy. This study aims to investigate impact of the GenAI apps among the students using survey of technical and non-technical disciplines. Survey is mainly focused on: use of GenAI apps, variations in observed effectiveness and student’s usage pattern, level of adoption and acceptance of GenAI apps. Reviews of existing literature on the implications of GenAI and emerging need for systemic changes are discussed with reference to result.
 
 
 
 Survey was developed to assess the integration of GenAI apps in the higher education. It was conducted with undergraduate and postgraduate students so as to find the adoption and acceptance rate of GenAI apps among the students; it has been partitioned into two categories: non-technical disciplines and technical disciplines. Students from the social science and pure sciences are in the non-technical disciplines, while students from computer science and engineering students are in the technical discipline. The questionnaire included a mix of multiple-choice questions, scale items and open-ended responses.
 
 
 
 This research is classified for students into technical and non-technical disciplines, revealing notable differences in adoption patterns. First, students from non-technical disciplines are not entirely using GenAI applications. Second, effectiveness of the usage can be analyzed by the purpose of usage of GenAI apps which is shown by graphs. However, technical students show higher inclination for AI usages. Third, regarding adoption or acceptance, many rural students initially adopt it through classmates or roommates. In contrast, students in urban areas, especially in technical disciplines, spend higher hours; here, they accept the technology and update themselves with new technology.
 
 
 
 The survey did not assess the accuracy or effectiveness of GenAI outputs. This is a limitation for drawing conclusions about the performance quality of these apps across disciplines.
 
 
 
 Students come from different parts of India, so it is also possible that the places where they previously studied lacked facilities such as internet connectivity and stable power supply. This influences the usage. Students from many disciplines participated in the survey, so their perspective to look at the GenAI apps is a unique feature. GenAI apps are accepted among technical students, and non-technical students are gradually adopting. Over-reliance may hinder the individual learning and creativity; it can be an aid to the learning but not as a supplement of human intelligence. Universities face challenges in formulating policies.

title_key: the current state and future prospects of artificial intelligence in dentistry|yermolaieva
title: THE CURRENT STATE AND FUTURE PROSPECTS OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN DENTISTRY
abstract:
Introduction. Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming the healthcare system, including the field of dentistry, thereby creating the conditions for the introduction of corresponding changes in dental education.
Objective: To assess the achievements and challenges of using artificial intelligence in dentistry, with a particular focus on dental education, and to identify the prospects for its future application.
Materials and methods. The study employed the bibliosemantic method, as well as systematic and comparative approaches. Information retrieval and analysis of scientific sources regarding the application of AI in dentistry and dental education were conducted using the scientometric databases of PubMed covering the last 10 years.
Results and Discussion. An analysis of scientific sources has shown that AI has become an integral part of dental practice and education worldwide and in Ukraine.
The exponential growth in the number of publications on this topic in recent years indicates that dentistry (and dental education in particular) is undergoing a period of active implementation of AI technologies and tools. Scientific publications in the PubMed scientometric database are primarily devoted to the integration of AI into dental practice and the training of dental professionals, ethical and safety issues related to the use of AI, and the comprehensive use of digital technologies and AI tools in the continuing professional development and professional practice of dentists. Currently, there is a lack of studies that thoroughly examine the effectiveness of LLMs in solving dental problems, particularly in the fields of restorative dentistry and endodontics, which hinders an understanding of their practical application and potential risks for the clinical training of dentists.
Despite the numerous possibilities of AI, its integration into educational programmes and clinical practice has limitations, due to issues and difficulties such as ethical concerns, data reliability, current and future legal frameworks, and the lack of adequate training for both educators and students. At the same time, AI technologies and tools can be used to complement educational programmes at all stages of dental training.
Conclusions. The use of artificial intelligence is having a profound impact on dental practice and education, prompting dentists to continually expand their skill set and expertise regarding the technologies and tools for its implementation, which can be used solely as a supplement to existing standards and programs.

title_key: copies are not confirmations how news duplication fools llm judges and continual learners|metales
title: Copies Are Not Confirmations: How News Duplication Fools LLM Judges and Continual Learners
abstract: Many news reports of a claim are copies of one source: wire stories, content shared within a media group, syndicated features and press releases. We ask whether LLM judges and continual learners treat such copies as independent confirmations. In 200,000 English CC-News articles, a MinHash detector links 18.9% to a near-copy from another outlet (precision 0.97 once boilerplate is removed); it links 92% of edited reprints to their originals but none of the LLM rewrites by phi4, Llama 3.2 or Gemini 2.5 Flash. Shown three identical reprints of a claim about an unknown person instead of one report, Llama 3.2 3B and phi4 14B raised the share of lies they accepted from 0.06 to 0.71 and from 0.21 to 0.90 and ignored a note that the reports came from one source; Gemini 2.5 Flash already believed a single report, and Gemini 2.5 Pro followed provenance notes and tables. In a simulated continual-learning stream, showing the judge one report per detected chain cut the copied lies it accepted by 0.10-0.24 across four judges, at a mean cost of no more than 4.2 percentage points of accepted truths. Against reworded copies, a test of how many of a report's named entities are absent from an earlier look-alike separates LLM rewrites from 100 labelled independent reports of the same event with AUC 0.98-0.99 and wrongly flags one; entity overlap alone does as well, TF-IDF and a current embedding model come close, and the test catches few natural same-source derivatives. With the miss patterns of generated rewrite networks, it cut the reworded-copy lies accepted from 0.67 to 0.20 (0.40 when the rewriter invents details). Counting reports or chains alone is not a reliable defence, the effect of provenance information depends on the judge, and colluding sources remain the open problem. title_key: mobilizing creativity in education from attention to the conditions of possibility|couillard
title: Mobilizing Creativity in Education: From Attention to the Conditions of Possibility
abstract: Creativity researchers have responded to early calls to fill gaps in the literature, and creativity is now considered a 21st-century competency across education policy and curricula. Yet naming it has not led to broad integration across education, and the rapid adoption of GenAI has complicated how we understand creativity. We treat “mobilization” as an analytical concept and offer a framework that identifies four points at which creativity fails to mobilize and reach teaching in practice: conception, pathway, conditions, and mechanism. We draw on a case study of five undergraduate instructors at a Canadian research university, showing a lack of training and support to develop and implement creative teaching approaches. We match this with OECD survey data from across ninety jurisdictions. We also examine historical contexts relevant to the mobilization problem and unpack some realities of GenAI and creativity in education. Our evidence and analytic framework show that mobilization requires considering the underlying issues. This paper gives creativity advocates clarity on how to ask for support and how to engage program developers, policymakers, and faculty heads.

title_key: colonial mediations and sovereign possibilities a synthesis derived decolonial heuristic layered equity framework for equitable generative ai integration in k 12 and higher education|krishnan
title: Colonial mediations and sovereign possibilities: a synthesis-derived decolonial heuristic layered equity framework for equitable generative AI integration in K-12 and higher education
abstract:
This critical integrative synthesis examines generative AI integration in K-12 and higher education through an explicit decolonial lens. It focuses on how colonial mediations shape opportunities, challenges and strategies for equitable access and outcomes aligned with UN SDG 10.
 
 
 
 Following a critical integrative review paradigm that fuses the integrative logic of Whittemore and Knafl (2005) with reflexive thematic analysis (Braun and Clarke, 2006) and decolonial theory, 58 sources (2020–2026) were identified through systematic search and purposive theoretical sampling. Sources prioritizing structural critique, Global South perspectives, K-12 evidence gaps, output-level neocolonial patterns and contextual agency were retained. Sources were appraised with the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool and analyzed through a seven-phase relational mapping protocol that translated thematic codes into the layered architecture of the Decolonial Heuristic Layered Equity Framework (DHLEF). Robustness of core pathways was confirmed through sensitivity analyses.
 
 
 
 Three interdependent themes – transformative opportunities, interlinked challenges and enabling strategies – emerge when read through decolonial theory. Opportunities appear as outer potential outcomes mediated by challenges whose effects are conditioned by data colonialism, epistemic colonialism, infrastructure dependence, governance colonialism and output-level neocolonial patterns. Strategies achieve moderating effects most effectively when reframed as sovereignty practices, including contextual hacking and language sovereignty. The DHLEF renders these colonial mediations visible in hypothesized relational pathways and supplies a context-differentiated implementation roadmap grounded in empirical evidence from low- and middle-income countries (LMIC) and K-12 contexts.
 
 
 
 Reliance on secondary and grey literature limits depth and generalizability. The DHLEF remains a synthesis-derived heuristic whose pathways constitute propositions requiring empirical validation through longitudinal and intersectional designs. The synthesis provides a transparent foundation for structural analysis rather than prescriptive protocols.
 
 
 
 The DHLEF supplies institutions and policymakers with a context-sensitive, non-prescriptive heuristic for navigating generative AI integration. It enables differentiated decision-making by educational level and geopolitical resource setting, positioning sovereignty-oriented practices – offline-first tools, community governance and Indigenous data protocols – as conditional moderators rather than sequential prerequisites. Educators and technology providers can apply the framework to diagnose infrastructure dependence, epistemic bias and accessibility barriers prior to deployment, while prioritizing institutional support structures empirically shown to strengthen equitable outcomes in low-resource and K-12 environments. Implementation remains iterative and locally calibrated rather than universally prescribed.
 
 
 
 By rendering colonial mediations analytically central, the DHLEF advances structural justice rather than distributional inclusion alone, interrupting asymmetries in knowledge validation and educational opportunity. It positions sovereignty practices – contextual hacking, language sovereignty, community data governance and offline-first infrastructures – as necessary interruptions of data, epistemic and infrastructural extraction, with particular urgency for marginalized learners in Global South and low-resource contexts. The framework reframes equitable GenAI integration as an ongoing political and ethical project of refusal and resurgence, rather than a technical optimization problem, thereby aligning educational practice with the structural demands of UN SDG 10.
 
 
 
 The DHLEF advances understanding by converting thematic synthesis into a relational structure that makes colonial mediations analytically central. It extends prior static ethics and education frameworks through decolonial integration and synthesis-derived pathways. It incorporates contextual differentiation by educational level and geopolitical setting, positions 2025–2026 trends as amplifiers of colonial dynamics and offers a tool for equitable GenAI integration that centers sovereignty rather than diffusion. The framework resolves three persistent tensions in existing scholarship: the absence of dynamic relational modelling, the dominance of distributional over structural equity framings and Northern-centric biases that have limited applicability to Global South and K-12 contexts.

title_key: peculiarities of developing high school students critical thinking in mathematics lessons|starykova
title: PECULIARITIES OF DEVELOPING HIGH SCHOOL STUDENTS’ CRITICAL THINKING IN MATHEMATICS LESSONS
abstract: The relevance of the research is determined by the need to prepare high school students to consciously process large amounts of information, verify the reliability of data, make well-reasoned decisions, and use digital technologies responsibly. Developing critical thinking in mathematics lessons is particularly important because the logical and evidence-based nature of mathematics provides considerable opportunities for fostering students’ independence, analytical abilities, sound reasoning, and reflection. The article aims to theoretically substantiate the peculiarities of developing high school students’ critical thinking in mathematics lessons and to identify effective ways of implementing this process. The research employed a set of theoretical methods: analysis of pedagogical and methodological literature to clarify the essence and peculiarities of critical thinking development; comparison to examine different scholarly approaches; systematization and classification to organize relevant teaching methods, techniques, and types of mathematical tasks; and generalization to determine effective ways of developing critical thinking in high school mathematics. The study defines critical thinking in mathematics learning as students’ ability to consciously analyze mathematical information, establish relationships between a problem’s conditions and requirements, formulate and test hypotheses, select rational solution strategies, evaluate the validity of reasoning, justify conclusions, and reflect on their own learning activities. The findings substantiate the principal peculiarities of this process: problem-oriented learning, variability of solution strategies, evidence-based mathematical judgments, the use of errors as a didactic resource, dialogic interaction, project- and inquiry-based learning, staged organization of cognitive activity, and critical use of digital technologies and generative artificial intelligence. Effective implementation involves the systematic use of open-ended, problem-based, and inquiry tasks; proof and refutation activities; analysis of erroneous solutions; mathematical discussions; educational projects; digital mathematical environments; verification of AI-generated solutions; and reflection. The integrated application of these approaches facilitates the transition from reproducing standard algorithms to independent, inquiry-based, evidence-based, and reflective mathematical activity.

title_key: surpassing technical and teaching constraints a review of intelligent tutoring systems existing limitations and future research directions|ahluwalia
title: Surpassing Technical and Teaching Constraints: A Review of Intelligent Tutoring Systems, Existing Limitations and Future Research Directions
abstract: ITS (Intelligent Tutoring Systems) can be seen as an important use of artificial intelligence in education. These systems offer the same benefits as one-on-one human tutoring such as customized training and feedback. This review reviews the innovations in system design, pedagogy, tools facing students, and what has been reported to have been achieved in the 2020-2026, although the field dates back to 1956. Current literature shows that ITS is capable of improving test results and attitudes of students, but their impact on the independent learning in the long-term is unclear. ITS have also helped in giving more clarity in step by step work, like solving mathematical proofs. Although these benefits exist, there are a number of issues, such as that algorithmic bias, simplified models of learners, limited scalability, behavioural data collection and human feelings, privacy issues, and mistakes made by tutors when using Large Language Models (LLM) are all still present. In this paper, five main fields of future research were acknowledged: the better explainability of ITS, the creation of the system that can recognize emotions and multi-modal input, the development of human-AI collaboration models, the system’s design that will take into account cultural and linguistic diversity, and the longitudinal research to measure the long-term learning outcomes. The review is supposed to be a resource that will benefit all researchers, developers and policymakers who are involved in promoting smart educational technologies.

title_key: strategic vectors of educational literature modernization in the context of higher medical education digitalization based on student centered learning|bodnar
title: STRATEGIC VECTORS OF EDUCATIONAL LITERATURE MODERNIZATION IN THE CONTEXT OF HIGHER MEDICAL EDUCATION DIGITALIZATION BASED ON STUDENT-CENTERED LEARNING
abstract: Digitalization of medical education requires textbook modernization based on student needs.Aim. To substantiate textbook quality criteria.Material and Methods. A survey was conducted among 120 senior medical students at BSMU. Descriptive statistics and content analysis were used.Results. 90.83% of students use digital literature, 70.83% use Moodle and YouTube, 95% need interactive e-textbooks. The ideal book model includes conciseness (95%), case-based methods (95%), evidence-based content (90%), and atlas-quality visuals (80%). Book purchasing decisions depend on illustrations (79.16%) and writing style (58.33%).Conclusions. The future of educational literature lies in the hybridization of printed formats and mobile e-textbooks with AI assistants, quizzes, and QR codes.

title_key: integrating generative ai in csd education a practical tutorial for faculty and students|walker
title: Integrating Generative AI in CSD Education: A Practical Tutorial for Faculty and Students
abstract: The rapid adoption of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in higher education has created both opportunities and challenges for Communication Sciences and Disorders (CSD) programs. This tutorial provides a structured, discipline-specific framework to support the ethical and effective integration of GenAI into academic and clinical education. The Foundational-Developmental-Analytical-Advanced Artificial Intelligence (FDAA-AI) framework is introduced alongside a six-step process to guide assignment design, align AI use with learner readiness, and promote independent clinical reasoning. Grounded in Bloom’s Taxonomy and the Kirkpatrick Evaluation Framework, the model emphasizes making student thinking visible, aligning assessment with cognitive processes, and maintaining accountability for clinical decision-making. Ethical considerations, including confidentiality, transparency, and competence, are integrated throughout. Practical clinical scenarios illustrate application across training levels. This tutorial aims to support faculty and students in leveraging AI as a tool for learning while preserving the foundational competencies essential for professional practice.

title_key: more knowledge more use the relationship between self assessed knowledge and generative ai use among students|dusek
title: More Knowledge, More Use? The Relationship Between Self-Assessed Knowledge and Generative AI Use Among Students
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) is increasingly used in education; however, the relationship between students’ self-assessed knowledge and their actual patterns of tool use remains insufficiently understood, particularly in the secondary school context. Classroom observations suggest that students who assess their knowledge of generative AI more highly may not necessarily use these tools more intensively for academic tasks, but may instead apply them more selectively. The aim of this study was to examine the relationship between self-assessed knowledge of GAI, duration and frequency of use, and the educational purpose of GAI tool use among secondary school students. The study employed a quantitative structured survey method with a sample of 281 students aged 15 to 19 years; the data was analysed using descriptive statistics, correlation analysis, and hierarchical regression analysis. Results indicate that self-assessed knowledge is statistically significantly and positively associated with the duration of GAI tool use (r = 0.277, p < 0.05; weak to moderate association), while educationally oriented GAI use for school learning and task completion is negatively associated with both self-assessed knowledge (r = −0.266, p < 0.05) and duration of use (r = −0.395, p < 0.05; moderate negative association). Exploratory factor analysis confirmed a single dimension of educational purpose of GAI use, and regression models demonstrated that experience and self-assessed knowledge are significant predictors, whereas demographic variables do not contribute significantly. The findings suggest that greater perceived knowledge of GAI does not automatically lead to more intensive educational use, highlighting the need to promote critical, purposeful, and reflective use of generative AI in education.

title_key: impact of an unplugged intelligent tutoring system on flow and learning gains in physics a quasi experimental study in low infrastructure brazilian public schools|queiroz
title: Impact of an Unplugged Intelligent Tutoring System on Flow and Learning Gains in Physics: A Quasi-Experimental Study in Low-Infrastructure Brazilian Public Schools
abstract: This paper presents the design and quasi-experimental evaluation of STI-Física, an unplugged Intelligent Tutoring System (ITS) for Physics education in low-infrastructure Brazilian public schools. The system integrates local Bayesian Knowledge Tracing (BKT) for adaptive student modeling, generative-AI step-level hints precomputed for offline use, QR-based session access without student registration, and deferred synchronization with a teacher analytics dashboard. All of these components operate on students' personal smartphones without internet dependency. We evaluated the system in a public high school in the semi-arid Northeast region of Brazil with 31 second-year students for flow analysis (control group [CG]: n = 18; experimental group [EG]: n = 13) and 29 for learning analysis (CG: n = 13; EG: n = 16) on a thermodynamics unit. The EG used STI-Física in 90-minute sessions while the CG performed equivalent paper-based exercises. The 10-item learning instrument was built from a BNCC-aligned content matrix with teacher validation. The EG maintained significantly higher flow states than the CG (ANCOVA, F (1, 28) = 4.417, p = .045, η2 = .127) and showed greater learning gains (Mann-Whitney, U = 57.0, p = .041, rrb = .452). These findings provide preliminary, proof-of-concept evidence that unplugged ITS architectures combining BKT with generative-AI hints can support science education in resource-constrained settings.

title_key: teachers attitudes and behavioural intentions towards ai integration in chinese higher education a qualitative interview study|xiong
title: Teachers’ attitudes and behavioural intentions towards AI integration in Chinese higher education: a qualitative interview study
abstract:
The rapid expansion of generative AI has intensified scholarly and policy debate over its role in higher education, yet university teachers’ attitudes towards its integration remain complex and context-dependent. This study explores how university teachers perceive, experience, and respond to AI integration in their teaching. Guided primarily by the three-component attitude model and informed by the technology acceptance model and the theory of planned behaviour, the study examines cognitive appraisals, affective responses, behavioural intentions, and perceived support needs.
 
 
 
 The study draws on semi-structured interviews with 14 university teachers from four higher education institutions in China. The interview data were analysed using codebook-informed thematic analysis combining deductive and inductive coding.
 
 
 
 The findings indicate that teachers generally perceive AI as a supportive rather than substitutive educational tool, valuing it for improving efficiency, supporting lesson preparation, and enriching pedagogical design. Emotional responses varied from enthusiasm and a sense of accomplishment to caution, neutrality, and, in some cases, declining satisfaction. Across the interviews, teachers’ primary concerns centred less on their own replacement than on the perceived risks of inappropriate AI use for students’ independent thinking, reasoning, originality, and authentic understanding. Teachers’ intentions to adopt AI were therefore conditional and bounded, shaped by pedagogical purpose, disciplinary context, student readiness, and the need to maintain teacher control. Teachers also emphasised that sustainable AI integration requires more than general encouragement, calling instead for AI literacy development, discipline-sensitive support, specialised tools, and enabling institutional infrastructure.
 
 
 
 Overall, these findings extend contextual understandings of teachers’ AI acceptance by showing how adoption intentions are pedagogically negotiated and highlight the importance of supporting professional judgement and students’ independent thinking in higher education.

title_key: qraftai a prompt free adaptive cognitive learning loop framework for multi modal assessment|s
title: QraftAI: A Prompt-Free Adaptive Cognitive Learning Loop Framework for Multi-Modal Assessment
abstract: Current online testing systems are mainly based on static question banks and predetermined levels of difficulty which do not allow for personalization possibilities and restrict the learner to predetermined types of assessments. Recently, Generative AI-based educational systems gained a lot of momentum and have enabled much advancement in automatic content creation, assessment, grading, and feedback provision. Yet many such systems require the user to use prompt engineering which is a recurring element in the generation of questions and response evaluation. Moreover, existing solutions tend to treat question generation and answer evaluation separately rather than unifying these processes into a coherent adaptive learning process. The paper presents QraftAI, a novel Adaptive Cognitive Learning Loop (ACLL) framework that has taken personalization in learning to a whole new level. In QraftAI, a learner is required to specify only the subject they want to learn, the complexity level, and the type of assessment. The system automatically devises prompts for a Large Language Model (LLM) using the Groq API to generate questions and hints for the assessment. The system allows for typing and handwriting using Optical Character Recognition (OCR) and semantic evaluation. Furthermore, QraftAI provides a constantly updated dashboard with ongoing activities to understand how well the learner is doing. The technical stack used to develop QraftAI consists of Next.js/React, FastAPI, Firebase Authentication, Firestore, EasyOCR, Groq API, Vercel, and Render.

title_key: design of an ai feedback type adaptation model in english professional writing training|zhang
title: Design of an AI feedback type adaptation model in English professional writing training
abstract: The deep integration of generative artificial intelligence and foreign language writing teaching makes accurate feedback modeling for English professional writing training an important direction to improve training efficiency and personalized guidance level. Aiming at the shortage that the unified feedback mode is difficult to take into account the differences of writing problems and the individual characteristics of learners, this paper constructs an AI feedback type adaptation model, which is designed around the key links of feedback label system, learning process state coding, semantic feature extraction of pre-trained language model, multi-dimensional feature fusion and discrimination, learner portrait constraint matching, rule enhancement and confidence calibration. The experiment was carried out based on 4800 essays, 21600 sentence segments and 12600 feedback labeled samples. The results show that the Accuracy, Precision, Recall and F1-score of the proposed model reach 93.8%, 93.1%, 92.4% and 92.7%, respectively. The feedback matching rate reaches 93.8%, and the overall performance is better than the comparison model, which indicates that the proposed method can provide effective technical support and practical significance for intelligent feedback generation and precision teaching intervention in English professional writing training.

title_key: status and influencing factors of artificial intelligence readiness among nursing students|qin
title: Status and influencing factors of artificial intelligence readiness among nursing students
abstract:
To investigate the current status of artificial intelligence (AI) readiness among nursing students and analyze its influencing factors, providing evidence for the cultivation of AI literacy in nursing education.
 
 
 
 A total of 684 nursing students from two universities in Hubei Province were recruited as study participants. Data were collected using a general demographic questionnaire and the Chinese version of the Medical Artificial Intelligence Readiness Scale for Medical Students (C-MAIRS-MS). Descriptive statistics, univariate analysis, and multiple linear regression analysis were employed for data processing.
 
 
 
 
 The overall mean score of AI readiness among nursing students was 3.47 ± 0.31; the cognitive dimension scored the highest (3.57 ± 0.44), while the competency dimension scored the lowest (3.32 ± 0.48). Multiple linear regression analysis revealed that education level, Self-rated academic performance, Student cadre, Innovation and entrepreneurship project, Large language model use frequency, AI course learning, Programming foundation were significant predictors of AI readiness, collectively explaining 33.3% of the total variance (R

 Nursing students’ AI readiness remains suboptimal with room for improvement. Targeted interventions addressing key predictors are essential to strengthen AI competency among nursing students.

title_key: a study of the formation of an artistic image in modern ai screen art using the example of kelly boesch s ai art|zaitsev
title: A study of the formation of an artistic image in modern AI screen art using the example of Kelly Boesch's AI-art
abstract: The subject of this article is the process of artistic image formation and the specifics of visual language in modern screen art, considered on the basis of the work of AI-artist Kelly Boesch. The object of the research is audiovisual works created using artificial intelligence technologies. The author analyzes in detail the genre features and key themes of Kelly Boesch's work, examines her unique methodology and coloristic strategy. Special attention is paid to the paradoxical nature of her method and the mechanisms for maintaining copyright control. The article reveals how the artist defends her creative sovereignty and aestheticizes algorithmic rigidity, turning the technical limitations and errors of the neural network into an expressive means and an integral part of the artistic narrative. The research methodology is based on a comprehensive art historical analysis. Cultural-historical, semiotic, and formal-stylistic methods have been applied to study the artist's visual language. The main conclusion of the study: Boesch's work proves that generative AI does not replace the author, but transforms his role from a traditional artist into an architect of algorithmic concepts, where a person acts as the final filter and carrier of meanings. The author's special contribution to the research and the novelty of the work is the primary comprehensive analysis of the works of a modern creator experimenting with AI tools. The study also introduces the concept of "algorithm poetry" as an aesthetic phenomenon, where technological determinism paradoxically enhances the subjectivity of the author. The research results can be used to develop criteria for evaluating and selecting high-quality works created using neural networks. The proposed parameters for evaluating the neuro-artist's work can be used in educational programs and courses on digital art and AI design.

title_key: trustworthy educational outputs in online language assessment student and expert views|ramli
title: Trustworthy Educational Outputs in Online Language Assessment: Student and Expert Views
abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence has created new challenges for online language assessment because a strong performance may not always reflect a learner’s independent ability. This study examined how students and language assessment experts viewed the trustworthiness of educational outputs in online speaking assessment. The study used a mixed-methods secondary analysis of data collected from 186 Malaysian university students who completed an Online Semi-Scripted Dialogue Assessment and five experts in language assessment and educational technology. Quantitative questionnaire data were analysed using descriptive statistics, while students’ open-ended responses and experts’ semi-structured written interview responses were analysed thematically. The findings showed that students generally viewed the online speaking assessment as clear, fair, and capable of measuring their speaking ability. However, students and experts also recognised that ChatGPT, other artificial intelligence tools, translation applications, second devices, prepared scripts, and help from other people could influence assessment performance. These forms of assistance may improve the quality of a response without providing accurate evidence of the learner’s independent language ability. The findings also highlighted the importance of clear rules, real-time interaction, spontaneous questions, oral verification, and professional judgement. The study concludes that trustworthy educational outputs in online language assessment depend on authentic performance, transparent expectations about artificial intelligence use, and meaningful human verification.

title_key: student llm interactions during math learning limited epistemic proactivity overall but within chat change predicts performance without ai|abdelghani
title: Student-LLM Interactions During Math Learning: Limited Epistemic Proactivity Overall, but Within-chat Change Predicts Performance Without AI
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for learning, raising a key question: can learners remain epistemically proactive, retaining responsibility for the cognitive and regulatory activities through which learning is produced while working with AI? Because this responsibility may change as interactions unfold, we examine epistemic proactivity as a developing process. We conceptualize epistemic proactivity through self-regulated learning (SRL) moves, complemented by help-seeking strategies and manifestations of epistemic vigilance. We analyzed these behaviors in 880 substantive turns from 112 secondary-school students completing open-ended mathematical-modeling practice with a general-purpose LLM (Mistral). Overall, students showed limited observable epistemic proactivity: their interactions were strongly request-dominated, with planning, monitoring, and evaluation relatively rare, although low-quality AI responses elicited more explicit evaluation. Temporal analyses qualified this picture: explicit SRL-related moves increased modestly over the chat, but help-seeking strategies became less understanding-oriented. Crucially, these temporal trajectories in help-seeking strategies predicted their post-test performance without AI beyond pre-test and aggregate patterns: students whose requests became more understanding-oriented performed better once AI assistance was removed. Thus, while students had a limited epistemic proactivity overall, its temporal development still was a critical predictor of post-test performance without AI. These results underscore the importance of examining the temporal organization of epistemic proactivity, rather than isolated prompt types, for understanding AI-supported learning. We release our fully-anonymized dataset publicly in an OSF repository.

title_key: research on the development mechanisms and implementation pathways of ai empowered productive teaching projects|lv
title: Research on the Development Mechanisms and Implementation Pathways of AI-Empowered Productive Teaching Projects
abstract: Against the backdrop of deepening industry-education integration in vocational education and AI-driven digital transformation, productive teaching projects face not only the perennial challenge of transforming authentic production tasks into teachable activities, but also new challenges such as rapid resource obsolescence, heterogeneous learner foundations, and insufficient evidence for process-based assessment. Taking the “Deployment and Maintenance of a Navigation Data Storage Platform” task from the Yangtze River Trunk-Line Ship Water Pollutant Joint Supervision and Service Information System as a case, this study builds on the six-stage process of Select→Deconstruct→Define→Transform→Integrate→Extend and develops a human–AI collaborative mechanism characterized by real projects as the carrier, job competencies as the main line, and AI-supported cognition as the support. To strengthen AI empowerment across project development and implementation, AI is embedded in project selection, work-process deconstruction, competency definition, teaching-task transformation, curriculum integration, and resource expansion, and is integrated with IDEAL project-based learning, multi-stakeholder whole-process assessment, “dual-teacher + AI assistant” collaboration, and a blended virtual–real training environment. This study provides a reference for IT-related programs seeking to build replicable and iteratively improvable AI-empowered productive teaching projects.
venue: Journal of Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence

title_key: replay for llm continual learning with multi teacher on policy distillation|qiu
title: Replay for LLM Continual Learning with Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation
abstract: Multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) distills several domain experts into one student and is used in the post-training of recent large language models. It trains on all domains at once, so every expert must be available at the same time. In practice, capabilities often arrive one after another, and the experts of earlier domains may be gone when a new domain is learned. Distilling the experts in sequence then suffers from catastrophic forgetting of the earlier domains. Some recent pipelines store a snapshot after every stage and end with a multi-teacher recovery stage taught by all snapshots. The number of stored models then grows with the number of stages. Different from these pipelines, this paper formulates continual MOPD by what is kept from earlier stages and studies replay toward the previous student. Inside every stage, prompts of earlier domains are replayed with the student of the previous stage as their teacher, so neither earlier experts nor stage snapshots are kept. Two design choices of replay are explored. The replay budget of a stage is either shared among the earlier domains or fixed per earlier domain. Replay steps either distill the token distribution alone or add alignment of hidden states, region-pooled self-attention scores and value relations. A five-domain benchmark of logic, math, code, safety and instruction following is built from public experts of one 1.5B student. Experiments on its 14 benchmarks show that, without storing any snapshot, replay toward the previous student closes most of the gap between sequential distillation and joint MOPD. With a fixed replay share per earlier domain, it performs on par with recovery from all stored snapshots.
