title_key: the effect of generative ai and gamification on enhancing students motivation based on the arcs model|wen
title: The Effect of Generative AI and Gamification on Enhancing Students’ Motivation Based on the ARCS Model
abstract: High school biology learning is often hindered by abstract concepts and cognitive overload, leading to low student motivation. Although generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) and gamification show instructional potential, their combined motivational effects remain underexplored. Grounded in the ARCS model, this study examined the impact of integrating ChatGPT-based GenAI and gamification on students’ Attention, Relevance, Confidence, and Satisfaction. A longitudinal quasi-experimental repeated measures design was conducted with 52 high school biology students over eight weeks. Motivation was measured at four time points using a validated ARCS questionnaire and analyzed with Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. Results showed significant improvements across all ARCS dimensions from pre- to post-intervention (p < .001). Attention and relevance increased steadily, confidence improved in later stages, and satisfaction rose overall. Reported challenges included limited personalized AI feedback, competition-induced anxiety associated with leaderboard-based competition, and increased cognitive load resulting from complex AI-generated content. The findings indicate that GenAI-supported gamification can enhance motivation in biology learning when supported by careful pedagogical design.

title_key: development of mathematics learning design using ai based deep learning approach to enhance students conceptual understanding|widayanti
title: Development of Mathematics Learning Design Using AI-Based Deep Learning Approach to Enhance Student’s Conceptual Understanding
abstract: This study aims to develop a deep learning-based mathematics learning design integrated with artificial intelligence for fractions, intended to improve third-year pupils’ conceptual understanding, as well as to test its validity, practicality and effectiveness. A research and development approach was employed, following five stages: analysis, design, development, implementation and evaluation. The instructional design, developed using ChatGPT integrated with the Polypad application, was validated by three experts, whilst its effectiveness was tested on 22 Year 3 pupils using a single-group pre-test–post-test procedure analysed with the Wilcoxon Signed Ranks test, and its practicality was measured through a pupil feedback questionnaire. The findings indicate that the instructional design was highly valid according to the experts’ assessment, and that the pre-test and post-test instruments were both valid and reliable. There was a significant increase between pre-test and post-test scores, indicating that the design was effective in enhancing pupils’ conceptual understanding of fractions. Student feedback also indicated that the design was practical to use. These findings suggest that a systematically designed learning approach integrated with artificial intelligence can meaningfully support the conceptual learning of fractions in early primary school mathematics education.

title_key: scripted reflective prompts vs free exploration in ai assisted programming learning a quasi experimental study|siqueira
title: Scripted Reflective Prompts vs. Free Exploration in AI-Assisted Programming Learning: A Quasi-Experimental Study
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into programming education, raising questions about how much structure such tools require to support learning. This quasi-experimental study investigated whether scripted reflective prompting enhances learning over unstructured exploration in LLM-assisted programming. Twenty-four Brazilian high school students learned Python loops using Google Gemini under guided or free exploration. ANCOVA revealed no significant differences between conditions F(1,21)=1.097, p=.307, although both groups showed gains. Results suggest scripted scaffolding may not outperform free exploration in brief interventions, and instructional sequencing may influence learning trajectories in AI-assisted contexts.

title: Reimagining adolescent education with ephegogy: generative AI and active learning in practice
abstract:
This paper introduces ephegogy, a theory addressing the gap between traditional educational models and adolescents' developmental needs in artificial intelligence (AI)-augmented societies. Blending constructivism, connectivism and generativism, it explores how integrating generative AI (GenAI) and active learning can scaffold motivation, autonomy, and relevance for adolescent learners.
 
 
 
 A mixed-methods case study conducted in a single secondary-school geography course during 2024–2025. Quantitative data came from matched pre- and post-intervention surveys measuring motivation and self-efficacy (N = 17; N = 11 for the self-efficacy composite) and locus of control (N = 12), using instruments adapted for an under-14, predominantly English-as-an-additional-language cohort. A separate matched engagement survey (N = 24) and an end-of-course co-creation survey (N = 33) provided further data. Qualitative data comprised 74 individual student reflections analysed thematically using the cultural-historical activity theory (CHAT) framework, alongside open-text survey responses from 74 students. The study was designed using three frameworks (self-determination theory, ephegogy and CHAT).
 
 
 
 Findings are associational and exploratory, specific to this pilot. Composite motivation increased significantly (p = 0.043, d = 0.53), led by a significant rise in school enjoyment (p = 0.028). On a separate instrument, confidence in using AI tools showed the largest single increase (p = 0.016) and motivation relative to traditional courses also rose (p = 0.040); as several items were examined, these are treated as exploratory. Self-efficacy and locus of control showed no reliable change. Qualitatively, choice, the learning contract, and resource autonomy were dominant themes; most students disclosed and reflected on their AI use, and the modal student experience was ambivalent, valuing autonomy while finding it demanding.
 
 
 
 As a single pilot case study with small, matched samples, no control group and a single teacher-researcher as sole coder, findings are context-specific and cannot support causal claims. Future research should evaluate the framework with larger samples, control conditions, and across diverse cultural contexts and disciplines.
 
 
 
 Ephegogy provides actionable strategies for scaffolding student autonomy and ethical AI use within project-based learning. Tools such as the Student-Author Voice (SAV) rubric support metacognitive reflection and responsible co-creation, assessing authored voice rather than relying on AI detection.

title: Ecosistemas de Aprendizaje Aumentado
abstract:
The emergence of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI) in higher education has led to a refounding of the contract between subjects and machines. This article explores how this technology becomes a mediator in reading and writing practices, transforming students' relationship with knowledge within a new learning ecosystem. 
This work is part of a segment of doctoral research on university students' representations of screen reading and the use of AI for academic purposes, situated within the interpretive paradigm with a qualitative approach and inductive logic, utilizing a grounded theory design. The data corpus was obtained through theoretical sampling that included students from diverse disciplinary areas and stages of their degree programs, employing techniques such as in-depth interviews, participant observation, and the Think Aloud Method.
              The findings reveal a displacement in reading practices and a learning process mediated and assisted by GAI across various roles. This process is not purely individual but is integrated into collaborative network ecosystems where technology coexists with the necessity of human validation. 
              The research concludes that while GAI optimizes operational processes, its excessive and unguided use could pose the risk of cognitive debt and a disconnection from deep analytical processes necessary for comprehension. The study highlights that meaningful learning lies in the student's critical capacity to detect algorithmic errors and in the persistence of the human footprint as the foundation of the pedagogical process.

title_key: trusstutor bench benchmarking large language models on solution accuracy sycophancy and error detection in statics|apostolakis
title: TrussTutor-Bench: Benchmarking large language models on solution accuracy, sycophancy, and error detection in statics
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have rapidly become a default source of help for students in science and engineering courses. In foundational engineering mechanics courses such as statics, students routinely use these tools to check answers, work through partial solutions, and ask for explanations. Effective tutoring in this setting requires more than a correct final answer. A model must also confirm correct work when a student doubts it, and identify errors in flawed work. Existing benchmarks evaluate LLMs primarily on final-answer accuracy, so it is unclear whether models that can solve mechanics problems also have the other technical capabilities that tutoring depends on. Here we introduce TrussTutor-Bench, a benchmark of 200 verified two-dimensional truss problems paired with automatically generated student solutions, and use it to evaluate thirteen LLMs on solution accuracy, sycophancy, and error detection. Baseline accuracy ranged from 64.5% to 97.0%. Every model detected nearly all injected errors in synthetic flawed student work (90.4% to 100%), so error detection did not distinguish models under these clean conditions. Sycophancy did. When a student insisted that correct work was wrong, models rejected correct solutions to problems they had themselves solved in 1.6% to 50.0% of cases. These results show that performance varies widely across models: the leading models solve, check, and defend student work nearly perfectly, while others are far less reliable, particularly when a student doubts correct work. TrussTutor-Bench provides a verified, extensible standard for determining which models are technically reliable enough to put in front of students. Follow-up work must now focus on teaching rather than technical capability, drawing on learning science to determine whether LLM help leads students to understand the material or simply to reach the right answer.

title_key: from cheating to coaching how chemistry syllabi frame academic integrity in the age of generative ai|mehta
title:
From Cheating
to Coaching: How Chemistry Syllabi Frame
Academic Integrity in the Age of Generative AI
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly changing expectations for academic integrity in higher education, yet it remains unclear how institutional AI governance is translated into course-level guidance. This study examines how academic integrity and generative AI are framed in chemistry course documents and institutional policy documents. Using a hybrid inductive–deductive qualitative document analysis, I analyzed 18 publicly available chemistry course documents and 17 institutional policy documents from nine institutions across four countries. The analysis identified five higher-order themes in chemistry course documents: consequence-focused framing of academic integrity; academic integrity framed primarily as student responsibility; boilerplate policy language dominating over contextualized integrity guidance; generative AI addressed through silence, ambiguity, or prohibition; and faculty guidance and prevention rarely being explicit. A direct comparison revealed a substantial governance gap: 15 of 17 institutional policy documents (88.2%) explicitly mentioned generative AI, compared with only 2 of 18 chemistry course documents (11.1%). Institutional policies also more frequently addressed faculty guidance, research guidance, and AI governance than course documents. These findings suggest that institutional AI governance is developing more rapidly than its translation into chemistry course-level practice. Although policies and syllabi will continue to evolve as generative AI changes, the documented governance gap provides a baseline for examining how institution-level guidance is translated into instructional practice over time. The study concludes by proposing a coaching-oriented approach that shifts syllabus guidance from primarily punitive restrictions toward transparent, ethical, and pedagogically purposeful AI use.

title_key: beyond copy paste detecting and understanding students use of unauthorized aid when monitored|price
title: Beyond Copy-Paste: Detecting and Understanding Students' Use of Unauthorized Aid when Monitored
abstract: Students increasingly turn to Generative AI (GenAI) for help or quick solutions on programming practice problems, even when course policies prohibit this unauthorized aid (UA) because it can hinder learning. To address this, many tools detect UA by monitoring students’ programming processes. In this work, we deployed one such tool, Provena, in a non-majors CS1 course, and we evaluated the efficacy of 8 features for detecting UA, including code provenance, edit linearity and time-related features. Two instructors labeled students who likely used UA on one project based on submitted code and edit history. We investigated how well each feature aligns with instructor judgments of UA, as well as course outcomes. We found that most students inserted suspicious code manually in a very linear fashion (transcription), rather than by pasting it, a possible attempt to circumvent detection. Active Time, among other features, was quite effective at identifying "suspicious" students (PR-AUC = 0.93). Case studies and statistics suggest that many students who seem to use UA still struggle on assignments and may only use it on subsections of their code. We discuss concerns about using these features in practice, and the broader potential for an "arms race" between students and instructors.

title_key: an intelligent adaptive learning model to reduce novice students cognitive load in ai assisted code debugging|mustamin
title: An Intelligent-Adaptive Learning Model to Reduce Novice Students' Cognitive Load in AI-Assisted Code Debugging
abstract: Novice students in vocational mechatronics education frequently experience high cognitive load during programming code debugging. This challenge often leads to mental frustration and passive reliance on modern Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools. This study develops and evaluates an Intelligent-Adaptive Learning Model esigned to provide structured pedagogical scaffolding during Python code debugging. Utilizing a Research and Development (R&D) methodology within the ADDIE framework, the model was implemented across eight practical lab sessions involving 21 novice students. Data were collected via post-activity quantitative questionnaires (5-point Likert scale), qualitative reflection sheets, and interaction matrix logs. The findings indicate that logic errors (66.7%) and indentation issues (42.9%) are the primary sources of extraneous cognitive load. Adaptive prompting guidance effectively mitigated passive copy-paste habits (mean = 2.33) while significantly boosting independent debugging self-efficacy (mean = 3.62). Furthermore, 76.2% of students engaged in autonomous troubleshooting prior to consulting AI, and 85.7% achieved complete daily task completion. Psychologically, 76.2% experienced cognitive relief and conceptual clarity, while 23.8% exhibited heightened intrinsic motivation. The model successfully achieved Technology Readiness Level (TRL) 4, demonstrating that pedagogically integrated AI scaffolding effectively reduces extraneous cognitive load and fosters autonomous problem-solving in vocational technology education.

title_key: mapping review of tools developed for teaching academic writing|rybicki
title: Mapping Review of Tools Developed for Teaching Academic Writing
abstract: Academic writing is a core activity in higher education. Due to the increasing number of students, instructors are pressed for time and resources to guide students in their writing processes, ranging from undergraduate reports to master’s theses. As digital technologies become increasingly available, writing is supported using both commercial tools and open-source platforms. However, many popular tools are generic and not designed for teaching academic writing. Thus, instructors across disciplines, including computer science, engineering, and psychology, have developed their own tools to address specific challenges in writing processes, such as peer review or automatic writing evaluation. This mapping review surveys independently developed and open-source tools designed for teaching academic writing in English across various disciplinary contexts during 2000–2022. The results indicate that such tools have been developed and researched globally, with the English-speaking and East and South-East Asian regions increasingly developing custom tools to support writing instruction. This review helps instructors and educational decision-makers across fields make decisions about future tool development that may incorporate large language models. However, there is further need for research on educational technologies in academic writing instruction.

title_key: generative ai use and critical thinking among university students|yan
title: Generative AI Use and Critical Thinking among University Students
abstract: How students use artificial intelligence and what they learn from it cannot be ignored. According to how often people use AI tools, the groups were divided, and then descriptive statistics, Welch's ANOVA test and independent-sample t-tests were carried out to compare the critical-thinking scores of these groups. Based on the above description, the mean critical-thinking scores of the four groups using AI are relatively high. However, Welch's ANOVA showed that there were no significant differences among the four groups (F(3, 24.71) = 1.586, p = .218). The two groups were divided into regular and non-regular AI users; the mean critical-thinking scores of the regular-use group (50.06) and the non-regular-use group (45.42) were significantly higher for the regular-use group; t(100) = 2.948, p = .004, and Cohen's d = .750. Based on the above results, the impact of AI on students' critical thinking ability is not straightforward; it may vary according to how they use AI. AI can help students learn better by learning to think independently; however, if they rely on AI too much, they may not develop their own thinking skills. Given the small sample size, uneven distribution of groups, self-reported data, cross-sectional design, etc., only associations can be concluded from the results and not cause-and-effect relationships.

title_key: pengaruh human control terhadap kepercayaan mahasiswa teknik informatika dalam penggunaan claude ai di universitas malikussaleh|muksalmina
title: PENGARUH HUMAN CONTROL TERHADAP KEPERCAYAAN MAHASISWA TEKNIK INFORMATIKA DALAM PENGGUNAAN CLAUDE AI DI UNIVERSITAS MALIKUSSALEH
abstract: Generative AI assistants such as Claude AI are increasingly used by informatics students, yet trust in them depends not only on output quality but also on how much control users feel they have over the process. This study examines the effect of Human Control on trust among Informatics Engineering students at Universitas Malikussaleh using Claude AI. A cross-sectional survey of 55 students measured Human Control through four indicators (controlling AI decisions, correcting AI output, determining AI use, and retaining final decisions) and trust through an eight-item scale (1–5). Both Human Control (M = 3.95) and trust (M = 3.62) were high. The habit of checking AI output (M = 4.07) was stronger than the ability to fix wrong parts oneself (M = 3.76), and consistency of answer quality was the lowest-rated trust item (M = 3.49). Simple linear regression showed that Human Control had a positive and significant effect on trust (B = 0.733, β = 0.742, p < .001), explaining 55.1% of its variance (R² = .551). Perceived control is therefore a strong, but not the only, determinant of trust in generative AI, supporting learning designs that train students to verify and correct AI output.

title_key: readability of artificial intelligence generated responses to patient questions about hearing loss and dementia|kollia
title: Readability of Artificial-Intelligence-Generated Responses to Patient Questions About Hearing Loss and Dementia.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE
This study examines the readability of artificial intelligence (AI)-generated responses to public queries regarding hearing loss (HL), dementia, and the link between them.


METHODS
This cross-sectional study submitted 20 standardized patient-facing questions about HL, dementia, and their relationship, to three AI platforms (ChatGPT, Claude, and Perplexity AI). At the time of data collection, the default models were, respectively, GPT-5.3 Instant, Claude Sonnet 4.6, and Perplexity AI default "best" model selection. All 60 responses were assessed for readability using two validated metrics, Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level (FKGL) and Simple Measure of Gobbledygook (SMOG). The American Medical Association (AMA)/National Institutes of Health (NIH)-recommends eighth-grade reading level for patient education materials. Descriptive statistics were calculated for readability scores across platforms and 10 topic domains (SPSS 31.0).


RESULTS
Across the three AI platforms queried, FKGL median readability for responses to hearing-related questions was at the upper high school to junior college grade level (12.3-15.3) and 1-2 grade levels lower with SMOG (11.4-13.0). For dementia responses, the readability was at 15.2-16.3 grade level with FKGL and 12.9-14.1 using SMOG. No statistically significant differences were found between AI platforms overall and by domain. Claude mostly received high grade level scores for domains regarding symptoms and condition management, for both HL and dementia with FKGL and SMOG.


CONCLUSION
AI chatbots are used by the public to seek health information, yet this study found that ChatGPT, Claude, and Perplexity AI produced responses to questions about HL and dementia at 3-8 grade levels above the AMA/NIH-recommended eighth-grade benchmark. These findings align with a growing literature showing that AI-generated health content routinely exceeds recommended readability thresholds across many medical specialties. This is particularly concerning for the aging populations most affected by HL and dementia. The authors urge relevant professional organizations to audit their public-facing materials for readability compliance.

title_key: generative ai assisted learning in islamic religious education its effects on students critical religious thinking and learning autonomy|hapiz
title: Generative AI-Assisted Learning in Islamic Religious Education: Its Effects on Students’ Critical Religious Thinking and Learning Autonomy
abstract:
Purpose of the study: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly integrated into educational practices, yet its use in Islamic Religious Education (IRE) raises concerns regarding students’ critical evaluation of religious information and independent learning. This study examined the effect of structured GenAI-assisted learning on students’ critical religious thinking and learning autonomy. 
Methodology: A quantitative quasi-experimental pretest-posttest control-group design involved 60 third-semester students in the Islamic Religious Education program at Universitas Islam Yasni Bungo, comprising 30 students in the experimental group and 30 in the control group. The experimental group participated in an eight-session GenAI-assisted intervention involving problem identification, initial reasoning, ChatGPT-supported inquiry, critical evaluation of AI-generated responses, religious-source verification, independent argument construction, reflection, and integrated case discussion. The control group received conventional lecturer- and textbook-guided inquiry. 
Main Findings: The experimental group showed greater improvement in critical religious thinking (64.10 to 71.60) and learning autonomy (109.10 to 118.70) than the control group. ANCOVA revealed statistically significant group effects on critical religious thinking, F(1,57) = 87.22, p < .001, partial η² = .605, and learning autonomy, F(1,57) = 134.57, p < .001, partial η² = .702. These findings indicate that structured GenAI-assisted learning was associated with improved critical religious thinking and learning autonomy when integrated with reasoning, critical evaluation, religious-source verification, independent argumentation, and reflection.
Novelty/Originality of this study: This study introduces a structured GenAI-assisted learning framework that positions ChatGPT as cognitive scaffolding rather than cognitive substitution in Islamic Religious Education. Its novelty lies in integrating initial reasoning, AI-supported inquiry, critical evaluation, religious-source verification, independent argument construction, and reflection within one intervention, while empirically examining its effects on both critical religious thinking and learning autonomy.

title_key: incorporating cognitive load and knowledge transfer for multi domain knowledge tracing|zhang
title: Incorporating Cognitive Load and Knowledge Transfer for Multi-Domain Knowledge Tracing
abstract: Knowledge Tracing (KT) aims to assess students' dynamic knowledge states from their learning histories. While most existing KT methods focus on single-domain learning with notable success, real-world learning scenarios often involve multiple domains simultaneously, introducing two critical factors: 1) Cognitive load, arising from managing learning across domains in both temporal and knowledge dimensions. 2) Knowledge transfer, where knowledge states in one domain influence related states both within and across domains. In this paper, we focus on exploring these factors to improve students' knowledge state assessment in multi-domain learning scenarios and propose a novel method incorporating cognitive Load and knowledge Transfer for Multi-domain Knowledge Tracing (LT-MKT). Specifically, to bridge isolated domains, LT-MKT first integrates textual information from questions and their associated concepts to construct a Multi-domain Hierarchical Graph, leveraging the advanced representational capabilities of large language models (LLMs). Then, cross-domain features in both the temporal and knowledge dimensions are explicitly modeled to capture the effects of cognitive load. Additionally, a knowledge transfer module is designed to model the propagation of knowledge states within and across domains. By jointly modeling these factors, LT-MKT enables more accurate prediction of students' future performance. Finally, extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance. Code is available at https://github.com/sosweetzhang/LT-MKT.

title_key: beyond syntax and tracing a multidimensional diagnostic framework for novice code comprehension|cavalcanti
title: Beyond Syntax and Tracing: A Multidimensional Diagnostic Framework for Novice Code Comprehension
abstract: Understanding code is a major challenge for beginning programming students, especially as Large Language Models (LLMs) have made code generation easier than understanding. Despite the availability of various assessment instruments, many approaches still analyze this skill through isolated tasks and results based solely on correct answers or grades. To address this problem, this work proposes the Three-Dimensional Comprehension (3DC) model, a multidimensional approach to diagnosing code comprehension. To operationalize the model, the LIFC process was developed, integrating multiple assessment instruments and tasks to collect and triangulate evidence generated by students during program reading and interpretation activities. The proposal also defines the LOAD diagnostic profiles, which represent different comprehension patterns observed among beginning students. Preliminary results indicate that integrating multiple pieces of evidence enables the identification of specific difficulties that traditional assessments based solely on final performance cannot adequately capture. Thus, the 3DC model seeks to support more detailed diagnoses and more targeted pedagogical interventions in introductory programming education.

title_key: can generative artificial intelligence interpret culture assessing chatgpt s role in qualitative health research|malova
title: Can Generative Artificial Intelligence Interpret Culture? Assessing ChatGPT's Role in Qualitative Health Research.
abstract: The rapid integration of artificial intelligence into research has raised urgent questions about whether generative models can contribute meaningfully to qualitative inquiry, particularly in health contexts where cultural nuance and contextual interpretation are essential. This study evaluates ChatGPT's capacity to support ethnographic analysis by comparing AI-assisted outputs with a previously conducted human-led analysis of 20 interviews with college students managing Type 1 diabetes. Guided by Spradley's four-phase ethnographic interview method, it examines ChatGPT-4o's ability to identify cultural domains, construct taxonomies, articulate contrastive dimensions, and synthesize higher-order themes. While ChatGPT efficiently generated surface-level summaries and facilitated early data organization, its analytic contributions remained largely descriptive. The model struggled to identify symbolic tensions, contextual meanings, and culturally embedded interpretations that human analysts derived through iterative reading, reflexivity, and familiarity with the lived experience of chronic illness. AI-generated taxonomies lacked internal structure, and thematic interpretations failed to account for the institutional, relational, and identity-based dynamics shaping students' experiences. These findings suggest that although generative AI can serve as a useful assistive tool for preliminary coding and pattern recognition, it cannot replicate the interpretive depth central to qualitative health research. The study highlights the methodological implications of incorporating AI into qualitative inquiry, underscoring the need for critical oversight and researcher reflexivity when integrating AI-assisted approaches. As the use of AI expands in health education and behavior research, understanding its limitations is essential for ensuring that culturally grounded, meaning-rich insights remain at the center of qualitative analysis.

title_key: genai powered postsecondary computer science education tools a systematic literature review|sizemore
title: GenAI-Powered Postsecondary Computer Science Education Tools: A Systematic Literature Review
abstract: The emergence of commercial Generative AI (GenAI) tools like ChatGPT has led to a large body of research investigating how these tools are used in postsecondary CS education (CSEd) and their impact on student learning. Instructors and researchers have built new tools that leverage the powerful capabilities of GenAI, providing a pedagogically-oriented alternative to commercial tools. This emerging phenomenon has created a large ecosystem of GenAI-powered CSEd tools, but there is a limited understanding of how these tools are developed, how they utilize existing knowledge of education and learning, and how they are evaluated. To answer these questions, we conducted a systematic literature review on GenAI-powered tools in postsecondary CSEd, screening 1,834 search results from ACM Digital Library, IEEE Xplore, Springer Link, and Scopus, resulting in 72 papers for analysis. Through inductive coding, we found that tool development is strongly motivated by desires to provide personalized learning experiences for students and to address the potential risks of commercial LLMs. Further, we found that tool development was often grounded in educational framings like scaffolding and cognitive load theory. Tools frequently included features to avoid giving direct answers to students and adapt to their responses over time. In terms of evaluation, the most common methods include post-surveys and logging usage data. We close with a discussion of broader trends we observed across the papers and offer considerations for improving the development of GenAI-powered CSEd tools in the future.
venue: Proceedings of the 26th Koli Calling International Conference on Computing Education Research

title_key: beyond the chatgpt divide|bilikozen
title: Beyond the ChatGPT Divide
abstract: This study explores faculty and student perspectives on the integration of ChatGPT in higher education, with a focus on its impact on academic integrity, critical thinking, creativity, and overall academic development for multilingual learners (MLLs) as they navigate writing across the curriculum. Conducted at a transnational American University in the United Arab Emirates with a highly diverse multilingual population, the study employs a sequential explanatory mixed-methods design grounded in an interpretive framework. Survey responses from 278 students enrolled in required academic writing courses and twenty-nine English department faculty members were analyzed, followed by semistructured interviews. The findings reveal a nuanced divergence: Faculty approach ChatGPT with caution, prioritizing ethical and policy concerns, while students use it across assignments yet remain ambivalent about its ethical limits and academic impact. Although both groups share concerns about academic integrity and critical thinking, they differ in their approaches; faculty favor stricter regulatory policies, whereas students seek guidance and transparency. For writing programs and language specialists, these findings highlight the need to integrate AI literacy into writing curricula, moving beyond punitive policies toward pedagogical strategies that support multilingual writers in making informed, ethical decisions about AI use across disciplines.

title_key: a deterministic ai pipeline for skill extraction and constraint based course recommendation using academic transcripts|shaikh
title: A Deterministic AI Pipeline for Skill Extraction and Constraint-Based Course Recommendation Using Academic Transcripts
abstract: University transcripts often reduce a student’s diverse skills and competencies to a single GPA, which does not adequately reflect the quality or relevance of their skills. A GPA does not provide a way for employers to distinguish between individuals who have trained for different careers (e.g cloud engineer vs machine learning engineer) if both graduates receive the same grade point average at the end of their respective programs. The hybrid AI pipeline element identified through the review of the literature consists of two individual key components that will assist in facilitating the use of academic transcripts as occupation-based career guidance: (a) Weighted Ridge Regression (with European Qualifications Framework (EQF) Calibration) for regression analysis; (b) Cognitive Diagnosis Model (CDM)-based mastery estimator with enforcement of hard prerequisites; (c) Sentence-BERT semantic matching to all taxonomy of The European Skills, Competencies, Qualifications and Occupations (ESCO) framework. The assessment of the performance of our hybrid AI pipeline when tested against four zero-shot unconstrained LLMs (GPT-4o Mini, DeepSeek, Gemini 2.0 Flash and Claude Haiku & Sonnet) using a total of ten (10) synthetic student transcripts and produced zero violations of hard prerequisites. All performance measures produced by our hybrid AI pipeline outperformed all four LLMs tested on each of the four validity measurements in this controlled study. The results indicate that when using a validated occupational taxonomy as well as information from the synthetic student’s grade records, the resulting guidance is more accurate, more reliable, and more dependable than the general-purpose language model’s guidance in this controlled evaluation.

title_key: a role based agentic ai framework for personalized learning recommendation using lms learning analytics|wibowo
title: A Role-Based Agentic AI Framework for Personalized Learning Recommendation Using LMS Learning Analytics
abstract: Learning Management Systems (LMS) record student interactions with learning materials, assessments, and online activities, but these records are rarely transformed into personalized learning support. This paper presents a role-based agentic AI framework that uses LMS learning analytics to generate personalized learning recommendations. Using the Open University Learning Analytics Dataset (OULAD), the framework integrates learning analytics feature engineering, Random Forest-based final result prediction, structured recommendation planning, and an LLM-based recommendation writer. The predictive component achieved 0.7300 accuracy, 0.6886 balanced accuracy, 0.6822 macro precision, and 0.9147 macro One-vs-Rest ROC-AUC. Since the Fail class remained challenging, mitigation experiments improved the Fail F1-score from 0.5040 to 0.5649 through probability-threshold adjustment. The agentic evaluation processed 30 student cases across three repeated runs, resulting in 90 successful executions with a 1.0000 output success rate, 0.9917 plan-tag alignment, and 0.9667 risk-recommendation consistency. Additional ablation, groundedness, and LLM-writer comparison results indicate that the structured role-based pipeline can produce aligned and grounded recommendations within the evaluated proof-of-concept setting. The framework combines student engagement, assessment performance, submission behavior, and student profile indicators to support risk interpretation and intervention planning. It also applies guardrail validation to check output format, forbidden patterns, duplicate cases, and consistency with the recommendation plan. Overall, the study demonstrates a structured approach for connecting predictive learning analytics with personalized recommendation generation while maintaining measurable workflow reliability, output validity, and recommendation consistency.

title_key: a generative ai based technology for developing level based instructional tasks in grade 9 informatics education|sattarova
title: A Generative AI-Based Technology for Developing Level-Based Instructional Tasks in Grade 9 Informatics Education
abstract: Developing level-based instructional tasks for secondary school informatics is a time-consuming and complex process that requires alignment with curriculum objectives, competency requirements, and students’ cognitive levels. This paper presents a Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI)-based technology for automatically developing differentiated instructional tasks for Grade 9 Informatics education. The proposed technology integrates curriculum analysis, prompt engineering, large language models (LLMs), expert validation, and a structured workflow to generate instructional tasks at three learning levels based on Bloom’s taxonomy. The overall process is represented using an IDEF0 functional model, which describes the interactions among curriculum standards, competency requirements, AI-assisted content generation, pedagogical review, and classroom implementation. The developed technology was applied to Grade 9 Informatics lessons, and a quasi-experiment was performed in secondary schools to examine its effectiveness. Results indicate that the AI-supported approach reduced the workload associated with preparing teaching materials, while improving the quality of differentiated learning tasks and student achievement. The developed technology shows that generative AI can be used successfully to help teachers create high-quality leveled teaching tasks.

title_key: designing teaching agents for human ai collaborative classrooms a designbased study of students sense of presence and learning engagement|qi
title:
Designing Teaching Agents for Human‐
 AI
 Collaborative Classrooms: A Design‐Based Study of Students' Sense of Presence and Learning Engagement
abstract:
Generative artificial intelligence has expanded the possibilities for teaching agents to provide instructional explanations and feedback. However, limited research has examined how such support can be integrated into teacher‐guided classroom instruction and how students experience and engage with this form of teaching.
 
 
 
 This study aimed to iteratively design and refine teaching agents within a teacher‐guided undergraduate classroom and to examine changes in students' sense of presence and learning engagement across three design iterations.
 
 
 
 A single‐group design‐based research study was conducted in a 10‐week Introduction to Educational Technology course. 36 first‐year undergraduate students majoring in educational technology participated in three design iterations: gesture‐supported presentation, teacher‐mediated real‐time Q&A, and individualized text‐based Q&A. Data were collected through questionnaires, classroom observations, student feedback, question records, and discussion texts. Repeated‐measures analyses were used to examine changes in students' sense of presence and learning engagement, and epistemic network analysis was used to examine changes in co‐occurrence patterns among presence‐related codes in students' post‐class reflections.
 
 
 
 The findings show that students' sense of presence significantly increased across the three iterations, whereas learning engagement did not show a statistically significant change, although the descriptive means showed a small upward pattern. Epistemic network analysis identified changes in co‐occurrence patterns among presence‐related codes in students' post‐class reflections. The strongest connections involved direct instruction, affective expression, and resolution in the first iteration, and affective expression with direct instruction, exploration, and integration in the third iteration. Given the single‐group sequential design, these findings should be interpreted as observed changes during the iterative implementation process rather than causal evidence for the independent effects of specific design strategies. The study contributes process‐oriented evidence and design considerations for integrating teaching agents into teacher‐orchestrated human‐AI collaborative classrooms.
authors: ["Meng-Meng Qi", "Bing Liu", "Hong-Tao Huang", "Ji-Xin Wang", "Lin Yu", "Bo-Wen Liu"]

title_key: algorithmic advice and professional judgment in a high stakes educational vignette a contrastive analysis of teacher responses and generative ai outputs|bao
title: Algorithmic Advice and Professional Judgment in a High-Stakes Educational Vignette: A Contrastive Analysis of Teacher Responses and Generative AI Outputs
abstract: Artificial intelligence systems are increasingly used to predict, recommend, and guide educational interventions, yet less is known about how educators at different professional stages respond to high-stakes, AI-framed recommendations or how such responses differ from generative AI textual outputs produced under comparable scenario conditions. This vignette-based mixed-methods study examined responses to an algorithmic directive recommending that an artistically gifted student be redirected from an economically uncertain arts pathway to a statistically safer mathematics-related pathway. Participants included pre-service teachers (n = 119) and in-service teachers (n = 49). The study also constructed a contrastive textual corpus of 50 AI-generated outputs from five large language models under two prompt conditions. These outputs were not treated as equivalent to human responses, but as textual comparators for examining how different sources organized language around risk, agency, care, and alternative pathways. Open-ended responses and AI outputs were analyzed using qualitative coding, Epistemic Network Analysis, and Classification and Regression Tree modeling. In-service teachers showed the highest proportion of Accept responses, often citing economic risk and future security. Pre-service teachers more often rejected the directive, linking rejection to student-centered reasoning and meta-cognitive gating. In the AI corpus, no output selected Accept, although the balance between Reject and Other outputs varied by model; outputs most often proposed integrated alternatives while using language coded as humanistic concern and expressed tension. The findings indicate how risk, care, agency, and responsibility are textually and professionally organized in high-stakes AI-framed educational decisions.

title_key: can ai guide testing without generating tests a comparative study of ai assisted unit testing|fang
title: Can AI Guide Testing Without Generating Tests? A Comparative Study of AI-Assisted Unit Testing
abstract: Recent advances in generative AI have enabled assistants to generate increasingly sophisticated executable unit tests. However, novices may accept these outputs without independently identifying what to test, evaluating test-suite completeness, or verifying correctness, potentially limiting opportunities to develop essential testing skills. Although prior work has explored AI-assisted test generation and feedback-oriented programming tutors, little is known about whether AI can support novices'testing practices without generating tests for them. To investigate this, we introduce TestCompass, a generative AI tutor that provides targeted feedback on weaknesses in students'test suites without generating executable tests. In a classroom study with 18 students, we compared TestCompass with a general AI assistant across two Java unit-testing tasks, examining students'testing behaviors, test-suite quality, and subjective experiences. We found that participants using the general-purpose AI assistant produced more tests, whereas TestCompass participants spent more time developing and verifying tests themselves. However, most test-suite quality measures were comparable between conditions, and TestCompass participants achieved similar requirement coverage with significantly fewer test methods ($p=0.012$) in one task. Neither group reported short-term improvements in perceived testing knowledge or confidence. These findings suggest that feedback-oriented AI can support meaningful testing outcomes while preserving opportunities for hands-on testing practice, offering a complementary approach to AI-assisted testing education.
authors: ["Zi-Han Fang", "Ron Asoulin-Handelman", "Helen Wu", "Yu Huang", "Gina R. Bai"]

title_key: enhancing students speaking skills through small group discussion supported by chatgpt voice at smpn 4 koto baru|monica
title: Enhancing Students Speaking Skills Through Small Group Discussion Supported by ChatGPT Voice at SMPN 4 Koto Baru
abstract: This study aimed to examine the effect of Small Group Discussion supported by ChatGPT Voice on student’s speaking skills at SMPN 4 Koto Baru. A quantitative approach with a pre-experimental one-group pretest-posttest design was employed. The participants considered of 27 seventh-grade A student’s selected through total sampling. Data were collected using speaking tests assessing pronunciation, fluency, vocabulary, and grammar. The data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, the Shapiro-Wilk normality test, and Wilcoxon Signed-Rank Test. The results showed that the students mean score increased from 34.81 in the pre-test and 44.44 in the post-test. The Wilcoxon Signed-Rank Test yielded a significance value of 0.000 (p < 0.05). Therefore, the null hypothesis (H0) was rejected, and the alternative hypothesis (Ha) was accepted. Indicating that Small Group Discussion supported by ChatGPT Voice has a significant positive effect on students speaking skills. These findings suggest that integrating collaborative learning with AI-assisted speaking practice can serve as an effective strategy for improving students speaking skills.

title_key: generative ai acceptance among students in lis programs in turkiye|ozturk
title: Generative AI acceptance among students in LIS programs in Türkiye
abstract:
This study aims to examine the levels of acceptance of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI) tools among undergraduate Library and Information Science (LIS) students in Türkiye, and how these levels of acceptance vary according to selected demographic and technology-related variables.
 
 
 
 A quantitative survey method was adopted. The sample consisted of 434 undergraduate students from 14 LIS departments across Türkiye. Data were collected using the “Generative Artificial Intelligence Acceptance Scale”, grounded in the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) model, and analysed using SPSS.
 
 
 
 The findings reveal that LIS students exhibit a high level of GAI acceptance, with performance expectancy emerging as the dimension most strongly associated with overall acceptance. Frequency of use, technological proficiency and participation in GAI training were significantly associated with acceptance levels across the UTAUT dimensions, whilst gender and duration of use showed comparatively limited associations. The vast majority of students (96.1%) believe that GAI tools can be integrated into information centre services.
 
 
 
 The findings offer important insights regarding the development of AI-focused curricula in LIS education, the enhancement of digital literacy, and the future integration of AI-based applications in information centres.

title_key: a syntax driven code analysis framework for assessing structure logic and quality in academic submissions|kedar
title: A Syntax-Driven Code Analysis Framework for Assessing Structure, Logic and Quality in Academic Submissions
abstract: The increasing number of computer science students has created difficulties in the ability for teachers to accurately grade assignments manually. Manual grading is slow and requires a lot of subjective judgment about the work. Because of the complexity of programming languages such as C, there are often hidden errors both in the code structure and the way memory is managed. To resolve these issues, the authors present CodeLens, an automated full stack assessment framework. Unlike the simple auto-grading systems that just check to see if the code executes successfully, CodeLens uses a dual-engine process by combining static analysis (checking the structure and complexity of the code before executing) with dynamic analysis (with executing the code under controlled conditions). CodeLens is built on a FARM stack (FastAPI, React, MongoDB) and uses custom Abstract Syntax Tree parsing to calculate metrics such as Cyclomatic Complexity and Nesting Depth. CodeLens also uses Generative AI to provide students with non-technical feedback regarding technical error logs generated during grading. This research contains details regarding the architecture of the system, and the consistency and scalability improvements that CodeLens provides to the delivery of programming education.

title_key: teaching in the ai era|
title: Teaching in the AI Era
abstract:
Generative artificial intelligence is changing what teaching, learning, and assessment look like, but the practical questions facing educators are still poorly served by either enthusiastic promotion or alarmist warning. This book occupies the middle ground by offering a practitioner-facing approach. 
It explains the technology in plain language then offers concrete, evidence-informed strategies for prompt engineering, lesson planning, materials creation, assessment design, academic integrity, and the human-in-the-loop oversight that responsible classroom use requires. Case studies from K–12 and higher education show what works, what fails, and why. The result is a measured handbook for teachers, teacher educators, school leaders, instructional designers, and academic-integrity professionals navigating the move from AI as an outside force to AI as a present feature of everyday teaching.

title_key: doublefree exploiting exploration history for rollout free multi task llms training|wang
title: DoubleFree:Exploiting Exploration History for Rollout-Free Multi-Task LLMs Training
abstract: Multi-task post-training can develop domain specialists through independent reinforcement learning (RL) and consolidate their capabilities through multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD). However, standard MOPD generates on-policy student responses and keeps multiple teachers online throughout consolidation, introducing substantial system costs. We view this pipeline as domain-wise exploration followed by cross-domain exploitation. Domain RL produces not only the final specialists, but also the trajectories collected throughout their training. Existing methods primarily use the former while leaving the latter underutilized. We introduce DoubleFree, which reuses these historical trajectories for rollout-free consolidation and precomputes teacher supervision for online-teacher-free student training. To understand why this works, we analyze when updates from historical trajectories can approximate on-policy distillation updates and how combining trajectories across exploration stages can better support an evolving student. DoubleFree requires only minimal changes to existing post-training frameworks. Across math, code, and instruction following on Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-8B, and SmolLM3-3B, DoubleFree achieves $2.99$-$5.75\times$ consolidation speedups and reduces GPU-hours by $80.9$-$90.1\%$, while maintaining comparable multi-domain performance.
authors: ["Ying-Ping Wang", "Min Cai", "Chen-Yu Yuan", "Xi Ye", "Zhijiang Guo", "Jia-Yi Huang"]

title_key: generative ai and academic writing in higher education a thematic review of student perceptions and learning practices|kamaludin
title: GENERATIVE AI AND ACADEMIC WRITING IN HIGHER EDUCATION: A THEMATIC REVIEW OF STUDENT PERCEPTIONS AND LEARNING PRACTICES
abstract: In higher education classrooms, Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is rapidly transforming the way students approach academic writing, thereby shifting learning practices and the ethical challenges students face. To better understand this phenomenon, this paper thematically analyses qualitative insights into the students’ GenAI-assisted academic writing experience, guided by the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA). Through this review, three main themes emerged. First, students view GenAI as a helpful cognitive assistant but with a potential risk of over-reliance and authenticity of their academic voice. Second, the academic writing process is shifting away from traditional drafting toward prompt engineering and editing skills. Third, students describe uncertainty navigating the ethical boundaries between acceptable assistance and academic misconduct. This paper recommends that educational institutions move beyond simply policing GenAI use towards supporting educators to actively teach critical AI literacy. By understanding how students perceive the usage of these tools, educational stakeholders can develop practical, ethical guidelines that support responsible learning and uphold the core values of higher education.

title_key: does low confidence drive reliance on ai or does reliance erode confidence a four wave ri clpm study of chinese language and literature undergraduates|du
title: Does low confidence drive reliance on AI, or does reliance erode confidence? A four-wave RI-CLPM study of chinese language and literature undergraduates
abstract: Generative AI tools are now routinely used by Chinese Language and Literature majors for tasks once considered the province of individual literary craft: drafting verse, shaping narrative prose, revising fiction. Two competing accounts describe what this means for students’ confidence in their own creative writing. A cognitive-offloading account holds that repeated reliance on AI displaces the mastery experiences through which writing self-efficacy is built, so reliance erodes confidence over time. A compensatory-use account holds the reverse: students whose confidence is already low turn to AI to avoid the discomfort of unassisted composition, so low confidence drives reliance. Cross-sectional and standard cross-lagged designs cannot separate these accounts because they confound stable between-person differences with genuine within-person change. We addressed this using a random-intercept cross-lagged panel model (RI-CLPM) across four waves spanning one academic year among Chinese Language and Literature undergraduates (N = 390 recruited; N = 387 analyzed under full-information maximum likelihood, of whom 298 supplied complete four-wave data). Generative AI writing reliance (GAWR) and literary creative writing self-efficacy (LCWSE) were assessed at each wave. The trait-level association between the two constructs was negative and could not be distinguished from zero (r = −.342, Δχ²(1) = 2.26, p = .133). At the within-person level, declines in self-efficacy predicted subsequent increases in reliance (β = −.276, p < .001). The reverse path, from reliance to subsequent self-efficacy, was smaller and fell short of the conventional threshold (β = −.085, p = .072). We state explicitly that this second result is not interpretable as evidence against erosion: a Monte Carlo power analysis put this design's power to detect an effect of that magnitude at 53.2%, close to a coin flip, so the erosion pathway is undetermined in these data and this null supplies no basis for concluding that erosion does not operate. A direct comparison of the two cross-lagged paths favored compensation (Δχ²(1) = 8.83, p = .003; bootstrap 95% CI for the difference [.020, .218] across 5,000 resamples), with the qualification that this comparison sets an adequately powered estimate against an underpowered one and therefore describes what this design was able to detect. Compensation is the pathway this study establishes; whether reliance also erodes confidence over a longer horizon is an open question. We discuss implications for writing pedagogy in Chinese Language and Literature programs and for how underpowered null results should be interpreted in AI-in-education panel research.

title: Верификация ответов систем искусственного интеллекта как средство развития компетенций будущих учителей физики при анализе физико-географических процессов
abstract:
В условиях цифровой трансформации искусственный интеллект (ИИ) становится неотъемлемой частью повседневной жизни современного человека, наш особый интерес касается его применения в образовательной среде. Его применение может нести в себе прогресс, однако бессистемное внедрение нейросетей в учебный процесс создает серьезные риски, основным из которых является снижение когнитивной активности обучающихся при получении ими готовых, некритически осмысленных ответов. В данной статье предлагается к рассмотрению методика «Верификация ответов систем искусственного интеллекта», разработанная для подготовки будущих учителей физики. Научная новизна подхода заключается в трансформации характерных ограничений нейросетей (например, склонности к генерации неполных или односторонних ответов) в эффективное дидактическое средство формирования профессиональных компетенций. Методика сфокусирована на развитии способности выстраивать устойчивые причинно-следственные связи между фундаментальными физическими и географическими законами и явлениями. За основу взят пример анализа темы «Океанические приливы». В данной методике демонстрируются неточные ответы ИИ, который проигнорировал региональную специфику образования приливов, это позволяет учителю инициировать управляемый межпредметный познавательный конфликт. Для систематизации учебного процесса предлагается оригинальная шестикомпонентная модель задания, включающая целевой, технологический, прогностический, аналитический, практический и наглядный этапы. В работе детально описан цикл перехода учащегося от пассивного потребления контента к активному синтезу знаний: от выявления неточных ответов ИИ к созданию визуализации физико-географических явлений на примере океанических приливов. Реализация данной методики может позволить рассматривать ИИ не просто как источник информации, а как активный инструмент верификации и глубокого междисциплинарного анализа. Внедрение предложенного подхода может способствовать не только качественному усвоению межпредметного материала, но и развитию критического цифрового мышления, а также повышению цифровой и профессиональной грамотности учителей в условиях высокотехнологичного общества.
 Against the backdrop of digital transformation, artificial intelligence (AI) has become an integral part of modern everyday life. Of particular interest is its application within educational settings. While AI integration holds significant pedagogical potential, its unstructured implementation in teaching and learning poses serious risks. The primary concern is a decline in students’ cognitive engagement, as they tend to accept ready-made outputs without critical evaluation. This paper presents the “Verification of AI System Responses” methodology, designed for the training of prospective physics teachers. The scientific novelty of this approach lies in transforming the inherent limitations of generative AI-such as its tendency to produce incomplete or one-sided outputs-into effective didactic tools for developing professional competencies. The methodology focuses on developing students’ ability to establish robust cause-and-effect relationships between fundamental physical and geographical laws and phenomena. The approach is illustrated through an analysis of the topic “Ocean Tides”. It demonstrates how AI inaccuracies-specifically, the omission of regional factors in tidal formation-can be leveraged by educators to initiate structured, cross-disciplinary cognitive conflicts. To systematize the learning process, an original six-component task model is proposed, comprising goal-setting, technological, predictive, analytical, practical, and visualization stages. The paper details the learner’s transition cycle from passive content consumption to active knowledge synthesis: moving from identifying AI inaccuracies to creating visualizations of physical-geographical phenomena, using ocean tides as a case study. Implementing this methodology enables educators to reposition AI not merely as an information source, but as an active tool for verification and in-depth interdisciplinary analysis. Adopting this approach is expected to foster not only deeper mastery of crossdisciplinary content but also the development of critical digital thinking, alongside enhanced digital and professional literacy among educators in today’s high-tech landscape.

title_key: evaluation of artificial intelligence driven research methodologies on lecturers productivity in lagos state owned universities nigeria|gbesoevi
title: Evaluation of Artificial Intelligence Driven Research Methodologies on Lecturers’ Productivity in Lagos State Owned Universities, Nigeria
abstract: This study examined the influence of Artificial Intelligence (AI)-driven research methodologies on lecturers' productivity in Lagos State University (LASU), Ojo Campus. The growing integration of AI tools such as Machine Learning (ML), Natural Language Processing (NLP), and ChatGPT into academic research and teaching, alongside concerns about lecturers' research efficiency, publication output, and teaching effectiveness in Nigerian universities, motivated the study. Specifically, the study sought to ascertain lecturers' awareness of AI-driven research methodologies, examine their knowledge of ML, NLP and ChatGPT, determine their perception of these tools in enhancing research quality and academic productivity, and establish the influence of the tools on research efficiency, publication output, and teaching effectiveness. A descriptive survey research design was adopted, with a sample of 165 lecturers drawn from seven faculties and two schools across Lagos State Owned Universities. Data were collected using a researcher-designed instrument, the Artificial Intelligence Driven Research Methodologies and Lecturers' Productivity Questionnaire (AIDRMLPQ). Out of 189 copies of the questionnaire distributed, 165 were properly completed and returned, giving a response rate of 89.2%. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics (mean and standard deviation) and Pearson Product Moment Correlation at the 0.05 level of significance. Findings revealed a significant positive relationship between the adoption of AI-driven research methodologies and lecturers' research efficiency (r = 0.742), between knowledge of ML, NLP and ChatGPT and academic productivity (r = 0.781), between lecturers' perception of AI tools and research quality (r = 0.766), and between AI tools utilisation and research efficiency, publication output, and teaching effectiveness (r = 0.754). The study concluded that AI-driven research methodologies play a significant and positive role in enhancing lecturers' productivity at LASU, and that institutional support and structured training remain critical to maximising the benefits of AI in higher education. It was recommended, among others, that the University organise regular training on AI tools, develop clear policies on ethical AI use, and invest in AI-compatible infrastructure to support lecturers' effective adoption of AI in research and teaching.

title_key: self reported ai competency and educational needs for integrated ai and digital rehabilitation education among occupational therapy students a cross sectional survey|park
title: Self-Reported AI Competency and Educational Needs for Integrated AI and Digital Rehabilitation Education Among Occupational Therapy Students: A Cross-Sectional Survey.
abstract:
Background and Aim
The growing use of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in healthcare calls for occupational therapy education that combines critical appraisal, clinical reasoning, and digital rehabilitation. This study aimed to examine students' interest in AI, perceived AI competency, and needs for integrated AI and digital rehabilitation education, and identified factors associated with educational content needs.


Participants and Methods
An exploratory cross-sectional survey using convenience sampling and five researcher-developed scales without full psychometric validation was conducted among occupational therapy students from three universities. A total of 250 questionnaires were submitted, and 230 complete responses were analyzed. Descriptive statistics, reliability tests, Welch group comparisons, Pearson correlations, and hierarchical multiple regression with sensitivity analyses were used.


Results
Mean scores were 3.64±0.77 for AI interest, 3.42±0.67 for self-reported AI competency, 3.93±0.68 for educational content needs, 3.95±0.63 for educational priority, and 3.82±0.64 for instructional method preference. All five domains were positively correlated. Educational priority and instructional method preference showed the strongest correlation (r=0.701). AI interest (β=0.490, p<0.001) and self-reported AI competency (β=0.154, p=0.015) were associated with educational content needs in the conventional regression; the final model explained 34.3% of the variance. The competency association was sensitive to robust inference (HC3 p=0.0504).


Conclusion
Students expressed preferences for integrated, practice-oriented education addressing AI use, occupational therapy clinical reasoning, client-appropriate tool selection, assessment, and intervention planning.

title_key: students interaction patterns with chatgpt in solving image based mathematics problems|gusti
title: Students’ Interaction Patterns with ChatGPT in Solving Image-Based Mathematics Problems
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools such as ChatGPT are increasingly used by students to obtain explanations and solutions to mathematics problems. However, access to answers does not necessarily mean that students examine the underlying reasoning. This study aimed to describe students’ interaction patterns with ChatGPT when solving image-based mathematics problems, variations in these patterns across two problems, and how students responded to, sought clarification of, or challenged ChatGPT-generated solutions. A qualitative descriptive design was employed. The participants were Grade 9 students of one intact class (total sampling), and the records of 31 students who worked on two image-based problems, concerning the area of a trapezoidal footpath and the painted area of a photo frame, were analyzed. The primary data consisted of student–ChatGPT conversation transcripts exported from shared conversation links. The transcripts were analyzed descriptively and qualitatively using six predefined interaction patterns: requesting a solution and then ending the interaction; seeking clarification; requesting a re-explanation; checking an answer or testing a method; following a solution step by step; and connecting or redirecting the interaction. The unit of analysis was the student–problem episode, and overlapping codes were permitted. The findings indicate that students did more than request answers. Some asked for the rationale behind a solution step, proposed strategies for confirmation, requested further explanations, responded to practice questions posed by ChatGPT, and made connections between the two problems. Two students questioned the complexity or necessity of ChatGPT’s chosen method. Differences between the problems were primarily reflected in the content of students’ questions. These findings are descriptive and are not intended to establish the prevalence of interaction patterns, learning outcomes, or causal relationships. The findings suggest a need for task design and teacher guidance that encourage students to verify and evaluate AI-generated solutions.

title_key: pathwise empowering teachers with a generative ai authoring system for personalized robot assisted learning|rahman
title: PATHWiSE: Empowering Teachers with a Generative AI Authoring System for Personalized Robot-Assisted Learning
abstract: Homework assignments often lack the personalized guidance and social interaction crucial for learning. Social robots offer a promising way to bring personalization and interactive support into learning activities; however, teachers rarely have the technical expertise needed to operate robots, let alone create or customize robot-assisted learning (RAL) lessons. To address this challenge, we introduce PATHWiSE, a robust, no-code authoring system designed to empower teachers to create custom RAL activities. Developed through participatory co-design activities with middle school science teachers and students and iteratively refined through multiple user studies, PATHWiSE enables educators to author, preview, and personalize RAL activities that can be tailored to different robot platforms and delivered with either in-person or on-screen robots. The system maintains a flexible trigger-action programming model to define robot expressions contextually related to lesson materials. Through integrated teacher- and student-facing portals, teachers can deploy RAL lessons using a lightweight and portable browser-based approach that affords integration with a wide range of systems. AI-assisted comment and emotion-expression generation tools augment teacher lesson creation while preserving teacher autonomy and expertise in content design. In this paper, we present the design and implementation of PATHWiSE, including its authoring workflow, interface architecture, backend integration, and representative use cases drawn from iterative studies to illustrate the capabilities of the full system.

title_key: instructional strategies for responsible genai use in computer science education|sizemore
title: Instructional Strategies for Responsible GenAI Use in Computer Science Education
abstract: The emergence of commercial Generative AI (GenAI) tools like ChatGPT has led to a large body of research investigating how these tools are used in postsecondary CS education (CSEd) and their impact on student learning. GenAI offers students personalized and timely academic support, but its use also raises concerns about over-reliance and impacts on critical thinking skills. Instructors have therefore taken many different approaches toward the use of GenAI in their CS courses. Some instructors have limited the integration of GenAI in their courses through bans or restrictive assignments. Others have taken more proactive approaches that encourage using GenAI in a responsible way to support learning, facilitated by custom GenAI tools with pedagogical guardrails or instructor-provided guidance on how to best use commercial GenAI tools. My research is focused on instructional strategies for guiding students on how to use GenAI in CS courses; I have completed a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) on custom GenAI tools and plan to conduct another SLR on instructor-provided guidance on commercial GenAI use. The findings from both SLRs will be synthesized to understand best practices for teaching students how to use GenAI in a way that supports their learning. From this work I plan to develop instructional interventions that teach responsible GenAI use, iteratively refining the interventions through user studies and later evaluating them empirically through in-class deployments.

title_key: analysing influence of usage patterns and reliance of artificial intelligence ai on learners critical thinking in higher institutions of learning|thoronjo
title: Analysing influence of usage patterns and reliance of artificial intelligence (AI) on learners critical thinking in higher institutions of learning
abstract: AI tools (ChatGPT, Grammarly, Gemini, QuillBot) are increasingly used in higher education to support learning and writing, but concerns exist about learner dependency and its impact on critical thinking and independent learning. This study examined the association between AI reliance and critical thinking among students from five Kenyan universities. Using a sequential explanatory mixed-methods design, data were collected from 275 students via questionnaires. Quantitative analysis included descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation, regression, and ANOVA. Results showed moderate AI reliance for tasks such as assignment preparation and idea generation. A modest positive correlation was found between AI use and critical thinking (r=0.24, p < 0.05). Self-directed learning (β = 0.29) and purposeful AI use (β = 0.21) were significantly associated with critical thinking. ANOVA indicated that moderate AI users had higher critical thinking scores than those reporting low or excessive AI use.
