title_key: funatomy exploring student perceptions of low cost game based learning in first year anatomy|venter
title: FUNATOMY: Exploring Student Perceptions of Low-Cost Game-Based Learning in First-Year Anatomy
abstract: Background: Game-based learning (GBL) is increasingly used in anatomy education to promote active learning; however, little is known about students’ perceptions of multiple low-cost GBL activities embedded in routine anatomy practicals. This study explored first-year health sciences students’ perceptions of the benefits and limitations of FUNATOMY, low-cost GBL activities integrated into anatomy practical sessions. Methods: A qualitative exploratory study was conducted among first-year students in four health sciences programs at the University of Pretoria, South Africa. Written reflections from 200 consenting students were analyzed using an AI-assisted inductive thematic approach. Two large language models were used as exploratory tools to generate preliminary themes that informed subsequent researcher-led thematic analysis. Two researchers independently assigned themes to student responses, resolving discrepancies through discussion and consensus. Results: Eight themes were established: Enjoyment; Understanding and application; Memory and knowledge retention; Learning environment; Collaboration; Complementary learning strategy; Knowledge gaps; and Did not help. Students described the activities as enjoyable and engaging and felt they supported retrieval and reinforcement of previously learned knowledge, understanding and application, collaboration, and recognition of knowledge gaps. Students viewed FUNATOMY as complementary to, rather than a replacement for, specimen-based anatomy practical teaching. Conclusions: The findings reflect students’ perceptions of FUNATOMY and suggest that the activities were viewed as a useful supplement to traditional anatomy practicals. However, the study did not objectively assess learning outcomes or establish the activities’ effectiveness.

title: Эффективность применения искусственного интеллекта при обучении иностранному языку в техническом ВУЗе
abstract:
в данной статье анализируются как теоретические, так и прикладные вопросы, связанные с внедрением технологий искусственного интеллекта (ИИ) в образовательный процесс при обучении иностранному языку студентов технических направлений. В качестве основной задачи исследования выступает эмпирическая верификация результативности использования ИИ-технологий в обучении иностранному языку у представителей неязыковых специальностей в сопоставлении с традиционными педагогическими подходами. Развитие цифровых преобразований в высшем образовании вступает в стадию, характеризующуюся широким внедрением генеративных искусственно-интеллектуальных моделей. Быстрые изменения, инициируемые искусственным интеллектом, затрагивают образовательную сферу. В технических вузах, где овладение иностранным языком является неотъемлемым компонентом профессиональной подготовки, введение ИИ помогает росту результативности и качества учебного процесса. Данное обстоятельство обусловило интерес исследовательского сообщества к ИИ, проявляющему потенциал в адаптивных стратегиях, автоматизации процедур и создании иммерсивной языковой среды. Методологическая основа проведённого исследования определяется использованием интегративного подхода, подразумевающего совмещение традиционных методик преподавания иностранных языков с современными разработками в сфере обработки естественного языка и инструментов машинного обучения. В качестве эмпирической базы реализован педагогический эксперимент, осуществлённый со студентами первого курса магистратуры по направлению «Робототехника и мехатроника». В контексте эмпирического этапа дополнительно организовано анкетирование, посредством которого фиксируется отношение обучающихся к введению искусственного интеллекта в процесс освоения иностранного языка в условиях технического университета. Экспериментальные данные дают возможность определить аспекты языковой деятельности, эффективнее интегрируемые во взаимодействие с ИИ (освоение произносительных навыков, отработка грамматических структур), что высвобождает аудиторное время для формирования умений, требующих участия преподавателя (дискуссии, анализ профессиональных ситуаций, межкультурная коммуникация).Также результаты исследования служат основой для дифференцированного подхода при проектировании профессионально-ориентированных образовательных траекторий студентов. Сейчас функционирование искусственного интеллекта осуществляется с опорой на обширные и непрерывно пополняющиеся текстовые данные, доступные в цифровой среде. Что трансформирует способы восприятия языковых явлений и оказывает воздействие на процессы коммуникации и образования среди людей. Динамичное распространение ИИ-технологий, которое преимущественно фиксируется среди молодежи, обусловливает необходимость корректировки устоявшихся методов преподавания иностранных языков.
 this article analyzes both theoretical and applied issues related to the implementation of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies in the educational process of teaching foreign languages to students majoring in technical fields. The primary objective of the study is to empirically verify the effectiveness of using AI technologies in teaching foreign languages to students majoring in non-linguistic fields, compared with traditional pedagogical approaches. The development of digital transformation in higher education is entering a phase characterized by the widespread adoption of generative artificial intelligence models. Rapid changes driven by artificial intelligence are affecting the educational sphere. In technical universities, where foreign language acquisition is an integral component of professional training, the introduction of AI helps improves the effectiveness and quality of the educational process. This has sparked interest in AI within the research community, which demonstrates potential for adaptive strategies, process automation, and the creation of immersive language environments. The study is based on an integrative approach (combining classical foreign language teaching methods with advances in natural language processing and machine learning). The empirical basis was a pedagogical experiment conducted in a first-year group of a master's degree program in Robotics and Mechatronics. The empirical study also included a survey characterizing students' attitudes toward the use of artificial intelligence in foreign language teaching at a technical university. Experimental data make it possible to identify aspects of language activity that are more effectively integrated into interaction with AI (mastering pronunciation skills, practicing grammatical structures), which frees up classroom time for developing skills that require teacher participation (discussions, analysis of professional situations, intercultural communication). The study results also serve as the basis for a differentiated approach in designing professionally oriented educational trajectories for students. Today, artificial intelligence relies on vast and continually expanding text data available in the digital environment. This is transforming the way we perceive linguistic phenomena and influencing communication and education processes among people. The rapid spread of AI technologies, which is primarily observed among young people, necessitates adjustments to established methods of teaching foreign languages.

title_key: biology undergraduates use of ai enabled feedback to revise scientific writing recipience and barriers|weston
title: Biology Undergraduates’ Use of AI-Enabled Feedback to Revise Scientific Writing: Recipience and Barriers
abstract: Background Instructors and education researchers are increasingly developing feedback with the assistance of generative AI, which we refer to as AI-enabled feedback, yet we do not know whether established understandings of feedback uptake and effectiveness apply similarly in AI-mediated contexts. This makes the recipience of AI-enabled feedback a central concern to understanding how to best support students in developing their scientific writing skills. This study examined how two teams of undergraduate biology students used AI-enabled feedback to revise their scientific writing, and the extent to which their revisions addressed that feedback. The teams revised their research proposal drafts after receiving AI-enabled feedback developed by their instructor with the aid of a custom AI tool. Results Our findings show that AI-enabled feedback prompted actionable revision across both teams. Each team addressed approximately half of the feedback comments, indicating comparable levels of uptake despite their differing approaches to revision. We observed that both teams were inconsistent in providing the additional information and reasoning requested in the feedback, and they struggled to address comments requiring self-evaluation. Taken together, we see that students often addressed the more easily actionable parts of AI-enabled feedback while omitting more demanding revisions. Conclusions These findings provide behavioral evidence of how students used AI-enabled feedback to revise their scientific writing. The observed patterns suggest that the content of AI-enabled feedback supported meaningful revision, while limitations in students’ agency, strategies, and volition likely shaped their implementation of comments. Although the degree of uptake observed in this study is encouraging, it is unlikely that a single application of generative AI within the feedback process will resolve all the challenges associated with feedback uptake.

title_key: generative artificial intelligence use and applied higher order cognitive performance among health informatics students a multicenter cross sectional case based assessment study|alhur
title: Generative Artificial Intelligence Use and Applied Higher-Order Cognitive Performance Among Health Informatics Students: A Multicenter Cross-Sectional Case-Based Assessment Study
abstract: Background Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is widely used by university students, but evidence linking routine use with demonstrated higher-order cognitive performance is limited, particularly in Health Informatics education. Purpose To examine associations between GenAI use and applied higher-order cognitive performance among undergraduate Health Informatics students in Saudi Arabia. Methods In this multicenter cross-sectional study, a convenience sample of 431 students from seven Saudi universities completed an online questionnaire (May–July 2026). GenAI use was self-reported (duration, frequency, weekly hours, academic-use intensity, responsible use, and formal AI training). Performance was measured with a newly developed, expert-reviewed, 30-item case-based assessment of critical thinking, problem-solving, and decision-making (weighted 0–3 scoring; total 0–90), completed remotely without proctoring. Nonparametric tests and hierarchical regression with heteroscedasticity-robust (HC3) standard errors and university fixed effects were used. Results Of 431 participants, 425 (98.6%) reported prior GenAI use. The mean total score was 57.14/90 (SD 15.41). Frequency, duration, and weekly hours of GenAI use were not associated with performance. Academic GenAI-use intensity showed a weak unadjusted inverse correlation (ρ = −0.15) but no association after adjustment for university (B = 0.10; 95% CI −1.61 to 1.80). Adding university fixed effects increased R2 from 0.080 to 0.287. Formal AI training was negatively associated with performance (B = −3.48; 95% CI −6.40 to −0.56). Conclusion In this convenience sample, routine GenAI exposure was not independently associated with performance on a newly developed case-based assessment, whereas scores varied considerably between universities for reasons this study could not identify. Because the design was cross-sectional, exposure was self-reported, and independent completion could not be verified, the findings are associational and the instrument requires external validation. Health Informatics programs may benefit from attending to how students use GenAI rather than how often.

title_key: artificial intelligence on the literacy level of undergraduates in nigerian universities|adeyemi
title: Artificial Intelligence on The Literacy Level Of Undergraduates In Nigerian Universities
abstract:
Abstract 
Technology has taken over the 21st century in order of evolving intelligence and practice. Artificial Intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming global education, yet limited empirical research has examined its influence within Nigerian teacher-training institutions. This study investigates the impact of AI tool usage on academic performance among. A quantitative survey design was employed, involving 480 distributed questionnaires, of which 412 valid responses were returned, yielding an 89.96% response rate. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation, multiple regression, and moderation analysis. Findings reveal a remarkably high AI adoption rate of 84.95%, with ChatGPT as the most widely used tool (66.1%). AI usage demonstrated significant positive correlations with key academic performance indicators, particularly research project outcomes (r = 0.378, p < 0.01). Regression results show that AI self-efficacy (β = 0.298, p < 0.001) is the strongest predictor of academic performance, followed by usage frequency (β = 0.189, p < 0.001) and digital literacy (β = 0.156, p = 0.001), collectively explaining 38.7% of the variance (Adjusted R² = 0.379). Digital literacy, academic level, and gender significantly moderated the AI-performance relationship. The study concludes that AI tools, when used confidently and effectively, enhance literacy level and support research-driven learning. Strengthening AI literacy, improving digital infrastructure, and establishing ethical guidelines are recommended to maximize benefits and ensure equitable access in Nigerian teacher education.
venue: International Journal of Management and Business Applied

title_key: from awareness to academic use generative artificial intelligence awareness as a predictor of utilisation for learning among allied health undergraduates|osijirin
title: From Awareness to Academic Use: Generative Artificial Intelligence Awareness as a Predictor of Utilisation for Learning Among Allied Health Undergraduates
abstract:
Background:
 Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has moved quickly from novelty to an everyday learning resource in higher education. Yet frequent exposure does not necessarily mean that students understand how to use these systems critically, safely, and academically. This distinction is especially consequential in health-related education, where inaccurate outputs, privacy breaches, and uncritical reliance can shape learning habits with implications beyond the classroom.
 Purpose:
 This study examined GenAI awareness and learning-oriented utilisation among undergraduates in a specialised allied health sciences university in Nigeria and tested whether awareness statistically predicts academic use.
 Sample:
 The sample comprised 220 consenting first-year undergraduates drawn from 14 academic programmes.
 Design and method:
 An analytical cross-sectional survey was conducted from 6 to 10 September 2026. A study-specific questionnaire measured GenAI awareness with 10 items and utilisation for learning with 12 items, both on four-point scales. Internal consistency was high for awareness (Cronbach’s α = .86) and utilisation (α = .95). Descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation, and simple linear regression were used, with HC3 robust standard errors and Spearman correlation as robustness checks.
 Results:
 GenAI exposure was widespread: 96.8% had heard of GenAI and 94.5% reported prior use. ChatGPT was the most frequently used tool (60.0%). Mean awareness was 3.48 (SD = .45), while mean utilisation was 3.44 (SD = .52). Awareness was moderately associated with utilisation (r = .427, 95% CI [.313, .530], p < .001) and significantly predicted utilisation (B = .490, HC3 SE = .073, β = .427, 95% CI [.346, .634], p < .001), explaining 18.3% of the variance. The pattern remained in a sensitivity analysis restricted to self-reported prior users.
 Conclusions:
 Awareness matters for academic GenAI use, but it is not sufficient. Students were more aware of GenAI capabilities than of privacy, bias, and academic-integrity risks, revealing a descriptive capability-criticality gap. Allied health institutions should therefore move beyond tool exposure towards structured AI literacy that combines practical use with verification, ethical judgement, confidentiality, and discipline-specific reasoning.

title_key: fostering equity and learning effectiveness in hybrid education through microsoft copilot vision an extended study of ai supported classrooms|vargas
title: Fostering Equity and Learning Effectiveness in Hybrid Education through Microsoft Copilot Vision: An Extended Study of AI-Supported Classrooms
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) continues to transform educational practices by providing innovative approaches to teaching, learning, and learner support. Within blended learning environments, AI-powered technologies offer new opportunities to enhance engagement, improve comprehension, and promote more inclusive educational experiences. Among these emerging technologies, Microsoft Copilot Vision provides multimodal capabilities that enable real-time visual interpretation, contextual assistance, and adaptive learning support. Despite these potential benefits, concerns regarding digital accessibility, educational equity, and responsible AI use remain important considerations for effective implementation. This study examined the role of Microsoft Copilot Vision in enhancing student engagement, learning comprehension, and perceived learning effectiveness within blended learning environments. Using a convergent mixed-methods research design, quantitative data were collected through survey questionnaires, while qualitative insights were obtained through focus group discussions involving 160 senior high school students enrolled in blended learning programs. Findings revealed high levels of student engagement, learning comprehension, and perceived learning effectiveness associated with the use of Microsoft Copilot Vision. Participants reported that AI-generated visual explanations and contextual assistance supported understanding of complex concepts, encouraged self-directed learning, and enhanced overall learning experiences. However, digital accessibility challenges, particularly those related to internet connectivity and device availability, continue to influence the equitable implementation of AI-supported learning. The findings further highlight the importance of responsible AI usage in maximizing educational benefits while preserving critical thinking and learner autonomy. The study contributes to the growing body of knowledge on Artificial Intelligence in Education (AIEd) by providing empirical evidence on the educational value of Microsoft Copilot Vision in blended learning environments and offers practical insights for educators, institutions, and policymakers seeking to foster equitable, resilient, and technology-enhanced learning ecosystems aligned with Sustainable Development Goal 4 (SDG 4).

title_key: exploring ai tools for accessible scientific documents|power
title: Exploring AI Tools for Accessible Scientific Documents
abstract: This field note addresses the critical challenge of accessing mathematical content in PDF documents for students using screenreader technology. Standard PDF exports often discard structural tags and fail to convey the complex meaning of mathematical notation, hindering full student participation in learning activities. To overcome these barriers, this exploratory project investigates improved document-production workflows that preserve mathematical structure from source code to final output. Utilizing Large Language Models (LLMs) like Anthropic’s Claude Code, the project prototyped methods for embedding structural information within LaTeX source code to generate inherently accessible PDFs and HTML documents featuring MathML. Furthermore, the note outlines a comprehensive future evaluation framework involving subject experts, accessibility specialists, and skilled screenreader users to rigorously validate these prototypes against real-world educational tasks. Ultimately, by both human expertise and AI, this initiative aims to develop an authoring toolchain for educators. This approach ensures mathematical documents are accessible upon creation, thereby enabling independent and more equitable participation for all students in mathematics education.

title: ДИНАМИКА МОРАЛЬНОГО САМОКОНТРОЛЯ В АКАДЕМИЧЕСКОЙ СРЕДЕ ПОД ВЛИЯНИЕМ ЦИФРОВЫХ ТЕХНОЛОГИЙ
abstract:
The rapid development of generative artificial intelligence tools has changed not only how students complete academic assignments but also the psychological mechanisms that regulate their attitudes toward academic honesty. This article examines the dynamics of university students' moral self-control under the digitalization of the educational environment through the lens of A. Bandura's theory of moral disengagement. 
The aim of the study is to identify the leading mechanisms of moral rationalization behind AI tool use in academic activity and to empirically test how the division of labor between student and AI affects the responsibility for the outcome that the student subjectively accepts. Two methods were used: a survey employing an original scale of AI-use rationalization, developed on the basis of Bandura's classification of moral disengagement mechanisms, and an experimental comparison of three conditions for completing an academic task (independent work, AI as an auxiliary tool, and full delegation of the task to AI). 
The results indicate the relative strength of individual moral disengagement mechanisms and differences in accepted responsibility between the experimental groups. The findings help clarify which cognitive mechanisms make AI use psychologically “safer” for students' moral self-perception than traditional forms of academic dishonesty, and can inform the development of preventive and educational programs at the university.

title_key: llm graph neural network collaborative exercise recommendation for dynamic knowledge state characterization|qiu
title: LLM-graph neural network collaborative exercise recommendation for dynamic knowledge state characterization
abstract: Under the background of deep integration of artificial intelligence into education and teaching, personalized exercise recommendation faces problems such as insufficient semantic understanding of exercises, coarse-grained description of students 'knowledge state, and insufficient recommendation stability under cold start conditions. This paper proposes LMGN, an exercise recommendation framework that integrates large language models and graph neural networks. The framework uses LLM to semantically encode the problem stem, the knowledge point label and the difficulty description, and generates the initial representation of the exercise node. On this basis, the student-exercise multi-behavior heterogeneous graph is constructed, and the interactive signals such as "do right, do wrong, request prompts" are modeled as relational, and the knowledge state propagation and representation update are completed with the help of relation-aware GNN. The experiment was carried out based on ASSISTments2009 and KDDCup2010 datasets. The Recall@20 and NDCG@20 of LMGN reached 0.2372 and 0.2162 respectively, and 0.0876 and 0.0763 respectively. It is better than MF, LightGCN, SimGCL and other baseline models. The results show that the proposed method can improve the recommendation accuracy under high sparse educational data, and provide a scalable technical solution for accurate learning guidance intelligent education system.

title_key: understanding non cs majors motivation to learn programming in the context of generative ai|orgill
title: Understanding Non-CS Majors’ Motivation to Learn Programming in the Context of Generative AI
abstract: Background: Computing educators have long advocated for non-CS majors to learn programming. Today, generative AI (GenAI) assistance makes coding more accessible than ever before. Does the presence of GenAI make learning programming basics more or less compelling for non-CS majors? Purpose: We investigate non-CS majors’ perceptions of the importance of learning programming, specifically in relation to programming with GenAI assistance. We focus on their beliefs when they have not yet studied programming to better understand the motivations of these learners as they enroll in CS courses. Methods: We conducted a survey in two introductory programming courses for non-CS majors in the first two weeks of a semester (N=197), followed by focus groups (N=20). Questions in both settings focused on constructs known to predict motivation according to Social Cognitive Career Theory: self-efficacy, outcome expectations (i.e., perceived career utility), and contextual factors. Results: A plurality of students agreed that today, less background knowledge is necessary in order to write code. Both self-efficacy and outcome expectations differed when students considered programming with and without GenAI assistance. While students had higher confidence programming with GenAI, they also believed that programming with GenAI has lower career utility. However, their self-efficacy and outcome expectations for programming without GenAI assistance were the only significant predictors of interest in learning programming. Contributions: Our findings suggest that GenAI does not inherently impact non-CS majors’ interest in learning programming; to increase interest in the age of AI, we need to make the applications and career value of programming more explicit to students.

title_key: designing ai integrated teaching materials for pre service english teachers a lesson from teachers professional education practices|syathroh
title: Designing Ai-Integrated Teaching Materials For Pre-Service English Teachers: A Lesson From Teachers Professional Education Practices
abstract: Lesson planning is a core professional skill for pre-service teachers, particularly within Indonesia’s Kurikulum Merdeka, which emphasizes the development of Modul Ajar as flexible, creative, and learner-centered teaching modules. With the growing presence of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in education, this study investigates how pre-service English teachers integrate AI tools into Modul Ajar development, exploring their perceived benefits, challenges, and professional implications. Employing a qualitative descriptive design, data were collected from seven pre-service teachers enrolled in the Pendidikan Profesi Guru (PPG) program through lesson plan documents, reflection journals, and focus group discussions. Thematic analysis was used to examine patterns of AI use, perceptions, and reflections across data sources. Findings reveal that participants used a range of AI tools, such as ChatGPT, Grammarly, Quillbot, and Canva, to support lesson planning. These tools assisted in drafting objectives, generating activities, refining language, and creating visual materials, enabling participants to focus on higher-order pedagogical considerations. Reported benefits included efficiency, improved clarity, enhanced creativity, and support for differentiated instruction. However, participants also identified significant challenges, including over-reliance on AI outputs, contextual misalignment with the Indonesian curriculum, occasional inaccuracies, and the irreplaceable need for human judgment in adapting lessons to learners’ needs. The study underscores that while AI can serve as both a scaffold and a catalyst for reflective practice, its effective integration requires critical evaluation, pedagogical guidelines, and professional judgment. Recommendations highlight the need for AI literacy training, context-sensitive frameworks, and further research on the long-term impact of AI integration on teaching competence and student outcomes.
venue: Journal of Language and Literature Studies

title_key: a humanai collaborative readthinkwrite framework for esp oriented college english education development and pedagogical applications|fan
title: A Human–AI Collaborative Read–Think–Write Framework for ESP-Oriented College English Education: Development and Pedagogical Applications
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) offers adaptive materials and rapid feedback for language education, but its classroom use often remains fragmented and weakly connected to disciplinary learning and student reasoning. This framework-development study proposes a Human–AI Collaborative Read–Think–Write Framework for ESP-oriented College English education in large science and engineering classes at a local application-oriented university in Guangxi, China. Developed through practice-informed problem identification, contextual needs analysis, theoretical synthesis, interdisciplinary co-design, and three rounds of refinement, the framework integrates Reading-to-Write Pedagogy with Human–AI Collaboration. It comprises one core—human–AI collaborative personalized learning; two drivers—content customization and feedback immediacy; and three loops—AI-assisted reading, AI-guided thinking, and AI-supported writing. A process-evidence assessment chain connects the initial draft, AI interaction records, revised draft, and reflective statement. Its pedagogical application is illustrated through an ESP unit on autonomous vehicles and road safety. the framework offers a teacher-governed, tool-neutral approach that positions GenAI as a scaffold rather than an author. Its effectiveness requires future external review, classroom piloting, and mixed-method validation.

title_key: from lookups to lessons turning retrieved knowledge into parametric memory|han
title: From Lookups to Lessons: Turning Retrieved Knowledge into Parametric Memory
abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) helps large language models (LLMs) answer factual questions beyond their training data, but it adds storage and inference costs. Distilling previously retrieved information into parametric memories enables reuse without online retrieval. However, training the memory to mimic a retriever rewards accurate independent predictions, which do not necessarily improve the final output quality when combined with the LLM's existing predictions. To address this, we introduce ResMem, in which the LLM reads retrieved text offline to generate teacher targets. This design avoids storing massive token representations, unlike existing parametric memory approaches such as MLP Memory, which relies on k-nearest neighbor (kNN) datastores. Furthermore, by using the LLM as an offline teacher that reads privileged retrieved evidence alongside the input, we train a parametric memory to learn an additive logit residual. This residual aligns the predictions of a student sharing the same backbone with the teacher distribution, while self-distillation updates remain confined to the parametric memory. On a Wikipedia subset, ResMem reduces the storage retained for teacher construction by 94.7% compared with the evaluated kNN pipeline. Across five question answering datasets, ResMem raises mean token F1 from 32.83% for the frozen LLM to 34.48%. It also breaks 21% fewer of the LLM's correct answers than a kNN-trained memory. These findings validate our motivation of treating retrieval as a learning resource, with parametric memory shaped by how retrieved knowledge is used to inform the model's future predictions. Code and model weights are available at https://github.com/SSRand/From-Lookups-to-Lessons and https://huggingface.co/RandHan/ResMem-Mistral-7B-v0.3.

title_key: beyond the final code understanding student programming behaviors through process journals|chao
title: Beyond the Final Code: Understanding Student Programming Behaviors through Process Journals
abstract: As students can now use Generative AI to easily solve introductory programming problems, there is a greater need to focus pedagogy on the programming process, not just the final product. Process journals, where students document their problem-solving steps while working on a coding problem, can encourage students to reflect on their learning and make their thinking visible to instructors. We qualitatively analyzed 48 process journals from an introductory programming course to understand student behaviors and interpret these behaviors through the theoretical lens of self-regulation. Our findings revealed ways in which students understand and approach the programming task, how they test and debug their code, how they consulted resources, and how they reflected or managed their learning. We classified these behaviors as positive, negative, or neutral based on how much self-regulation and engagement they showed. Although some students were not able to complete the basic requirements or showed little extra engagement after satisfying the base requirements, most students showed behaviors beyond the minimum requirements with the process journal and some demonstrated thinking beyond solving the problem. In addition, we found that the behaviors students showed were not strongly related to their exam score or their self-reported metacognitive self-regulation metric. Our study presents process journals as a tool that can give educators insight into both desirable and undesirable behaviors of the stages students go through when solving programming problems. This allows educators to stage interventions that support student learning and metacognitive development.

title_key: between verification and delegation the use of generative artificial intelligence in a public high school in mazatlan mexico|meza
title: Between verification and delegation: the use of generative artificial intelligence in a public high school in Mazatlán, México
abstract: This article addresses a study conducted at a public upper secondary school of the Universidad Autónoma de Sinaloa in Mazatlán, Mexico, on how students use generative artificial intelligence (AI) in their schoolwork, with the aim of understanding what happens to their autonomy when these tools become part of their academic life. A cross-sectional design was applied through an online questionnaire, which was answered anonymously by 206 students aged 15 to 18 in May 2026. Among the results, it was found that two out of three students (67.5%) use AI at least once a week, with ChatGPT and Gemini as the most commonly used tools, mainly to request explanations of complex topics. It is worth noting that 78.2% report using AI to verify their own answers and only 26.7% acknowledge that they could not complete some tasks without it; however, those who use it daily rely on it to solve mathematics exercises and write essays up to three times more often than the rest of their peers. Based on the above, it can be inferred that there is a gap between the autonomy students claim and the practices they themselves report; therefore, the challenge for teachers, families and institutions lies in teaching the correct and ethical use of these tools, so that AI supports learning rather than replacing the student’s own effort.

title_key: generative ai use in higher education cognitive offloading and epistemic curiosity examining psychological mechanisms of ai assisted learning|hussain
title: Generative AI Use in Higher Education, Cognitive Offloading, and Epistemic Curiosity: Examining Psychological Mechanisms of AI-Assisted Learning
abstract: This study examines the relationship between generative artificial intelligence (AI) use, cognitive offloading, and epistemic curiosity among university students, with particular emphasis on the mediating role of cognitive offloading. A quantitative, cross-sectional research design was employed, using primary data collected through a self-administered Google Forms questionnaire from a sample of 301 undergraduate and postgraduate students enrolled at selected public and private universities in Pakistan. Participants were recruited through convenience sampling. The analysis included descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation, regression analysis, and mediation analysis using PROCESS Macro Model 4 with 5,000 bootstrap samples and 95% confidence intervals in IBM SPSS. The findings indicate that generative AI use is positively associated with cognitive offloading, and that cognitive offloading is negatively associated with epistemic curiosity. The indirect relationship between generative AI use and epistemic curiosity through cognitive offloading was negative, suggesting that greater reliance on AI may reduce curiosity by encouraging students to offload cognitive effort. In contrast, the direct effect of generative AI use on epistemic curiosity was positive, indicating a pattern of inconsistent mediation. These results suggest that generative AI may simultaneously support and undermine students’ intellectual curiosity, depending on the extent to which it replaces independent thinking. The study contributes to the understanding of how AI-assisted learning relates to students’ cognitive strategies and curiosity, and it offers guidance for educators seeking to balance technological support with independent reasoning and active knowledge exploration.

title: Методологический базис: интеграция искусственного интеллекта в курс высшей математики для направления «Экономическая безопасность»
abstract:
в статье рассматриваются теоретические и практические аспекты интеграции технологий искусственного интеллекта в процесс преподавания высшей математики для студентов, обучающихся по направлению подготовки «Экономическая безопасность». Актуальность исследования обусловлена необходимостью формирования у будущих специалистов в области обеспечения экономической безопасности не только фундаментальных математических знаний, но и компетенций в области применения современных инструментов искусственного интеллекта (ИИ) для решения профессиональных задач, связанных с финансовым мониторингом, экономическим анализом и прогнозированием рисков. Целью работы является разработка методологического базиса интеграции ИИ-технологий в образовательный процесс по математическим дисциплинам с учетом специфики экономической безопасности. В ходе исследования проанализированы существующие подходы к применению нейросетевых алгоритмов в обучении, выявлены педагогические и технологические условия эффективного использования ИИ-ассистентов, а также определены направления адаптации учебных материалов для студентов-экономистов. Практическая значимость работы заключается в создании дидактической модели, позволяющей повысить качество математической подготовки будущих специалистов по экономической безопасности за счет персонализации обучения, автоматизации рутинных вычислительных задач и формирования навыков работы с современными интеллектуальными системами в контексте экономического анализа.
 the article examines theoretical and practical aspects of integrating artificial intelligence technologies into the process of teaching higher mathematics to students enrolled in the field of study «Economic Security». The relevance of the research is driven by the need to develop in future specialists in the field of economic security not only fundamental mathematical knowledge but also competencies in applying modern artificial intelligence tools to solve professional problems related to financial monitoring, economic analysis, and risk forecasting. The aim of the study is to develop a methodological framework for integrating AI technologies into the educational process in mathematical disciplines, taking into account the specific nature of economic security. The research analyzes existing approaches to the use of neural network algorithms in education, identifies pedagogical and technological conditions for the effective use of AI assistants, and determines directions for adapting educational materials for economics students. The practical significance of the work lies in creating a didactic model that improves the quality of mathematical training for future economic security specialists through personalized learning, automation of routine computational tasks, and the development of skills in working with modern intelligent systems in the context of economic analysis.

title_key: it takes two to vibe code profiling student ai programming interactions processes and their high order structure|misiejuk
title: It Takes Two to Vibe Code: Profiling Student-AI Programming Interactions Processes and Their High Order Structure
abstract: Programming has evolved from writing machine code to compiler-based and interpreted languages, and now to natural language that Large Language Models (LLMs) translate into code, transforming not only software development but also programming education. Programming with an LLM is interdependent: student engagement and AI response continually shape one another, turn by turn, yet most prior research has examined only the learner’s actions through aggregated measures, overlooking this interdependence. We adopt a process-oriented perspective to analyze 15,650 student-AI interactions from 88 students across seven programming assignments, employing Heterogeneous Transition Network Analysis to model the dialogue as a Markovian system of interdependent actor states. Our findings reveal two distinct interaction profiles: a constructive-facilitative profile, characterized by a recurring explain-demonstrate-explore loop, and a passive-directive profile, characterized by a solve-evaluate-debug cycle in which students repeatedly requested further solutions; importantly, these profiles were unrelated to final grades. Using higher-order networks and Hypergraph-based Pathway Analysis, we further identify recurring multi-step conversational structures that first-order Markov models obscure. In doing so we provide an empirical basis for understanding how distinct interaction patterns shape the programming process and student-AI interdependence.
venue: Proceedings of the 26th Koli Calling International Conference on Computing Education Research

title_key: using chatgpt teacher mode to teach a design based research protocol and implementation framework|khushalani
title: Using Chatgpt “Teacher Mode” To Teach: A Design-Based Research Protocol and Implementation Framework
abstract: The unstructured use of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in education may encourage passive answer-seeking rather than active learning. This study introduces ChatGPT Teacher Mode, a structured framework designed to position generative AI as a guided instructional partner that promotes critical thinking, metacognition, and evidence-based reasoning. Using a design-based research approach, the study develops a protocol for implementing Teacher Mode across mathematics, history, civics, and geography. The framework incorporates discipline-specific learning activities, including articulating mathematical reasoning, evaluating primary sources, explaining constitutional principles, and interpreting climate maps. It integrates pedagogical scaffolding, formative assessment, verification routines, and transparent AI-use policies to support responsible implementation. The proposed framework targets four outcomes: improved learning through structured reasoning, enhanced metacognitive awareness, higher-quality feedback aligned with assessment rubrics, and greater transparency in AI use. Potential challenges, including inaccurate outputs, over-reliance, and inequitable access, are addressed through verification strategies, AI-assisted and AI-free assessments, and institutional guidelines. This study contributes a socio-technical framework, an empirically testable research protocol, and practical guidance for educators integrating generative AI into teaching and learning. Teacher Mode offers a structured approach to leveraging generative AI while maintaining academic integrity and supporting meaningful student engagement. Its effectiveness, however, requires empirical validation across educational contexts

title_key: preserving academic integrity in the ai era video stimulated recall vsr for cognitive accountability|majid
title: PRESERVING ACADEMIC INTEGRITY IN THE AI ERA: VIDEO STIMULATED RECALL (VSR) FOR COGNITIVE ACCOUNTABILITY
abstract: Maintaining academic integrity has become incredibly challenging in the era of Generative AI tools like ChatGPT and Gemini. In programming education, these tools can seamlessly generate complete solutions for assignments, leading to a fundamental shift in how students approach their work. Rather than actively developing the code themselves, many now simply rely on AI to generate the implementation. This study examines how we can adapt to this reality through a new assessment technique. Rather than attempting to prohibit AI use, this research explores how changing the assessment design can ensure that students still involve their own critical thinking. By redesigning the way we evaluate, we can hold students cognitively accountable, forcing them to actively engage their minds and truly understand the task even when they utilise AI assistance. Video Stimulated Recall (VSR), combined with live oral questioning was implemented as an alternative assessment in a Mobile Application Programming course at Universiti Kebangsaan Malaysia involving 91 undergraduate students. Over a 14-week period, students recorded VSR videos in which they explained and justified their code, including AI-assisted code, for five laboratory tasks and two projects. They were subsequently required to modify the code in real time during question-and-answer (Q&A) sessions. At the end of the semester, a questionnaire measuring four constructs such as passive AI dependence, cognitive-active AI use, the washback effect of VSR and code ownership was administered, yielding 89 valid responses. The findings indicate that passive AI dependence was low (M=2.54), whereas cognitive-active AI use was high (M=3.93), suggesting that students tended to perceive AI as a learning support rather than a substitute. The VSR requirement produced a positive washback effect (M=3.51), with 81% of students reporting that they spent additional time studying their own code to prepare for the recordings. Students also reported a strong sense of code ownership (M=3.72). The study provides the conclusion that VSR serves as a useful tool in establishing cognitive accountability and turning AI from a danger to the integrity of education into a structured learning partner.

title_key: harnessing authentic student tool interaction traces to develop and evaluate llms for cs1 programming feedback|solano
title: Harnessing Authentic Student-Tool Interaction Traces to Develop and Evaluate LLMs for CS1 Programming Feedback
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) offer promising avenues for scalable, on-demand support in introductory programming (CS1) courses. However, proprietary LLMs demonstrate tendencies that run counter to educational objectives, and their use raises concerns regarding student privacy and institutional oversight. This project investigates how CS1 tool traces can be used to fine-tune and evaluate open-source LLMs for specific programming feedback applications. We draw on usage records from compiler error and unit test feedback systems to ground model development in authentic student-tool interactions, and support iterative refinement and evaluation. By training small models for specific programming feedback tasks, we can reduce reliance on proprietary models and facilitate low-cost, private deployment. Initial work demonstrates an effective approach to improving smaller open-source models through supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on authentic student compiler errors, and establishes a combined expert-annotation and LLM-as-judge evaluation pipeline. Current work extends this approach by using student unit-test activity surrounding LLM interventions to support feedback evaluation and further model specialisation. This project aims to assess both the short- and long-term effects of these specialised LLM-integrated tools on student learning, and provide institutions with a practical framework for their deployment, evaluation, and refinement.
venue: Proceedings of the 26th Koli Calling International Conference on Computing Education Research

title_key: dialogic co creation with generative ai reconciling parallel thinking channels intuition and epistemic transformation in higher education|chandiona
title: Dialogic Co-Creation with Generative AI: Reconciling Parallel Thinking Channels, Intuition, and Epistemic Transformation in Higher Education
abstract: AI as a cognitive partner whose knowledge disagreements can enhance learning and intellectual development rather than merely as a technological instrument. This research paper combines theories of dialogic pedagogy, cognitive dissonance, and epistemic humility via conceptual analysis. It looks at how Parallel Thinking Channels promote critical thinking, introspection, and the innovative combination of computational reasoning with human intuition. The purpose of this study is to advance the concept of dialogic cocreation by examining the revolutionary potential of generative AI in higher education portrays. This study utilized a quantitative approach with 419 undergraduate and post-graduate students as participants. The data analysis, conceptual model and hypotheses were evaluated employing Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM) in SmartPLS version 4.1.1.8 to analyse the associations between the constructs of the study. The results of study show that the disparities arising from the conflict between machine-generated results and human reasoning serve as triggers for transformative learning. By merging intuition with computational thinking, students enhance their ability to manage uncertainty, broaden their understanding, and cultivate flexible intellectual resilience. As a cooperative partner in knowledge development, this study offers a novel framework for incorporating generative AI into higher education. To prepare graduates for complex and uncertain digital futures, it emphasizes co-creation, critical reflection, and epistemic flexibility.

title_key: operationalising humanai interaction requirements through digcomp 3 0 for translator education|qudah
title: Operationalising human–AI interaction requirements through DigComp 3.0 for translator education
abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is changing the landscape of translation, expanding translators’ involvement in interaction configurations, evaluation of AI-generated outputs, and governance of risks within augmented translation environments. This study defines Human–AI Interaction in Translation (HAIT) as GenAI-mediated component of the human-centred augmented translation process, where GenAI is integrated into translation technologies and conversational large language models. Translation education lacks a developmental structure that connects these emerging requirements and their related digital competences to curriculum design. This study proposes a workflow-derived operationalisation of HAIT for translator education. A conceptual functional analysis of augmented translation workflows produced eight HAIT requirements, which were mapped to the 21 competences of the European Digital Competence Framework (DigComp 3.0) by assessing 168 potential relationships for functional correspondence, scope fidelity, and traceable justification. The analysis accepted 37 relationships among 16 competences and identified translation-specific residues that require curricular supplementation. The operationalised requirements were organised into a proposed four-level progression informed by DigComp proficiency levels. An exploratory mixed-methods pilot with 42 second-year translation students examined perceived relevance after contextualised exposure in a course-embedded intervention. Students broadly perceived DigComp as relevant to translation education and practice, particularly focusing on competences related to familiar topics such as privacy protection, device security, copyright, information retrieval, communication and collaboration, with limited attention to information evaluation and programming competences. Their responses were less explicit about AI-generated output evaluation, prompting and in-context steering, grounding configuration, and risk-responsive actions, highlighting the value of a spiral curriculum for competence development and Quality Education (SDG4).

title_key: flawed but memorable student critical reception of interest personalized genai analogies in computing education|bernstein
title: Flawed but Memorable: Student Critical Reception of Interest-Personalized GenAI Analogies in Computing Education
abstract: Motivation: Undergraduate computing students increasingly turn to generative AI (GenAI) tools to understand abstract concepts, sometimes receiving explanations built around analogies. Analogies work by comparing an unfamiliar concept to something familiar, but this creates a trap. To tell whether the comparison actually holds, a student needs to know both the concept and the everyday thing it is compared to, and a learner may be missing either one. GenAI may also embed assumptions about who the learner is. Research on GenAI in computing education centers on output correctness at the code and explanation level, leaving students’ critical reception of analogies largely unexamined. Method: We investigate how undergraduate students evaluate the accuracy, appropriateness, and embedded assumptions of GenAI-generated analogies, and how they perceive interest-personalized analogies relative to generic technical explanations. Ten students who had completed CS2 participated in this study, with each finishing a pre-survey, a think-aloud annotation task with personalized analogies and generic explanations for linked lists and recursion, and a semi-structured interview grounded in the Paul-Elder critical thinking framework. Students judged analogies along separable dimensions, treating accuracy, clarity, engagement, and trust as distinct standards. Results: Most participants described the interest-personalized analogies as more engaging or memorable than the generic technical explanations, while their accounts of trust were mixed. Some reported trusting the tailored analogies more; others scrutinized them more closely or distrusted the tailoring itself. Participants who demonstrated deep knowledge of an analogy’s source domain identified structural flaws that required source-domain knowledge to recognize. Because personalization and explanation format differed together, these findings do not isolate an effect of personalization alone. Implications: A familiar source flips the student’s role. On the concept they are still learners, but on the familiar source it is compared to they are the expert, and that is the position from which an analogy can be judged. We call this two-sided analogy auditing. GenAI systems should therefore ask what students know, not just what interests them, and treat a flawed analogy as something to inspect and fix rather than accept.

title_key: exploring the influence of ai tools on critical thinking development in english major undergraduates|chen
title: Exploring the Influence of AI Tools on Critical Thinking Development in English Major Undergraduates
abstract: Generative AI tools are increasingly embedded in higher education, where English majors are frequent users. Although they reduce cognitive load and boost efficiency, over-reliance may weaken independent thinking and logical reasoning, both core to critical thinking. This study examines how AI use influences critical thinking among undergraduate English majors at a university in Shanghai, focusing on usage frequency and question types. A mixed-methods design combines a questionnaire with semi-structured interviews. Questionnaire data are analyzed in SPSS using descriptive statistics, correlation, and regression; interviews capture perceived cognitive effects. The findings identify how frequency and question types relate to different dimensions of critical thinking, revealing both facilitating and constraining effects. Theoretically, the study extends research on AI in humanities education; practically, it informs strategic AI integration and critical thinking cultivation in English language teaching and digital transformation.
venue: Journal of Social Science and Human Research Studies

title_key: generative ai in c programming education pedagogical strategies and educational risks|secaf
title: Generative AI in C Programming Education: Pedagogical Strategies and Educational Risks
abstract: Teaching C programming involves challenges, particularly in pointers and memory management. With the widespread adoption of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI), new learning opportunities have emerged, although these tools may obscure subtle technical errors. This Systematic Mapping Study analyzes studies published between January 2022 and December 2025 to identify pedagogical uses, instructional strategies, and the impacts of GenAI in C programming education. The analysis is based on a corpus of 12 primary studies. The results indicate risks of cognitive passivity when AI is used without instructional mediation and suggest a shift from code production to code auditing. This study synthesizes recent evidence and highlights strategies for integrating GenAI without compromising students' conceptual understanding.

title_key: stem teacher education in the age of artificial intelligence less memorization more questions|bilek
title: STEM TEACHER EDUCATION IN THE AGE OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE: LESS MEMORIZATION, MORE QUESTIONS
abstract:
Artificial intelligence has made its way into education at a remarkable pace. What until recently seemed to be the subject of discussions about the future has now become part of everyday educational reality. Students are using generative AI to search for information, draft texts, solve problems, formulate explanations, and prepare coursework. Meanwhile, teachers are faced with an increasingly difficult question: what exactly should pupils and students know and be able to do when artificial intelligence can provide a seemingly convincing answer in a matter of seconds?
For STEM education, and particularly for the education of future STEM teachers, this issue is of paramount importance. Science education has traditionally been associated with the acquisition of a relatively extensive body of factual and conceptual knowledge. However, the availability of AI does not mean that such knowledge is no longer necessary. Paradoxically, its importance may even increase. A person who knows almost nothing about a particular topic has a limited ability to formulate meaningful questions, assess an AI-generated answer, recognise inaccuracies and, ultimately, take responsibility for the final output. In other words, access to information cannot replace understanding.

title_key: hybrid intelligence as a tool for textual decoding integrating the literary detective framework in higher education|parinos
title: Hybrid Intelligence as a Tool for Textual Decoding: Integrating the Literary Detective Framework in Higher Education
abstract: This paper explores the transformative integration of Hybrid Intelligence (HI) within the landscape of higher philological education, specifically operationalized through the innovative 'Literary Detective' pedagogical framework. Amidst the shifting cognitive baselines of the digital era, this study addresses the crisis of sustained deep attention by proposing a synergistic model of textual archaeology. The research focuses on the intricate process of multidimensional decoding, wherein human cultural intuition collaborates with the computational power of Large Language Models (LLMs) to excavate latent intertextual layers across a diverse literary corpus.The study provides a comparative analysis of foundational and modern texts, demonstrating how a structured Decoding Matrix facilitates the identification of complex cultural codes in the cosmological epics of Vaja-Pshavela, the impressionistic prose of Niko Lortkipanidze, and the tragic war poetry of Mirza Gelovani, alongside the works of Homer, Margaret Atwood, and Ana Kalandadze. The findings reveal that Artificial Intelligence, when utilized as a cognitive scaffold rather than a replacement for authorial voice, significantly amplifies the student's capacity to navigate intertextual networks and resolve “artificial hallucinations” through intuitive filtering. Empirical evidence suggests that this hybrid approach not only increases the efficiency of thematic identification by approximately 38% but also fosters advanced critical thinking and digital literacy. Ultimately, the paper argues for a paradigm shift in the humanities, positioning the student as an active investigator in an AI-augmented hermeneutic environment, ensuring the continued relevance of philological rigor in a post-digital academic world.
venue: International journal of technology in education and science

title_key: exploring students use of ai assisted tools for autonomous vocabulary learning a case study in secondary education|nada
title: Exploring Students’ Use of AI-Assisted Tools for Autonomous Vocabulary Learning: A Case Study in Secondary Education
abstract: Vocabulary learning is a gradual process that requires students' autonomy to support their vocabulary development. Metacognitive strategies encourage students to plan, monitor, and evaluate their learning progress. Furthermore, in the digital era, AI-assisted tools can support students to maintain self-regulated learning. Using a case study design, this inquiry uses interviews and questionnaires to collect data from a group of senior high school students. Twenty students participated in the investigation during a four-week implementation of a metacognitive strategy in a narrow reading program. The questionnaire was distributed before and after the program. To capture students' experiences during the program, students were instructed to write a reading journal. All data sources were analyzed descriptively. The results show that most senior high school students are familiar with using ChatGPT and Google Gemini. Indeed, in the context of vocabulary lookup, they have utilized the combination of Google Lens and Google Translate. The way students use AI-assisted tools has varied according to their level of proficiency. Students with limited vocabulary coverage used AI tools to improve their comprehension. Conversely, students with a sufficient vocabulary level used AI as a partner to enrich their knowledge and learn vocabulary productively. These findings yield two instructional implications: first, teachers need to guide students in using AI responsibly while integrating it into the learning process. Second, having access to AI tools is not enough; students must be prepared to become autonomous learners so they become lifelong learners.
venue: Journal of Language and Literature Studies

title_key: intelligent matching platform for university students employability|li
title: Intelligent Matching Platform for University Students' Employability
abstract: Therefore, this paper will introduce an intelligent matching platform for the employment prospects of college students and address the above issues. The Platform has been divided into a front-end and a back-end. Vue 3 and Element Plus are used for the user interface, Spring Boot and MyBatis for the back-end service, and JWT is used to ensure stateless authentication. Kafka is used for real-time data processing as a message queue, Flink performs stream-based intelligent matching calculations, and ClickHouse stores the matching results and statistics. The five dimensions of the multi-dimensional weighted scoring model are city, education level, major, salary and skills; accurate job recommendations are thus generated. An AI job-seeking assistant based on the DeepSeek-V3 large language model will offer real-time career advice. The three types of users for the system are students, enterprises and administrators, and all have data dashboards for employment monitoring. Experimental tests of less than 100 concurrent users showed that the average response time was less than 500 milliseconds, and thus the platform had effectively improved the accuracy of work matching, simplified employment management, and raised the general standard of university employment services.

title_key: effects of generative ai assisted revision on arabic writing performance a randomized counterbalanced within subject study|siregar
title: Effects of Generative AI-Assisted Revision on Arabic Writing Performance: A Randomized Counterbalanced Within-Subject Study
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used to support writing and revision, yet evidence regarding its effects on Arabic writing performance remains limited. This study examined differences in Arabic writing performance and linguistic error patterns between human-only and AI-assisted conditions. We used a randomized, counterbalanced, within-subject design with 72 students in an Arabic Language Education Program at UIN Sunan Gunung Djati Bandung, Indonesia. Participants were randomly assigned to two counterbalanced sequences: human-only followed by AI-assisted writing, or AI-assisted followed by human-only writing. Each participant completed two equivalent Arabic writing tasks of approximately 150–200 words under identical constraints. In the AI-assisted condition, participants used ChatGPT as a revision and feedback tool to help them identify, evaluate, and revise their writing rather than generate essays. Performance was assessed across seven dimensions: content, organization and coherence, grammar (nahwu), morphology (sharaf), vocabulary, syntax, and orthography (imlā'). Linguistic errors were classified into six categories: grammar, morphology, lexical, syntax, orthography, and coherence, while error transitions were separately examined as corrected, persistent, and AI-induced errors. Results indicated higher writing performance in the AI-assisted condition. We interpreted dimension-level improvements descriptively unless we tested them separately. Error analysis showed a reduction in linguistic errors under AI-assisted writing, although some errors persisted and a smaller number were AI-induced. These findings suggest that GenAI can support Arabic writing performance through revision and feedback, but do not establish durable gains in writing proficiency. GenAI is therefore best understood as a mediated resource that complements students' linguistic knowledge, agency, and judgment rather than replacing independent writing.

title_key: design of an ai literacy liberal arts curriculum and competency change analysis a case study of d university|kim
title: Design of an AI Literacy Liberal Arts Curriculum and Competency Change Analysis: A Case Study of D University
abstract: This study designed a mandatory general education course to cultivate the practical AI literacy required in the generative AI era and empirically analyzed changes between preand post-course scores. To complement the technology-centered approaches of existing computational thinking education, a lesson plan for a practice-based general education course centered on no-code tools and generative AI was developed on the basis of four design principles: low threshold, principle-based experience, practical utilization, and critical and ethical reflection. In pre- and post-course surveys of 340 students, post-course scores were significantly higher on all 12 items, and the reliability of the measurement instrument was satisfactory (α = .890–.938). These results suggest that the curriculum may be associated with improvements in AI literacy, although the single-group, unlinked-data design limits causal interpretation. A ceiling effect was suggested for the item on confidence in the course's relevance to one's major and career, indicating a need to consider strengthening career linkage and introducing advanced project-based learning (PBL). In addition, the time × group interactions by college affiliation and gender were not statistically significant.

title_key: sentiment analysis of students towards the use of chatbots in the learning process using the support vector machine svm algorithm|alfandi
title: Sentiment Analysis of Students Towards the Use of Chatbots in the Learning Process Using the Support Vector Machine (SVM) Algorithm
abstract: The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) platforms like ChatGPT within higher education environments has generated diverse responses among students. This study aims to analyze the sentiment trends of STMIK Kaputama students regarding the adoption of ChatGPT in their learning process using the Support Vector Machine (SVM) algorithm. A dataset comprising 520 student opinion entries was gathered through questionnaires administered across multiple academic levels. The text data underwent comprehensive preprocessing, including case folding, cleansing, tokenizing, stopword removal, and stemming, followed by feature extraction using Term Frequency–Inverse Document Frequency (TF-IDF). The sentiment distribution analysis revealed that student opinions were predominantly negative at 55.6% (289 entries), while positive responses accounted for 34.6% (180 entries), and neutral sentiments comprised 9.8% (51 entries). Model performance evaluation via a Confusion Matrix on 156 test samples achieved an overall accuracy of 80.77%. On a per-class evaluation level, the model obtained its highest F1-score in the negative class at 88%, followed by the positive class at 76%, and the neutral class at 57%, yielding a overall weighted average F1-score of 81%. Further examination of the decision function distribution f(x) confirmed high classification stability, with the majority of test samples situated far from the boundary hyperplane (spanning the 2.0 to 2.3 interval). Overall, these findings indicate that while ChatGPT is acknowledged for facilitating independent study and task comprehension, students at STMIK Kaputama remain critical and cautious regarding academic challenges and reliance on AI tools

title_key: rpt an llm powered tutoring system to support the learning of code refactoring|oliveira
title: RPT+: An LLM-Powered Tutoring System to Support the Learning of Code Refactoring
abstract: Code quality affects how programs are read, tested, and maintained. To improve code quality, professional developers refactor code. Writing code of good quality and refactoring code are taught in several CS programs. To support students’ learning of code refactoring, prior work has introduced RPT, a tutoring system with method-level refactoring exercises that relies on predefined rules to provide feedback and hints on refactoring steps. However, implementing these rules in the tutor requires significant manual effort, and automatically recognizing all variations of student code is difficult. To address this limitation, we investigate whether LLMs can provide feedback and hints for students’ refactoring steps. In this paper, we present RPT+, a redesigned version of RPT that replaces its rule-based backend with an LLM-powered backend. We evaluated the systems’ ability to detect code quality issues, and they identified roughly the same number of issues (RPT+: 77%, RPT: 76%). We also conducted an expert assessment to evaluate the quality of the hints provided by RPT+, and found mixed results. Although we rated 81% of the generated hints as appropriate, the use of generic instructions combined with the non-deterministic behavior of the LLM results in hints that may at times be misleading or unclear. Finally, we conducted two pilot studies in which students tested RPT+. The system worked as intended for detecting quality issues and suggesting refactoring hints. Students mostly rated the feedback and hints as helpful, but a few students suggested that the feedback on incorrect refactoring steps should be more detailed.

title_key: exploring values enhanced development in a software requirements engineering course|li
title: Exploring Values-Enhanced Development in a Software Requirements Engineering Course
abstract: Software requirements engineering lies between social demands and technical implementation. In the present course, several problems occur, including inconsistent lectures and value building, unpractical cases, lack of absorption pathways and insufficient evaluation. In this paper, we present a generative AI-based framework to reform the software requirements engineering course. It includes the entire teaching-learning process, from pre-class preparation to class participation and after-class reflection. During the teaching process, we obtain empirical data through the use of "Smart Senior Care system". The results indicate that this approach can enable students to pay attention to the consideration of values in requirement analysis. The key aspect of this method is to improve the students' ability to make decisions concerning the coordination of stakeholders' interests and value trade-offs.

title_key: ai enabled social engineering and deepfake fraud in higher education an integrative review of threats human detection limits and layered defences with a research agenda for the global south|sada
title: AI-Enabled Social Engineering and Deepfake Fraud in Higher Education: An Integrative Review of Threats, Human Detection Limits and Layered Defences, with a Research Agenda for the Global South
abstract: Purpose: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has changed the economics of social engineering. Large language models write fluent, personalised phishing at near-zero cost, voice-cloning tools imitate a lecturer or parent from seconds of audio, and real-time deepfake video can impersonate an official on a call. Universities combine an open culture, high staff and student turnover, large financial flows and young, heavily connected users, which makes them attractive targets. Yet the literature on AI-enabled deception and the literature on cybersecurity in higher education have developed largely in parallel. This review brings them together. Method: An integrative review following Whittemore and Knafl's (2005) approach. Structured searches of Scopus, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, SpringerLink, IEEE Xplore and the ACM Digital Library (2017–2026), supplemented by citation chasing, identified empirical studies, systematic reviews and authoritative reports on AI-enabled social engineering, human deepfake detection, phishing susceptibility and literacy-based interventions. The evidence was synthesised thematically and mapped onto a conceptual model. Findings: Four findings stand out. First, generative AI amplifies six threat vectors relevant to universities, from large language model (LLM) spear-phishing to synthetic-persona scholarship and romance fraud. Second, pooled human deepfake detection accuracy is close to chance (about 55% across 56 papers), and people consistently overestimate their own ability. Third, awareness training and media-literacy interventions produce real but modest and decaying gains, and they work better against misinformation than against targeted fraud. Fourth, research on students is concentrated in high-income countries, with very little from sub-Saharan Africa despite the region's specific exposure to financial fraud.
