title_key: medical school curriculum reform and the missing debate on artificial intelligence as an educational agent|choi
title: Medical School Curriculum Reform and the Missing Debate on Artificial Intelligence as an Educational Agent
abstract: In 2024, revision of the Enforcement Decree of the Higher Education Act in Korea abolished the rigid division between the 2-year premedical phase and the 4-year medical phase, allowing medical schools to design 6-year curricula autonomously for the first time in a century. Universities nationwide have begun redesigning their programs accordingly. This historic reform coincides with the rapid spread of generative artificial intelligence (AI) across society, including the ways students learn. In the current curriculum reform discourse, however, AI is discussed almost exclusively as content to be taught or as a supplementary tool to be used, whereas the more fundamental question of AI as an educational agent remains largely unexamined. Outside the formal curriculum, AI tutors already function as de facto teachers: a randomized experiment suggests that well-designed AI tutoring can outperform expert- led active-learning classrooms, and international surveys indicate that medical students routinely consult AI before, or instead of, their professors. This paper argues that the widening gap between the official, faculty-centered curriculum and the actual AI-mediated learning ecosystem may create discord: AI-mediated learning may become an unmanaged informal curriculum, faculty-designed assessment may lose authority, and trust in the formal curriculum may erode. Curriculum reform that merely rearranges the 6-year structure without addressing who teaches risks producing an elaborate design for an education that no longer reflects how learning occurs. Medical schools should explicitly define the position, scope, and governance of AI as an educational agent within their new curricula.

title_key: artificial intelligence ai integration in education teachers utilization perceptions and implementation challenges|cruz
title: Artificial Intelligence (AI) Integration in Education: Teachers’ Utilization, Perceptions, and Implementation Challenges
abstract: This study explored the integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools in chemistry instruction, focusing on teachers’ utilization patterns, perceptions, and the challenges they encounter. A sample of 18 chemistry teachers from various institutions participated, providing insights into the types and frequency of AI tools used, including ChatGPT, ChemCollective, and PhET Interactive Simulations. Findings indicate that generative AI tools—particularly ChatGPT—are the most widely adopted due to their accessibility, versatility, and ease of integration. In contrast, subject-specific and creative AI platforms remain underutilized, suggesting that familiarity, perceived complexity, and awareness significantly influence adoption patterns. Teachers demonstrated strongly positive perceptions of AI integration in both curriculum and instruction, recognizing its potential to enhance content delivery, student engagement, personalized learning, and the development of 21st-century skills. No significant differences were found across institutions, indicating a shared readiness to integrate AI in chemistry education. Despite these favorable perceptions, effective implementation is constrained by technical limitations, infrastructure gaps, data quality concerns, usability challenges, ethical issues, and privacy risks. Teachers also expressed concerns about over-reliance on AI and the potential reduction of meaningful teacher–student interaction, emphasizing the importance of maintaining a balanced, human-centered approach. Overall, the findings support the strategic and guided adoption of AI as a pedagogical enhancement tool rather than a substitute for professional judgment and instructional expertise. The results highlight the need for structured, discipline-specific professional development that emphasizes prompt literacy, critical evaluation of AI outputs, ethical awareness, and pedagogical alignment. Strengthening technological infrastructure, establishing sustained institutional support systems, and developing clear guidelines for responsible AI use are essential to ensure effective, equitable, and ethically grounded integration of AI in chemistry education.
authors: ["Aprille Mae A. Bunuan-Dela Cruz", "Elsa L. Cajucom"]

title_key: cognitive reserve depletion and learning autonomy recovery in generative artificial intelligence dependent educational environments|suardi
title: Cognitive Reserve Depletion and Learning Autonomy Recovery in Generative Artificial Intelligence Dependent Educational Environments
abstract: This study examines how generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) dependence relates to cognitive reserve depletion and learning autonomy among university students. Using a quasi-experimental design, the study involved 120 students from two universities in Padang, Indonesia, divided equally into intervention and control groups. Data were analyzed using linear regression and ANCOVA following a four-week learning autonomy recovery program. The statistical estimates showed a positive relationship between AI dependence and cognitive reserve depletion (B = 0.698, p < 0.001), while cognitive reserve depletion was negatively associated with learning autonomy (B = −0.482, p < 0.001). The intervention showed a positive adjusted effect (B = 0.334, p < 0.001), highlighting the importance of developing independent learning practices alongside AI use.

title_key: good questions sound measurement item writing quality psychometric functioning and competence level alignment of ai generated multiple choice assessments in chemistry education|rodemer
title: Good questions, sound measurement? Item-writing quality, psychometric functioning, and competence-level alignment of AI-generated multiple-choice assessments in chemistry education
abstract: Generative AI is increasingly used in education, yet evidence on the quality and validity of AI-generated assessments in science remains limited. This study examines whether large language models can support the development of high-quality multiple-choice tests in secondary-school chemistry. Using GPT-4, we generated an electrochemistry test from the curriculum and evaluated item quality against established item-writing criteria. The instrument was administered to 95 students at the end of an electrochemistry unit. Psychometric functioning was examined with Rasch modelling, and competence-level alignment was investigated through scale anchoring. The AI-generated items generally satisfied item-writing standards, with strengths in curricular alignment, alongside recurrent weaknesses in specialized language and option-length balance. Rasch analyses indicated acceptable fit and a stable item hierarchy, with measurement precision concentrated in the mid-ability range and distractor quality varying across items. Alignment between intended competence levels and empirical levels was weak, indicating that competence-level claims cannot be inferred from empirical difficulty alone. This study is, to our knowledge, the first in chemistry to generate a curriculum-anchored multiple-choice test with an LLM and evaluate it with mixed methods. Taken together, AI-generated items can serve as an initial draft requiring human oversight, with expert review and model-based checks before any consequential use.

title_key: jasalma intellekt dawirinde informatikan oqtwda oqwshlardn algoritmlik oylawn rawajlandrwdn sanl didaktikalq modelin joybarlastrw|
title: Jasalma intellekt dáwirinde informatikanı oqıtıwda oqıwshılardıń algoritmlik oylawın rawajlandırıwdıń sanlı-didaktikalıq modelin joybarlastırıw
abstract: This paper develops and substantiates a comprehensive digital-didactic model for fostering students' algorithmic and computational thinking in school computer science education amid the widespread adoption of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI). Analyzing the declining effectiveness of traditional programming instruction in the context of automated code generation, the authors show the need to shift the pedagogical focus from memorizing syntax to algorithmic decomposition, abstraction and conceptual modeling. The five-component didactic system consists of goal, content, technology-and-environment, activity-and-method and assessment-and-outcome blocks. The proposed system provides a structured pedagogical pathway for developing high-level problem-solving skills and critical computational competencies in AI-augmented learning environments.

title_key: generative ai as a catalyst for pedagogical transformation in higher education fostering 21st century competences in initial teacher training|nascimento
title: Generative AI as a catalyst for pedagogical transformation in higher education: fostering 21st-century competences in initial teacher training
abstract:
This study explores how structured engagement with generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) may support the development of transversal and 21st-century competences in initial teacher training. Specifically, it examines pre-service teachers' perceptions of how AI-based tools relate to creativity, critical thinking, problem-solving, collaboration, digital literacy, and AI literacy.
 
 
 
 A qualitative interpretative case study was conducted at a public higher education (HE) institution in Portugal, involving 78 undergraduate students enrolled in an initial teacher training program for early childhood and primary education. Participants worked collaboratively in nine groups and used customized versions of Google Gemini to design, adapt, and evaluate educational resources and lesson plans. Data consisted of nine collective reflective reports and were analyzed using thematic analysis.
 
 
 
 Across the collective reports, the groups associated AI-supported learning activities with collaboration, creativity, critical reflection, problem-solving, and digital literacy. The reports also indicated greater awareness of ethical issues, including bias, reliability, and responsible technology use. At the same time, the groups identified challenges related to uneven digital competence, institutional readiness, and the pedagogically appropriate integration of AI tools.
 
 
 
 The study draws on collective self-reported reflections from a single institutional context, which limits the potential transferability of findings. Future research should incorporate longitudinal and cross-institutional designs, together with additional data sources, to examine the development of AI literacy and professional competence over time.
 
 
 
 The findings highlight the need to embed AI literacy within teacher education curricula through structured opportunities for critical, ethical, and creative engagement with AI technologies. Teacher education programs should provide appropriate pedagogical scaffolding to support equitable participation and responsible AI use.
 
 
 
 This study contributes to rethinking HE pathways by examining how five transversal competences intersect with four dimensions of AI literacy in a structured GenAI-supported teacher training experience. By connecting creativity, ethics, and digital innovation, it provides an analytical lens for integrating AI into teacher education in alignment with contemporary educational challenges and Sustainable Development Goals, particularly SDG 4 (Quality Education) and SDG 10 (Reduced Inequalities).
venue: Education Innovations: Systems and Future Learning

title_key: perceived and demonstrated generative ai literacy in engineering problem solving the role of verification behavior|liu
title: Perceived and demonstrated generative AI literacy in engineering problem solving: the role of verification behavior
abstract:
Generative artificial intelligence is increasingly used in engineering education, but self-reported literacy may not establish whether students can evaluate its outputs. The distinction between perceived competence and performance on engineering-specific AI scenarios remains insufficiently examined. This study investigated their correspondence and whether reported verification frequency statistically accounted for the association between demonstrated literacy and engineering task performance.
 
 
 
 A cross-sectional online survey and assessment involved 1,206 mechanical engineering students at three Chinese universities. Measures comprised a 20-item perceived literacy questionnaire, a 12-item scenario test, an eight-item verification frequency scale, and two engineering tasks. Mediation and moderated mediation models controlled gender, year of study, AI use, AI course experience, and university fixed effects.
 
 
 
 
 Perceived and demonstrated literacy were modestly correlated,
 r
 = 0.265, 95% confidence interval [0.212, 0.317]. Demonstrated literacy was associated with verification frequency,
 b
 = 0.065, and the adjusted indirect association with engineering performance was 0.124, 95% bootstrap confidence interval [0.096, 0.154]. A small negative interaction suggested a weaker verification-performance association at higher perceived literacy, but its practical importance remains uncertain. A reverse-order model also produced a nonzero indirect association.
 
 
 
 
 The findings support assessing self-perception and scenario performance separately and investigating the quality of verification. Because the assessment was unproctored, the scores do not establish unaided competence; the cross-sectional associations do not establish a causal verification mechanism.

title_key: characterization of heterogeneous bioinformatics training needs in the ai era|geest
title: Characterization of heterogeneous bioinformatics training needs in the AI era
abstract: Bioinformatics training providers serve heterogeneous audiences, a challenge sharpened by fast-evolving technologies such as generative artificial intelligence (AI). Analyzing training-needs surveys in aggregate can mask this heterogeneity. We present a network-based clustering protocol that groups respondents by the similarity of their Likert-type topic ratings: respondents form a Spearman correlation network, and community detection groups them into learner profiles with shared training needs, independent of demographics. We demonstrate the protocol on the 2026 SIB Swiss Institute of Bioinformatics (SIB) training needs survey (n=260), covering topics, barriers, and formats. We identified four interpretable learner profiles: AI and data, infectious disease genomics, functional genomics, and biochemistry, imaging & AI. Each had distinct topic priorities, barriers, and format preferences that an aggregate analysis hides. For example, LLM-based knowledge extraction ranked 2nd overall but only 16th in the infectious disease genomics profile, whereas phylogenetics ranked 17th overall but first there. Across profiles, AI/LLM skills and reproducible data practices were in high demand, whereas AI-assisted learning was, unexpectedly, the least preferred format. Because the protocol requires only a shared Likert scale, it is reusable for other training-needs assessments; the implementation is openly available. Profile-based curricula can target each group’s topics, formats, and barriers. Biographical note the authors are members of the SIB Training group that provides training to ensure that life scientists make the best of the latest advances in computational biology. Key points We present a validated, openly available network-clustering method for identifying learner profiles from training-needs survey data. Applied to the 2026 SIB training needs survey, the method identified four thematically distinct, reproducible learner profiles, capturing training-need heterogeneity that demographics miss. AI/LLM skills are the top training gap across all profiles, alongside strong demand for FAIR/reproducible data practices — yet respondents prefer human-led formats over AI-assisted learning. Curricula should be tailored to learner profiles rather than demographics or aggregate topic rankings, which each hide profile-specific needs.

title_key: the impact of ai assistance on the academic writing self efficacy of undergraduates with different writing abilities|gong
title: The Impact of AI Assistance on the Academic Writing Self-Efficacy of Undergraduates with Different Writing Abilities
abstract: Against digital education background, generative AI has become common writing assistance for undergraduates. Existing studies mainly focus on second-language writing and ignore stratified comparisons across learners, while the dual effects of AI on academic writing self-efficacy remain understudied. Based on self-efficacy theory, this paper distributes questionnaires and divides respondents into three proficiency groups by CET-4 scores. Descriptive statistics, group difference tests and correlation analysis are adopted for empirical analysis. The results reveal prevalent AI over-dependence despite its polishing functions. Participants’ writing self-efficacy stays at medium-upper level yet hampered by writing anxiety. AI delivers short-term confidence promotion but impairs independent writing competence in the long run, with stronger influences on low-proficiency students. This stratified dual-path framework offers empirical references for standardized AI application in university writing teaching.
venue: Journal of Education and Educational Research

title_key: leveraging agentic coding for interactive education in electrical engineering|sawicki
title: Leveraging Agentic Coding for Interactive Education in Electrical Engineering
abstract: Large language models enable the automated synthesis of interactive educational software beyond conversational tutoring. This paper presents an authoring methodology using agentic coding (an autonomous, tool-augmented workflow based on the Reason-and-Act (ReAct) paradigm) to generate standalone, browser-based simulation modules for electrical engineering curricula. It was applied across three undergraduate courses, using three distinct agentic development environments: a transient commutation simulator for second-order RLC circuits (circuit theory), an eddy-current induction laboratory (electromagnetism), and an interactive benchmark of iterative linear solvers (numerical methods). We formalize a pipeline built on (1) strict decoupling of pedagogical specification from implementation, (2) formal mathematical notation constraints, (3) singlepass holistic generation to prevent context window degradation, (4) human-in-the-loop validation gates, and (5) prompt-level regeneration rather than conversational code patching. Recurring failure modes: notation drift, context saturation, feature creep, and physically invalid simulations ("vibe physics"); are analyzed together with their mitigations, and an independent analytical audit of two generated modules is reported. Modules are synthesized in 5–10 minutes over 3–5 specification iterations, shifting instructor effort from manual programming to requirements engineering and domain verification.

title_key: generative artificial intelligence in secondary education educational value motivation and ethical perceptions of students|bartovcak
title: Generative Artificial Intelligence in Secondary Education: Educational Value, Motivation, and Ethical Perceptions of Students
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) is becoming increasingly integrated into educational processes, particularly among secondary school students, where it is used to support learning, complete academic assignments, and develop a variety of skills. The aim of this study is to analyse how secondary school students perceive the educational value of generative artificial intelligence and to examine the role of motivation, sense of security, and ethical concerns in shaping that perception. The study was conducted on a sample of 281 secondary school students (Economics and Administrative Officer programmes) using a structured online questionnaire. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics, correlation analysis, exploratory factor analysis, and regression models. The results indicate that students most strongly recognise the contribution of generative artificial intelligence to the development of creativity and the adaptation of learning to individual needs, while its contribution to the development of critical thinking and teamwork was rated more moderately. Hypothesis testing revealed a statistically significant association between motivation for learning, sense of security, and ethical concerns with the perception of the educational value of GAI, albeit in unexpected directions. Students who reported a weaker motivational effect of GAI and a lower sense of security when using it tended to perceive GAI as a more educationally valuable tool. However, the mechanisms underlying these relationships require further investigation. At the same time, ethical concerns proved to be a weak but significant positive predictor of perceived educational value, suggesting an ambivalent relationship between students and this technology. The findings underscore the importance of pedagogically guided and ethically grounded integration of generative artificial intelligence into secondary education.

title_key: paradigm reconstruction and practical pathways of ai enabled physical chemistry teaching|ning
title: Paradigm Reconstruction and Practical Pathways of AI-Enabled Physical Chemistry Teaching
abstract: Physical chemistry is a core course for chemistry‑related majors. Its teaching faces problems such as abstract concepts, complicated mathematical deductions, and disconnection between theory and practice, making it difficult to improve teaching quality. Generative artificial intelligence offers new solutions to these teaching difficulties. This paper proposes strategies to reduce cognitive barriers, reshape classroom models, and optimize evaluations. Besides, it also puts forward risk prevention measures for “cognitive outsourcing” and “AI hallucinations”. This research holds that the essence of AI-enabled physical chemistry teaching lies in realizing the paradigm shift from unified content supply to the construction of an educational ecosystem through technology, and its effectiveness depends on consistently prioritizing the cultivation of students’ higher‑order thinking abilities.

title_key: use and perceptions of artificial intelligence tools among clinical medical students in selected nigerian universities a multi institutional survey|nwankwo
title: Use and Perceptions of Artificial Intelligence Tools among Clinical Medical Students in Selected Nigerian Universities: A Multi-Institutional Survey.
abstract:
BACKGROUND
AI tools are increasingly used in medical education for learning, clinical reasoning, and examination preparation, but there is limited data from Nigeria.


AIM
To examine AI use and attitudes among Nigerian medical students to inform policy.


METHODS
A cross-sectional online survey was conducted among medical students in three Nigerian medical schools from December 2025 to February 2026. The questionnaire covered demographics, awareness, and use of AI tools, perceived benefits and risks, attitudes toward integration, and barriers to adoption. Items were rated on a 5-point Likert scale. Descriptive statistics and Chi-square tests were used to analyze data.


RESULTS
A total of 328 responses were received. Respondents demonstrated generally positive attitudes toward AI use, although concerns regarding accuracy, academic integrity, and regulation were identified. 53.8% were males, (70.8%) aged 20-24, (55.7%) fourth-year students, and (43.1%) from the University of Nigeria. Smartphones (94.5%) and ChatGPT (98.2%) were mostly used. AI was useful for understanding difficult concepts (92.9%), self-directed learning (83.1%), and saving study time (81.2%). Concerns included misinformation (75.1%), academic dishonesty (60.7%), and reduced critical thinking (47.4%). Barriers included subscriptions (71.4%), poor connectivity (69.2%), and high data costs (66.8%). There was no statistically significant association between AI use and level of study ( P = 0.78), age group ( P = 0.12), and gender ( P = 0.82).


CONCLUSION
AI tools are widely adopted by medical students in Nigeria without clear guidelines for use, despite concerns regarding accuracy, dependence, and academic integrity. Curricula integration, along with clear guidelines and training, is recommended for responsible use.

title_key: motivations and gratifications in generative ai adoption a survey based uses and gratifications study of media and communication students at the university of gujrat pakistan|sarwar
title: Motivations and Gratifications in Generative AI Adoption: A Survey-Based Uses and Gratifications Study of Media and Communication Students at the University of Gujrat, Pakistan
abstract: In Pakistan, AI tools, including ChatGPT which are used as generative AI tools, have changed academic practice in higher education, but the motivations of students are under-researched. This quantitative survey uses the Uses and Gratifications Theory (UGT) to investigate generative AI usage by media and communication students in the University of Gujrat (UOG) in meeting academic needs, such as cognitive (content creation, research), tension-release (meeting deadlines), and personal integrative (learn media production) gratifications. A survey was conducted on 250 students of UOG who have been on the media-related programs using a structured questionnaire. The SPSS descriptive statistics demonstrated moderate awareness of AI (40.8%), dominating self-taught adoption (40.0%), and the frequency of usage being high (59.2% per week/day), with ChatGPT (30.0%), and virtual assistants (21.6%), prevailing in writing, brainstorming, and plagiarism. Integration was not even across the board as advanced tools (e.g., machine learning platforms, 4.0%) were barely utilized. Results are positive in favor of UGT, which demonstrates active selection of AI in terms of utilitarian and hedonic gratifications, but indicates shortcomings in formal training and ethical consciousness. Implications consist in the introduction of AI literacy in media curricula in order to maximize gratifications, and reduce the risks of dependency. This paper builds upon UGT to generative AI within Pakistani media education providing information on the fair implementation in resourceconstrained contexts.

title_key: beyond the score uptick foundational proficiency cognitive agency and ai era learning in indonesias pisa 2025|judijanto
title: Beyond the Score Uptick: Foundational Proficiency, Cognitive Agency, and AI-Era Learning in Indonesia’s PISA 2025
abstract: Indonesia’s PISA 2025 results present a paradox. Reading and science scores increased nominally from 2022, educational participation among 15-year-olds expanded substantially, and several indicators of curiosity, perseverance, teacher support, and self-regulation appear favourable. Yet the OECD concludes that average performance in mathematics, reading, and science did not change significantly from 2022, while proficiency remains critically low. Only 17% of Indonesian students reached at least Level 2 in mathematics, 27% in reading, and 37% in science. This qualitative literature review synthesises PISA 2025 evidence with recent peer-reviewed literature published predominantly between 2020 and 2026 to reinterpret Indonesia’s performance through an access–learning–cognition–digital ecology framework. The review identifies five interacting challenges: an access–quality paradox; a foundational-proficiency deficit, particularly in mathematics; a gap between teacher support and cognitive activation; socioeconomic and school-level constraints; and an emerging digital-learning paradox in which extensive device and generative-AI use can either augment or substitute for productive cognitive effort. The analysis argues that neither international ranking nor nominal score changes provide an adequate diagnosis. Indonesia’s next educational challenge is to convert expanded schooling, supportive learning environments, and digital access into deeper reading, mathematical modelling, scientific reasoning, self-regulated learning, and epistemically responsible AI use. Policy implications emphasise diagnostic remediation, cognitively demanding instruction, disciplined technology integration, AI literacy, family engagement, and proficiency-based monitoring

title_key: code commits and complexity in the genai era a longitudinal study of team based capstone projects|shakil
title: Code, Commits, and Complexity in the GenAI Era: A Longitudinal Study of Team-Based Capstone Projects
abstract: Generative AI tools are now widely available to students, but little is known about how team-based project codebases have changed since they appeared. This matters when project courses use repository activity as evidence of progress and learning. Existing studies have largely examined self-reports, controlled tasks, or short individual assignments, leaving open questions around how student codebases evolve in authentic project settings. We present a ten-semester analysis of N=260 capstone team repositories from 2021 to 2025, spanning pre- and post-AI cohorts. We examine three dimensions: code size (lines of code), code characteristics (comment density, error-handling density, and cyclomatic complexity), and development behaviour (commit volume, edit size, and commit frequency). We find that end-of-semester codebases roughly triple, from about 3.4 KLOC in 2021--2023 to about 10 KLOC in 2024--2025. Code characteristics show a clear decoupling: cyclomatic complexity and error-handling density increase, while comment density does not. Later cohorts commit far more often and in greater volume, but individual commit sizes are largely unchanged, suggesting a shift in development rhythm rather than edit granularity. Most changes appear from 2024 onwards and are not uniformly monotonic. We did not directly observe AI use, so we report these as changes that coincide with increased GenAI availability rather than as effects of AI use. Our findings highlight the need to reconsider how student-produced artefacts are used and assessed in project courses.

title_key: reimagining the role of a medical teacher in the era of artificial intelligence|mughal
title: Reimagining the Role of a Medical Teacher in the Era of Artificial Intelligence
abstract:
For the past three decades, the "Twelve Roles of the Medical Teacher" has been the key framework to determine the competencies required to be effective in the practice of medical teaching. It identifies twelve specific roles in six categories i.e. Information Provider, Role Model, Facilitator, Assessor, Planner, Resource Developer. 1 In Pakistan, it remains the key driver of almost all faculty development programs, including the short six-month Certificate in Health Professions Education (CHPE) and more comprehensive two-year Master in Health Professions Education (MHPE) programs. However, currently, there is a shift in Health Professions Education due to the rise of Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) and the explosion of big data which raises the question: are these traditional roles still sufficient? 
Contemporary literature clearly suggests that they are not. 2,3 The pace at which medical knowledge expands today far exceeds the capacity of traditional teaching tools, such as textbooks. Thus, the role of the health professions educator is moving away from being a deliverer of information and toward becoming a developer of digital platforms curated according to learners’ needs.

title_key: the influence of ai facilitated personalised education on improving student academic performance|han
title: The Influence of AI-Facilitated Personalised Education on Improving Student Academic Performance
abstract: AI has revolutionised the landscape of personalised learning, empowering learning systems to analyse learner data, tailor learning paths, provide feedback, suggest learning materials, and pinpoint learning challenges. This paper aims at answering the main question: What is the association between AI-facilitated personalisation and students' academic achievement, and what are the implementation conditions that influence this association? This paper introduces a systematic, evidence-based review that integrates findings from peer-reviewed systematic reviews, scoping reviews, meta-analyses, and selected empirical research in the fields of artificial intelligence in education, adaptive learning, intelligent tutoring, personalised recommendations, and digitally-delivered feedback. The findings suggest that personalised adaptive learning is linked with higher academic achievement in a significant number of the studies examined. A 2024 scoping review of 69 studies found that 41 studies (59%) showed improvements in student academic achievement and 25 studies (36%) showed improvements in students' engagement. A 125 study synthesis from the systematic review in the education sectors in 2025 found that adaptive learning, machine learning, natural language processing, recommendation systems, intelligent tutoring, and generative AI are key technical methods to personalisation. There were 29 empirical studies chosen for a 2025 meta-analysis of AI and academic outcomes, and 99 effect sizes from 32 RCTs used in a separate meta-analysis for the effects of AI for personalised STEM education. This suggests that, alongside automation, academic benefits for AI depend on adaptive feedback in instruction, diagnostic assessment, appropriate sequencing in instruction, control by the learner, involvement of the teacher, and pedagogical alignment. The paper presents a conceptual model that connects the concepts of AI-assisted Learner Profiling, Adaptive Content, Feedback, Engagement, Self-regulation, and Academic Achievement. The analysis also highlights data privacy, unequal access, algorithmic limitations, educator readiness, and over-reliance on automated outputs as conditions that need to be protected within institutional contexts. The results encourage a human-centred approach in which AI is used as an adaptive teaching layer, not to replace teachers.The topics include, but are not limited to, the following: artificial intelligence, personalised education, adaptive learning, academic performance, intelligent tutoring systems, learning analytics, student engagement, educational technology.

title_key: prompt engineering as an extension of information literacy implications for library instruction programmes|adewojo
title: Prompt engineering as an extension of information literacy: Implications for library instruction programmes
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is now a routine information tool for students and knowledge workers, and the quality of what they obtain depends in part on how they instruct it. This article argues that prompt engineering is best understood as an extension of information literacy, and that library and information professionals should lead its teaching in partnership with other units. Using conceptual analysis, it maps prompt competencies onto the six frames of the ACRL Framework for Information Literacy for Higher Education and, unlike earlier mappings, identifies where the analogy fails. The mapping holds for question formulation, evaluation and refinement. It fails where a language model generates text and does not retrieve documents, where its sources cannot be inspected, and where it fabricates citations. Those failures are the strongest argument for librarian involvement, because they call for verification skills that prompt technique alone does not supply. The article proposes an instructional design in four strands, including one for workplace settings, sets out how each can be assessed, and considers equity of access to instruction. It also addresses two objections: that prompt engineering is a transient skill, and that librarians are not yet prepared to teach it. The argument is conceptual and requires empirical evaluation.

title_key: human or machine efl students trust calibration in ai generated english content a study at the faculty of languages surman|altarabulsi
title: Human or Machine? EFL Students’ Trust Calibration in AI-Generated English Content:A Study at the Faculty of Languages, Surman
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used by university EFL students for language learning and academic tasks, yet fluent output may be inaccurate. This study examined self-reported trust and verification practices and students’ judgments of selected AI-generated English content among undergraduates at the Faculty of Languages, Surman, University of Sabratha. A quantitative descriptive-correlational design was applied to questionnaire responses from 38 students. The instrument included background questions, ten five-point Likert items, five evaluation tasks with confidence and verification-intention responses, and an optional open-ended item. Descriptive statistics, Cronbach’s alpha, and Spearman’s rank correlations were used. Mean self-reported trust was 3.36/5 and verification was 3.74/5. Students correctly judged 62.1% of task responses under the primary answer key. Use frequency was not significantly associated with trust (ρ = .279, p = .090), whereas verification was associated with accuracy (ρ = .473, p = .003), as was confidence (ρ = .648, p < .001). Findings are preliminary given the small sample, modest trust-scale internal consistency, and ambiguity in one evaluation item. In exploratory HC3 regression, confidence remained associated with accuracy (β = .51, p = .005), while reported verification did not uniquely reach p < .05 after confidence was included (p = .063). After Holm correction across 28 exploratory pairs, only confidence–accuracy and awareness–adaptive-trust correlations remained significant. The study highlights the value of teaching verification and interpreting trust relative to output reliability.

title_key: ai bias in special education|laconner
title: AI Bias in Special Education
abstract: Despite the rapid deployment of artificial intelligence (AI) to support K–12 educators in improving their practice, serious concerns remain unanswered about large-language model (LLM) output. This is especially true in special education, where educators report little training in disability theory, leading them to consult with AI systems without the background knowledge needed for objective analysis of the chatbot responses. To address this issue, we conducted a qualitative content analysis of the transcripts of responses from five major LLMs (Anthropic Claude, Google Gemini, OpenAI ChatGPT, Perplexity Sonar, and xAI Grok) to common questions from early-career educators. We found an overreliance in the chatbot output on the Medical Model of disability, as well as almost no engagement with the Human Rights Model. We also found a wide variability between the different LLMs, as well as internal variability within each LLM based on the wording of the prompt. We conclude by calling for explicit instruction on disability theory in teacher preservice programs to support critical engagement by teachers with AI tools, as well as improved LLM models that consider multiple models of disability. This article makes a practical contribution to special education practice by identifying imbalanced AI output and suggesting ways to minimize the negative impacts that may result from using these tools.

title_key: from static to dynamic parameter manipulation as adaptive ddl scaffolding in creative writing with generative ai|yu
title: From Static to Dynamic: Parameter Manipulation as Adaptive DDL Scaffolding in Creative Writing with Generative AI
abstract: Abstract Generative AI tools now pervade university classrooms, yet the field lacks empirical understanding of how technical AI configurations translate into adaptive Data-driven Learning (DDL) scaffolding. This gap is crucial in creative writing, where excessive structure can suppress authorship and insufficient support can stall exploration. This study investigates how large language model (LLM) parameter configuration functions as a pedagogical design lever for DDL scaffolding in poetry writing classrooms. Across a three-phase mixed-methods study with 30 university creative writing learners (a 2 × 2 factorial experiment, an offline classroom workshop, and an online classroom workshop), two parameter settings, temperature and top-p, reliably reshaped the distribution of three pre-coded interaction types: Constraint Repair (Type A), Exemplar Giving (Type B), and Surprise Harvest (Type C). Moving from a structured to an exploratory setting, Type C rose roughly seven-fold in Phase 1, with the same direction of effect in the two subsequent classroom phases. Triangulating chat logs, reflection templates, and panel transcripts, Type B was voted most helpful but linked to diminished authorship, while Type C was associated with the highest authorship and satisfaction. We position parameter literacy as a necessary instructor competence for adaptive AI scaffolding.

title_key: an ai generative ai assisted blended learning intervention for nursing undergraduates a quasi experimental study of attitudes toward ai ai literacy and autonomous learning competency|lan
title: An AI/generative AI-assisted blended learning intervention for nursing undergraduates: a quasi-experimental study of attitudes toward AI, AI literacy, and autonomous learning competency
abstract:
Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly shaping healthcare, highlighting the need for nursing graduates to develop relevant competencies. However, structured AI education remains limited in nursing programs, and evidence on the effects of AI-focused teaching interventions remains scarce.
 
 
 
 A quasi-experimental pretest–posttest study was conducted among 142 undergraduate nursing students at a university in southwestern Zhejiang, China. Seventy-two students participated in a 10-week AI/generative AI (GenAI)-assisted blended learning course comprising 12 h of self-paced online learning and 6 h of hands-on workshops, while 70 students received standard instruction. Attitudes toward AI, AI literacy, and autonomous learning competency were assessed before and immediately after the intervention using validated instruments. Post-test outcomes were compared using analysis of covariance (ANCOVA), adjusting for the corresponding baseline score, previous AI training experience, frequency of AI use, and digital literacy.
 
 
 
 
 In the intervention group, AI literacy increased significantly from 55.67 ± 9.84 to 65.01 ± 8.81 (
 P
  < 0.001), as did attitudes toward AI, which increased from 48.07 ± 6.77 to 51.72 ± 9.90 (
 P
  = 0.049). Neither outcome changed significantly in the control group. After adjustment for covariates, the intervention group had significantly higher post-test scores for AI literacy (adjusted mean difference = 11.01, 95% CI 8.55–13.47;
 P
  < 0.001) and attitudes toward AI (adjusted mean difference = 4.60, 95% CI 1.98–7.21;
 P
  < 0.001). Autonomous learning competency changed little in the intervention group (
 P
  = 0.578) but declined significantly in the control group (
 P
  < 0.001). The adjusted post-test difference also favored the intervention group (adjusted mean difference = 10.94, 95% CI 7.44–14.43;
 P
  < 0.001).
 
 
 
 
 AI/GenAI-assisted blended teaching was associated with higher AI literacy and more favorable attitudes toward AI, while autonomous learning competency remained relatively stable in the intervention group but declined in the control group. Structured AI education integrating conceptual learning, practical application, and responsible AI use may be a valuable addition to undergraduate nursing education.

title_key: a pedagogically guided llm framework for scaffolding human ai cocreation and preserving learners agency and creativity|haq
title: A pedagogically guided LLM framework for scaffolding human-AI cocreation and preserving learners'agency and creativity
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can generate alternatives, elaborate ideas and supply rationales, overlapping with cognitive work learners are expected to perform. However, human-AI cocreation still lacks a mechanism for determining how AI can scaffold learners'creative decision-making. This study develops a cognitive-pedagogical framework for deriving the behaviour of a pedagogically constrained LLM from an educator-approved specification of each activity in a cocreative process in project-based learning. The creative-process phase supplies the activity's purpose, typical processes and pedagogical conditions; the active section of a creative technique specifies how the group works on its ideas. For each task, an educator approves four fields: a cognitive and metacognitive objective, a pedagogical objective, the task and group artefact as context, and the learner-owned product. The objective identifies the creative operations and decisions about progress, focus, criteria and next steps that remain with the group. Four translation rules derive permitted support, timing, feedback scope and prohibitions. The framework is illustrated with Viacocrea's six phases and two activities: Plan Brainstorming and a constructed Build activity using PPCo (Pluses, Potentials, Concerns, Overcoming concerns). In the proposed workflow, a controller applies the approved specification to student requests and feedback offers. Prompt engineering and approved pedagogical guidance retrieved through retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) inform a draft, which is checked for form, pedagogical function and safety before delivery. The worked examples illustrate how support can differ between activities while its constraints remain traceable to educator decisions. The framework offers educators and researchers a reusable way to derive LLM support from creative activities while preserving learners'agency and creativity.

title_key: towards comparative comprehension in cs1 an exploratory study using structured code comparisons|eagal
title: Towards Comparative Comprehension in CS1: An Exploratory Study using Structured Code Comparisons
abstract: Software developers routinely evaluate code alternatives during code review, refactoring, debugging, maintenance, and when adapting examples from online resources or AI-generated suggestions. This skill, known as comparative comprehension, is fundamental yet difficult: developers must compare different implementations and reason about correctness and task alignment. Its importance is increasing as Generative AI tools produce plausible alternative solutions requiring critical evaluation. Despite its growing role in professional software development, CS1 instruction continues to emphasize producing working code over evaluating competing solutions. As a result, an increasingly important skill in programming practice may remain underdeveloped in CS1 instruction. We explore how structured code comparison activities support comparative comprehension in CS1 students transitioning from Snap! to Python. Drawing on work in mathematics education, we designed instructional activities that ask students to analyze alternative implementations, explain differences in program behavior, and justify solution choices. We evaluated these activities through a pilot study using pre- and post-tests and students’ responses to comparison prompts. While we did not observe statistically significant improvements across quantitative measures, our findings reveal patterns in how novice programmers engage with code comparisons. Students frequently relied on surface-level syntactic differences and struggled to reason about program behavior, particularly when comparisons contained multiple differences. These structured code comparisons also exposed misconceptions and false carryover that traditional code-writing tasks often failed to reveal. Our findings highlight both the challenges and opportunities of supporting comparative comprehension through structured comparison activities, particularly in terms of timing, scaffolding, and comparison design.
